candidates.how_in_gridiron: New exported function fitJamesStein(observations) in shrinkage-fit.js beside fitK(), sharing the same byGroup/grandMean bookkeeping already built; wire it as an alternate kOverride source for fit-shrinkage-weekly.mjs's existing comparison harness rather than building a new one.
candidates.expected_value: Brown (2008) found plain James-Stein (TSE ratio .525) slightly beat method-of-moments EB (.593) on real batting data — a modest but free-to-test improvement given the harness already exists; worth confirming whether the same ordering holds on Gridiron's own panel before assuming the current estimator is optimal.
candidates.exit_test: fit-shrinkage-weekly.mjs's existing CRPS/MAE-vs-hardcoded comparison, extended to a three-way comparison (hardcoded vs current MM-fit vs JS-fit); adopt JS only if it beats the current fit on held-out weeks, otherwise record the null and keep the current estimator.

candidates.candidate: Add a nonparametric empirical-Bayes (Robbins'-method / Efron g-modeling style) shrinkage option for any (metric, position) group whose population is visibly non-normal or bimodal (e.g. starter-vs-backup usage mixtures), to be tried wherever shrinkage-fit.js's ANOVA-based k currently assumes a single normal population.
candidates.mechanism: Instead of assuming one normal prior across a group (what the ANOVA method-of-moments k implicitly does), estimate the population density of the group means nonparametrically (e.g. a discrete grid deconvolution of observed means given their sampling variances) and shrink each unit toward its own posterior mean under that estimated, possibly multimodal, prior.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: A new estimator alongside fitK() in shrinkage-fit.js, applied first to a metric shrinkage-fit.js already flags as likely mixed-population (e.g. qb_attempt_share, which mixes clear starters and committee/backup QBs) before generalizing.
candidates.expected_value: Brown (2008) found NPEB was the single best-performing method tested (TSE ratio .508, beating James-Stein's .525) specifically because the real population was a visible mixture (pitchers vs. position players) — Gridiron's own starter/backup and rookie/veteran populations are plausibly similar mixtures the current single-normal ANOVA assumption cannot represent.
candidates.exit_test: Same fit-shrinkage-weekly.mjs CRPS/MAE harness, run on a metric first diagnosed as non-normal (histogram/QQ-plot check on the group means already available from fitK's intermediate output); adopt only where it beats the current ANOVA-based k on held-out weeks for that specific metric, not codebase-wide by default.

do_not_do: Don't fit, backtest, or query against the live fantasy-football-dashboard database or touch any of its processes — read-only tonight, a server is capturing Week 1 NFL games live.

Don't wire any new or refit team-strength/roster-strength shrinkage into a live betting or fantasy decision before it clears teamStrengthWalkForward's existing paired-bootstrap gate (>=2 of 3 seasons significant) — the project already has this gate; use it rather than bypassing it because the method is textbook statistics.

Don't assume the ranking of shrinkage methods (method-of-moments EB vs James-Stein vs nonparametric EB vs MLE-Bayes) transfers unmeasured from baseball to NFL team margins or fantasy usage rates — Brown (2008) shows the best method flips depending on whether the underlying population is a visible mixture or roughly homogeneous; each Gridiron surface needs its own held-out test.

Don't apply heavy population-level shrinkage uniformly to known outlier/elite units (a true top-5 QB, a historically dominant defense, a locked-in workhorse RB) without a flag or exemption path — Efron's own Clemente example is the standing caution that low aggregate error can conceal a materially worse point estimate for exactly the cases a user most cares about getting right.

Don't fit any new shrinkage constant globally across 'every season on record' the way nfl-preseason-blend.js's own module header documents having already fixed (Codex correction C10, a future-leaking global default) — copy its asOfSeason cutoff-safe calibration pattern for any new work instead of regressing to a global.

Don't use a non-parametric bootstrap variance estimator for NFL team-pair uncertainty — Ragain et al.'s own NFL result shows it fails exactly when many team-pairs share only one game ever played, which describes Gridiron's own division-heavy schedule; use a parametric (Fisher-information or parametric-bootstrap) variance estimate for any NFL cross-sectional shrinkage work.

result.label: Audit/CLV architecture consolidation
result.summary: Grepped the repo instead of assuming: the "5-7 duplicate audit engines" finding is caused by 37 separate services/*.js files each independently rolling their own sha256 content-addressing (codeHash/dataSignature/digest/configurationHash variants) with no shared identity primitive — nfl-blind-audit.js, audit-registry.js, and nfl-engine-registry.js each invented their own. The CLV finding is confirmed concretely: nfl-clv.js, nfl-execution-clv.js, nfl-execution-clv-downsize.js, and nfl-prop-clv.js compute CLV in different units (points vs implied-probability-percent) with different sign conventions (nfl-clv.js inverts totals sign explicitly; nfl-execution-clv.js assumes the contract key already pre-inverted it) writing to different tables. The single most important discovery: Gridiron ALREADY has a correctly-built, tested model registry (server/modeling/registry.js + sqlite-store.js + migration 005_model_registry_integrity.js, with dataset/feature version tables, promotion gates, and a passing test/model-registry-persistence.test.js) — but it is used only for ML-head training experiments and is never imported by the audit or CLV layer, which grew a parallel, worse, disagreeing copy instead. That reframes most of the fix as wiring existing infrastructure rather than inventing new architecture. Read 4 primary sources in full: Sculley et al.'s "Hidden Technical Debt in ML Systems" (names pipeline jungles/glue code/undeclared consumers, prescribes scrapping and redesigning rather than patching), Breck et al.'s "The ML Test Score" (28-test rubric across data/model/infra/monitoring, calibrated against 36 real Google production teams — even they implement most tests at under 80% adoption), the MLflow Model Registry paper (4-stage promotion state machine with role-gated transitions, self-reported millions of models managed), and Uber's Michelangelo blog (~10,000-feature shared store eliminated duplicate per-team feature builds via one training/serving DSL — the direct feature-layer analogue of Gridiron's own narrow, underused assertTimestampedObservation() leakage check in contracts.js). Candidates split 4 fix (consolidate the 4 CLV modules into one; wire nfl-blind-audit.js/audit-registry.js onto the existing-but-idle ModelRegistry schema; collapse the 3+ independent content-addressing functions into one shared identity module; extend the existing point-in-time leakage assertion from the fantasy pipeline to the NFL betting feature tables) and 4 new (an ML-Test-Score-style scored technical-debt rubric run in CI; a canary/shadow-serve gate before promotion, which does not exist anywhere today; a real point-in-time feature store for the unused 12.4M-row Polymarket tape and 251,591-row play-by-play; and a paired-significance "one evaluation harness" that can compare any two registered candidates, which ModelRegistry.compare() does not do today — it just returns raw records).

sources.title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
sources.authors: D. Sculley, Gary Holt, Eugene Davydov, Todd Phillips, Dietmar Ebner, Vinay Chaudhary, Michael Young, Jean-Francois Crespo, Dan Dennison
sources.sample: Position/taxonomy paper drawing on Google-internal production ML systems; no single quantitative benchmark
sources.key_result: Names pipeline jungles (accumulating ad hoc scrape/join/sample chains), glue code (can be 95%+ of a mature ML codebase), undeclared consumers, and configuration debt as concrete technical-debt categories; prescribes 'thinking holistically about data collection and feature extraction' and, when a pipeline jungle is bad enough, scrapping and redesigning from scratch rather than patching incrementally.

sources.title: The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction
sources.authors: Eric Breck, Shanqing Cai, Eric Nielsen, Michael Salib, D. Sculley
sources.sample: Structured interviews with maintainers of 36 real production ML systems at Google
sources.key_result: 28-test rubric across Data(7)/Model(7)/Infra(7)/Monitoring(7); score = 0.5pt manual+documented, 1pt automated+repeated per test, final score = MINIMUM of the 4 category sums (deliberately, so no strong category masks a weak one); measured result: none of the 28 tests was implemented by more than 80% of the 36 surveyed teams, and most tests scored nonzero for at least half the teams — even Google's own teams under-implement ML-specific production tests.

sources.title: Developments in MLflow: A System to Accelerate the Machine Learning Lifecycle
sources.authors: Andrew Chen, Andy Chow, Aaron Davidson, et al. (Databricks)
sources.sample: Descriptive system paper covering MLflow adopter feedback since 2018 launch; self-reported adoption, not a controlled experiment
sources.key_result: Model Registry adds a 4-stage promotion state machine (Development/Staging/Production/Archived) with request/approve transitions gated by data-scientist vs deployment-engineer roles; self-reported that adopters are 'managing millions of models' through it across energy, biotech, and retail — structurally the same pattern as Gridiron's own already-built ModelRegistry.promote()/REQUIRED_GATES, just not applied outside ML-head training.

sources.title: Meet Michelangelo: Uber's Machine Learning Platform
sources.sample: Primary industry source describing Uber's internal ML platform; not peer-reviewed, but the canonical origin of the 'feature store' architecture pattern
sources.key_result: ~10,000 features in one shared, versioned catalog computed once and reused by dozens of modeling teams; explicitly states duplicate per-team feature rebuilding was the problem the store solved; one DSL guarantees the same feature expression runs at training and serving time, and batch features flow through one HDFS-to-Cassandra pipeline shared by both paths to eliminate training/serving skew.

candidates.candidate: Delete the 4 independent CLV calculators (nfl-clv.js, nfl-execution-clv.js, nfl-execution-clv-downsize.js's own aggregation path, nfl-prop-clv.js) and replace their CLV-computation cores with one shared module exporting one signed-points function and one fair-probability function, used by all 4 call sites and writing to one clv_grades table (spread/total/moneyline/prop rows share a schema with a market column).
candidates.fixes_finding: Five independent, disagreeing CLV (closing-line-value) implementations exist over four different tables with different math and sign conventions
candidates.mechanism: nfl-clv.js explicitly inverts sign for totals-Under bets inside gradeClosingLineValue(); nfl-execution-clv.js's spreadClvPoints() assumes lines are already pre-inverted by the contract key and does no such inversion; nfl-prop-clv.js computes CLV as an implied-probability delta ×100 rather than points at all. A single canonical fair-probability + signed-points function, unit-tested once against both spread/total and prop cases, removes the possibility of the 4 modules ever disagreeing about the same bet again.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/clv/core.js exporting fairProbability(side,ourLine,closeLine,closeFairProb) and signedClvPoints(...); nfl-clv.js, nfl-execution-clv.js, nfl-execution-clv-downsize.js, nfl-prop-clv.js import from it instead of each defining spreadClvPoints/noVigProbability/probability-delta locally; one new clv_grades table replaces the 4 divergent storage locations, migration adds it and backfills from nfl_bet_log.
candidates.expected_value: Eliminates the specific 5-implementation disagreement finding outright; makes the -2.28 CLV / 78% adverse-move number auditable from one place instead of requiring reconciliation across 4 modules before it can be trusted.
candidates.exit_test: Re-run last week's graded bets through the new single module and the 4 old modules side by side; if the new module's clv_points/clv_pct for every bet falls within the old modules' existing disagreement range (i.e., it isn't introducing a 5th wrong answer) and the old modules are deleted (not kept as a fallback), the consolidation is done. Weekly CLV report must run on one query against clv_grades, not a UNION of 4 tables.

candidates.candidate: Wire nfl-blind-audit.js and audit-registry.js onto the already-built, already-tested ModelRegistry / SqliteModelStore + model_dataset_versions/model_feature_versions/model_backtests/model_metrics schema (migration 005_model_registry_integrity.js) instead of each maintaining its own bespoke codeHash()/dataSignature() freeze logic.
candidates.fixes_finding: 5-7 duplicate backtest/audit engines exist because the identity/versioning logic that should be one shared thing was independently reinvented per surface
candidates.mechanism: grep confirms model_dataset_versions/model_feature_versions/model_backtests are defined by migration 005 and used nowhere outside server/modeling/*.js and its own test, despite being exactly the versioned-dataset/versioned-feature-contract abstraction the audit layer needs and currently fakes with its own dataSignature() row-count snapshot. Each blind-audit run and each audit-registry preregistration should record a model_dataset_versions row (content_hash over the frozen INPUT_TABLES) and a model_backtests row (protocol='sealed_holdout' for the untouched forward 2026 ledger, 'walk_forward' for the historical replay) instead of a private hash nobody else can query.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: audit-registry.js's codeHash()+dataSignature() and nfl-blind-audit.js's freeze logic both call into server/modeling/registry.js's ModelRegistry.create()/promote() and write to model_dataset_versions (content_hash = current codeHash+dataSignature concatenation) instead of maintaining separate hash fields; nfl-audit-overview.js's compareAuditRuns() then compares registry-tracked dataset_version_id equality instead of its own result_hash convention.
candidates.expected_value: Turns 3+ non-interoperating audit/versioning systems into 1, using infrastructure that already passes test/model-registry-persistence.test.js — this is materially cheaper than inventing a new registry, and it is the literal ask ("one canonical research pipeline") for the surfaces named in the brief.
candidates.exit_test: After the change, a single query against model_backtests joined to model_dataset_versions returns every historical blind-audit run AND every audit-registry preregistration with no NULLs in dataset_version_id/feature_version_id; test/blind-audit-lookback.test.js and test/audit-registry-always-valid.test.js still pass unmodified in behavior (same leakage guarantees), and audit-registry.js's own codeHash()/dataSignature() functions are deleted, not kept alongside the registry call.

candidates.candidate: Collapse the 3+ independent content-addressing/identity functions (server/modeling/contracts.js configurationHash/stableJson, nfl-engine-registry.js's digest(), audit-registry.js's codeHash()+dataSignature(), and the ad hoc createHash('sha256') calls duplicated across 30+ other services/*.js files) into one shared identity module every one of those files imports.
candidates.fixes_finding: 5-7 duplicate backtest/audit engines — the root mechanism enabling the sprawl is that 37 separate files independently reinvent 'what code+data produced this number' with no shared primitive, so none of their hashes can ever be compared
candidates.mechanism: grep across server/services/*.js for codeHash/dataSignature/createHash('sha256') hits 37 files (nfl-bitemporal.js, nfl-contract-key.js, nfl-evidence-dataset.js, nfl-forecast-identity.js, nfl-model-growth.js, nfl-online-neural.js, nfl-postgame-truth.js, nfl-quote-tape.js, nfl-replay.js, nfl-team-card.js, nfl-teaser-execution.js, nfl-unified-engine.js, nfl-weekly-feature-store.js, weekly-learning.js, and 23 more). server/modeling/contracts.js already has the right primitive (stableJson canonical serialization + sha256), just scoped to one pipeline's use.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Promote configurationHash/stableJson out of server/modeling/contracts.js into a repo-root server/identity.js with zero pipeline-specific imports; replace all 37 files' local hash helpers with imports from it in one mechanical pass (codemod-able since the call shape — hash over a JSON-serializable value — is already uniform).
candidates.expected_value: Makes fix-2's registry migration tractable (one identity primitive to wire through instead of reconciling 3 different hash conventions first) and removes an entire class of future "why don't these two hashes match" bugs across the 37 sites.
candidates.exit_test: grep for 'createHash(.sha256.)' outside the new identity module returns zero hits in server/services/*.js; all 37 affected files' existing tests pass with only the import changed, proving the replacement is behavior-preserving.

candidates.candidate: Extend the existing assertTimestampedObservation() point-in-time leakage guard in server/modeling/contracts.js (currently scoped only to PIPELINE_VERSION='gridiron-fantasy-walk-forward@1.0.0') to run against the NFL betting feature tables (nfl_team_week_features, nfl_player_week_features, nfl_play_by_play) that nfl-blind-audit.js freezes and replays every week.
candidates.fixes_finding: nfl-blind-audit.js freezes INPUT_TABLES (including nfl_team_week_features, nfl_play_by_play, nfl_quote_tape) to prevent historical leakage at the table-mutation level, but nothing checks that individual rows inside those frozen tables are themselves point-in-time valid (available_at <= as_of) the way the fantasy pipeline already requires of its own features
candidates.mechanism: contracts.js's assertTimestampedObservation() already throws 'future-data leakage: ... available after prediction cutoff' for the fantasy walk-forward pipeline; the NFL betting side has an equivalent risk (e.g., a team-strength feature computed with data available only after the game it's predicting) but nothing calls this or an equivalent check against nfl_team_week_features/nfl_player_week_features rows before nfl-team-strength.js or the ensemble consume them.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: nfl-blind-audit.js's per-week freeze gains a call to assertTimestampedObservation() (or a betting-specific variant with the same available_at<=as_of contract) over every row read from INPUT_TABLES for that week before the replay runs; failure blocks the week the same way a mutation-journal violation already does.
candidates.expected_value: Closes a plausible but currently unchecked leakage vector in the exact tables the blind audit already treats as sacred, using a function that already exists and is already tested elsewhere in the repo — cheap insurance against exactly the kind of silent leakage that let the ensemble's -2.28 CLV go undetected for so long.
candidates.exit_test: Deliberately backdate one row's available_at to after its as_of in a copy of nfl_team_week_features and confirm the blind audit run for that week now throws/fails-closed instead of silently including it; on the real (clean) table, the check adds the assertion with zero false positives over the last 3 audited seasons.

candidates.candidate: Implement an ML-Test-Score-style scored technical-debt rubric (Breck et al. 2017's 28 tests across Data/Model/Infra/Monitoring) as a CI script that computes and tracks ONE number for Gridiron's own system health over time.
candidates.mechanism: The paper's own measured result (even 36 real Google production teams implement most of the 28 tests at under 80% adoption) shows this kind of scored rubric surfaces real gaps that ad hoc review misses; Gridiron's audit-registry.js grades hypotheses about NFL markets, never the health of the pipeline itself, so there is currently no single tracked number for 'how production-ready is this system.'
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New scripts/ml-test-score.mjs walks server/services/, server/modeling/, and test/ to check for the rubric's automatable subset (e.g. Infra 1 'training is reproducible' -> re-run an experiment twice and diff results; Monitor 3 'training and serving compute the same values' -> compare a feature computed via the audit freeze path vs the live serving path for one sample week) and writes a scored snapshot per category (min-of-4 per the paper) to a new gridiron_test_score table, trended over commits.
candidates.expected_value: Gives Nick one number to watch trend on as the consolidation work (fix-1..fix-4) lands, rather than relying on this one-time audit to notice architecture debt again next time it accumulates.
candidates.exit_test: The script runs unattended in CI and produces a score in [0,5] with a documented category breakdown; a deliberately broken build (e.g. remove a required promotion gate) measurably drops the Infra category score, proving the metric actually detects regressions rather than always reporting green.

candidates.candidate: Add a mandatory time-boxed canary / shadow-serve window (ML Test Score's Infra 6/7 pattern) before ModelRegistry.promote() can complete — a challenger must accumulate N days of forward, held-out predictions logged to model_metrics(split='forward') before promotion, not just pass the 5 static gates instantly.
candidates.mechanism: server/modeling/registry.js's promote()/assertPromotable() checks 5 static boolean gates (schema/leakage/data_quality/baseline_improvement/tests) and transitions immediately on approval — there is no requirement that the candidate has actually run against live, not-yet-seen data first. The MLflow paper's Staging stage exists structurally in Gridiron's registry naming but nothing enforces spending real time there before Production.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Add a REQUIRED_GATES entry 'shadow_window' checked by counting model_metrics rows with split='forward' and recorded_at spanning >= N days for the candidate's experiment_id; promote() throws until satisfied, mirroring the existing gate-check pattern in assertPromotable().
candidates.expected_value: Converts registry promotion from 'passed backtest gates' to 'survived real time,' catching regressions a purely retrospective gate can't (staleness, distribution shift) before a bad model reaches fantasy or betting production — directly serves the standing priority that fantasy edge beats betting edge, since a shadow window is cheapest to require first on fantasy heads.
candidates.exit_test: Attempt to promote a freshly-completed experiment with zero forward model_metrics rows and confirm it is blocked with a clear 'shadow_window' gate-failure message; after N days of synthetic forward metric rows are inserted for a test experiment, promotion succeeds without any other code change.

candidates.candidate: Build a real point-in-time feature store (Michelangelo/Feast-pattern: one shared, versioned, entity+timestamp-indexed table with a canonical as-of query) for the unused 12.4M-row Polymarket quote tape and the 251,591-row play-by-play table, so both are queried through one time-travel-correct interface instead of ad hoc per-consumer SQL.
candidates.mechanism: Uber's Michelangelo blog documents the concrete before/after: before the feature store, teams independently rebuilt identical features; after, ~10,000 features live in one shared catalog computed once via one DSL applied identically at training and serving time. Gridiron's Polymarket tape is 'essentially unused for anything beyond spread-ladder construction' and the 251,591 PBY rows are 'used only for hand-built features, never sequence models' per tonight's findings — both are raw tables with no shared, versioned, as-of-queryable feature layer sitting on top of them.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/feature-store.js exposing featureAsOf(entityId, featureName, asOfTimestamp) backed by a nfl_feature_store table (entity_id, feature_name, value, computed_at, available_at, version) populated from nfl_quote_tape and nfl_play_by_play by versioned builder functions; nfl-team-strength.js and any future PBP-sequence model call this instead of separate raw SQL per consumer.
candidates.expected_value: Makes the 12.4M-row quote tape and 251,591-row PBP table actually reusable across multiple future models (sequence models, team-strength state-space updates) with a single point-in-time-correctness guarantee, instead of each new consumer re-deriving its own leakage-prone query — directly unblocks 2 of tonight's separately-flagged "unused data" findings with one piece of shared infrastructure.
candidates.exit_test: Two different consumers (e.g. nfl-team-strength.js and a new PBP-sequence prototype) request the same feature for the same entity/timestamp through featureAsOf() and get byte-identical values; a deliberately future-dated quote-tape row is excluded from an as-of query for a timestamp before it existed, proving the time-travel guarantee holds.

candidates.candidate: Build one evaluation harness with paired statistical comparison: a service that takes any two registered candidates (two ensemble configs, two CLV formula versions, two audit runs) and returns a governed paired comparison — bootstrap CI, the existing alwaysValidPValue significance test, and a minimum-sample-size gate — before either can be promoted over the other.
candidates.mechanism: server/modeling/registry.js's ModelRegistry.compare(ids) today just returns the raw stored records side by side with no statistical test attached; audit-registry.js's alwaysValidPValue exists and is used for single-hypothesis preregistration but nothing pairs two candidates against each other with a governed test. This is the literal 'one evaluation harness' the topic names, and it doesn't exist as a callable service today — only as ad hoc manual comparison.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/evaluation-harness.js exporting compareCandidates(idA, idB, metric) that pulls each candidate's model_metrics rows (from fix-2's registry wiring), computes a paired bootstrap CI over matched weeks, runs alwaysValidPValue from backtest-significance.js, and refuses to return a verdict below a minimum matched-sample-size threshold; ModelRegistryPanel.tsx gains a 'Compare' view calling it.
candidates.expected_value: Gives every future consolidation decision (which CLV formula, which ensemble blend, which audit config) a governed, reusable statistical answer instead of eyeballing two dashboards — this is the actual mechanism that would have caught the ensemble's fake 20-component diversity or the -2.28 CLV drift earlier if it had existed and been run routinely.
candidates.exit_test: Feed the harness the ensemble's known-good vs known-bad historical configuration (the one with -2.28 mean CLV) and confirm it reports a statistically significant difference in the correct direction with a real p-value/CI, not just a raw metric diff; running it twice on the identical pair of frozen candidates returns byte-identical output (no hidden nondeterminism).

do_not_do: Do not build a 5th 'unified CLV module' while leaving the 4 existing ones importable elsewhere — remove their call sites in the same change or you've added a 6th disagreeing implementation, not fixed anything.

Do not invent a brand-new registry or feature-store framework from scratch — server/modeling/registry.js + sqlite-store.js + migration 005 already pass a real persistence/auth/promotion test suite (test/model-registry-persistence.test.js); extending that schema is cheaper and lower-risk than a parallel new one, and a second registry is literally the disease this research diagnoses.

Do not rewrite nfl-blind-audit.js's leakage-freeze logic (INPUT_TABLES, mutation-journal triggers) itself — that mechanism works and is load-bearing; consolidate only the identity/versioning primitive underneath it, not its freeze semantics.

Do not adopt an external feature-store product (Feast/Tecton) wholesale for a single-operator SQLite project — the point-in-time-join pattern is the transferable idea; the operational infrastructure (separate online/offline stores, Spark/Cassandra) is not worth it here.

Do not treat the ML Test Score's 28-point rubric as a merge-blocking gate — the paper's own finding is that even real Google production teams sit well under full marks; use it as a trended number, not a hard threshold.

Do not apply the new canary/shadow-serve window uniformly with the same duration for fantasy and betting candidates — per the standing fantasy-over-betting priority, keep the fantasy shadow window short and let betting-adjacent promotions wait longer.

result.label: F17-margin-distribution-lit
result.summary: Read 4 primary sources in full/near-full detail (Sides-Harvill-Sides 2022 and Glickman-Stern 1998 fully; Moyer-Railey-Daw-Gutekunst 2024 fully; Stern 1991 documented via 3 independent citing sources plus Glickman-Stern's direct reproduction of it) plus 4 corroborating practitioner analyses. Central finding: no continuous distribution (normal, Skellam, or independent Poisson) reproduces NFL key-number mass — every source that tested it found key numbers must be modeled as free/tilted point masses, exactly what Gridiron's own (already-built, currently unused-by-the-simulator) `margin-distribution.js` does. The literature's real value here is (a) giving concrete target numbers — margin SD in the 12.1-13.86 range depending on era/team-strength modeling, key-number masses ~14.7% at margin=3 and ~8.9% at margin=7 for 2015-2023, HFA ~3pt mean with ~2.3pt cross-team SD (never a discrete lump), and an exact empirical OT score-pair table (n=145, 2015-2023) — and (b) confirming that Gridiron's drive-sim has zero mechanism today to detect a key-number distortion even after F01's bugs are fixed, since `calibrationReport()` checks only mean/SD. Grepped nfl-drive-sim.js and confirmed the exact line (562) producing the flat-7-point HFA lump, confirmed simulateRemainder() (773) has no halftime/OT branch at all, and confirmed calibrationReport() (903) has no shape/key-number check.

sources.title: On the Probability of Winning a Football Game
sources.sample: NFL seasons 1981, 1983, 1984
sources.key_result: Margin of victory minus closing spread ~ N(0, 13.86^2); not significantly different from normal for RANGE questions (win/cover), but never claimed accurate for exact-margin (key-number) probabilities -- confirmed via Glickman & Stern (1998) direct citation and reproduction, plus two other independent citing sources.

sources.title: Converting College Football Point Spread Differentials to Probability
sources.authors: Ryan Sides, Jane L. Harvill, Victoria R. Sides
sources.sample: 2021 NCAA football season (SP+ vs. betting lines); historical differential table from Boyd (2015), 1980-2014
sources.key_result: Normal approximation fails at key numbers; fix is multiplying normal-model cell probabilities by empirical/normal frequency ratios (multiplier 2.7 at differential 3, 2.1 at 7) then renormalizing -- structurally the same idea as Gridiron's own margin-distribution.js tilt-times-atom model, independently derived. Worked example: 53.2% cover prob / 0.8% edge vs. naive normal's 51.06%/no edge. Authors explicitly flag their single validation season as compromised (COVID rosters, 6th-year seniors) -- honest limitation.

sources.title: A State-Space Model for National Football League Scores
sources.authors: Mark E. Glickman, Hal S. Stern
sources.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association, 93(441):25-35
sources.sample: NFL regular seasons 1988-1993 (28 teams); held out last 110 games of 1993 for validation
sources.key_result: AR(1) state-space team-strength model with separate between-week/between-season variances via MCMC. Posterior residual SD of score differential tau=12.78 (95% CI 12.23-13.35), lower than Stern 1991's cruder 13.86. Home-field advantage is continuous and team-varying (posterior means 1.62 to 7.28, cross-team SD~2.3), never a flat constant. Out-of-sample vs. real benchmark (Vegas line, n=110): model MSE 165.0 / MAE 10.50 beats the line's MSE 170.5 / MAE 10.84, correctly picks 64/110 vs line's 63/110 -- explicitly stated as suggestive, not large enough to generalize.

sources.title: Scorigami: Simulating the Distribution and Assessing the Rarity of National Football League Scores
sources.authors: Liam Moyer, Jameson Railey, Andrew Daw, Samuel C. Gutekunst
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Winter Simulation Conference, pp. 702-713
sources.sample: NFL play-by-play via nfl_data_py (49,664 plays, 2023 season); scoring-event data 1940-2023; OT-specific data 2015-2023 (n=145 OT games); primary benchmark population = 2015-2023 'current epoch'
sources.key_result: Naive independent-Poisson-per-scoring-event model underpredicts key-number mass by ~2x (margin=3: model 7.67% vs true 14.7%; margin=7: model 5.67% vs true 8.89%) and inflates mean margin (13.32 model vs 11.11 true). Their non-stationary, state-dependent Poisson PROCESS model (time-segmented rates + score-differential-tilted team weighting, garbage-time deceleration) cuts joint-PMF RMSE from 0.00335 to 0.00310 (7.8% improvement) and matches mean margin (11.25 vs true 11.11). Table 2 gives exact empirical OT score-pair frequencies (3-0:74, 6-0:49, 6-3:13, 0-0:7, 3-3:2, 2-0:0, n=145) directly reusable as ground truth. Authors explicitly state the fit could still be improved and that the two models' Scorigami forecasts are largely unvalidated going forward -- honest limitation.

sources.title: Margin Probabilities from NFL Spreads
sources.sample: not disclosed in fetched content
sources.key_result: Qualitative corroboration: NFL margins are 'somewhat normal' around the spread but key numbers (3,7,10) occur more often than a normal predicts; their multi-distribution model 'explains margins meaningfully better than a single normal.' No hard sample size or error numbers surfaced.

sources.title: NFL Key Betting Numbers: How Margins Changed with Longer Extra Point
sources.sample: NFL seasons 2003-2020 (full dataset) and 2015-2019 (post-rule-change focus)
sources.key_result: 2015-2019 key-number frequencies: 3=14.43%, 7=9.89%, 6=7.25%, 14=5.74%, 10=4.61% -- consistent with Moyer et al.'s 2015-2023 figures, used as cross-era corroboration.

sources.title: A Complete History of NFL Margins of Victory
sources.key_result: Key numbers {3,4,6,7,10,14} average 45.0% of games 1974-2014 (SD of that share across years = 3.55pp), spiking to 52.1% in 2015; used to show the aggregate key-number share is stable even as which specific numbers dominate shifts.

sources.title: What's the Correct Margin-of-Victory Cap For the NFL?
sources.sample: NFL 2002-2013 (32-team era), SRS ratings
sources.key_result: SD of game-level prediction error (actual margin minus SRS-implied margin) = 12.1 -- a fourth independent era-specific SD estimate, sitting between Glickman-Stern's 12.78 (1988-93) and the post-2015 figures, consistent with a slow downward drift in the 'true' margin SD.

candidates.candidate: Replace the flat 7-point post-OT home-field-advantage lump in simulateGame with a continuous per-drive HFA calibrated to the literature's team-varying estimate
candidates.fixes_finding: home-field advantage is a flat 7-point post-OT lump distorting the key-number distribution
candidates.mechanism: nfl-drive-sim.js:562 currently does `if (homeFieldPoints > 0 && random() < homeFieldPoints / 7) home += 7;` -- a Bernoulli(homeFieldPoints/7) all-or-nothing add of exactly 7 points, applied once after regulation+OT. This manufactures spurious mass at margin = true_margin +/- 7 that is not present in any empirical NFL margin distribution. Glickman & Stern (1998) show HFA is a continuous, team-varying quantity (posterior mean ~3.2 points, cross-team SD ~2.3, range ~1.6 to ~7.3 across 28 teams in their sample) that acts throughout the game via scoring/allowing rates, not as one discrete late jackpot.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: In nfl-drive-sim.js, convert `homeFieldPoints` from a probabilistic lump-sum add into a small continuous per-drive scoring-rate or expected-points nudge for the home offense/defense inside buildContext()/simulateDrive(), sized so its season-long expectation still matches homeFieldPoints (~1.6-3 pts) but its variance contribution is spread smoothly across ~11 drives/game instead of concentrated at one +/-7 jump. Optionally let it vary by team (team-level HFA table) rather than being a single league constant, matching Glickman-Stern's team-level posterior spread.
candidates.expected_value: Removes a specific, named, mechanically-verified source of key-number contamination in the simulator's margin output; makes the simulated distribution's mass at exactly +/-7 (relative to the no-fix baseline) closer to the true, non-jackpot shape without touching any other module.
candidates.exit_test: Re-run calibrationReport() (or the new key-number check in candidate F17-fix-2) before/after the change on the same 40 fixed matchups/seed; the excess probability mass at margin = (pre-fix expected margin) +/- 7, measured as simulated-minus-expected under a smooth null, should shrink toward zero; mean total/margin from the existing checks should not move by more than their current tolerances (do not regress the two checks that already pass).

candidates.candidate: Add key-number point-mass checks to calibrationReport(), scored against Gridiron's own already-fitted margin-distribution.js pmf
candidates.fixes_finding: home-field advantage is a flat 7-point post-OT lump distorting the key-number distribution
candidates.mechanism: calibrationReport() (nfl-drive-sim.js:903-960) currently runs exactly 3 checks -- mean total, mean home margin, margin SD, each with a +/-3 to +/-3.5 point tolerance. None of these three summary statistics can detect a shape distortion like the flat-7 HFA lump: a distribution that is +7-heavy at one margin and correspondingly light elsewhere can still have a mean and SD within tolerance. That is exactly how F01's bug shipped silently.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Extend calibrationReport()'s `checks` array with new entries comparing the simulated margin PMF's mass at |margin| in {3,6,7,10,14} (computed from simTotals/simMargins per-game samples, or better, from raw simulateMatchup() margin arrays if exposed) against margin-distribution.js's fitMarginModel()/marginPmf(spread).at(m) evaluated at each simulated game's own spread -- the exact ground truth already fitted on Gridiron's own game_lines, no new empirical work required. Add a chi-square-style or simple |diff| > tolerance check per key number, following the same pattern crossBothReproduction() already uses in margin-distribution.js.
candidates.expected_value: Turns a currently invisible failure mode into a visible, automatically-checked one; directly protects the fix in F17-fix-1 (and any future drive-sim change) from silently regressing the key-number shape again, using code that already exists in the repo rather than new empirical fitting.
candidates.exit_test: Run the extended calibrationReport() against the CURRENT (pre-fix) simulator: the new key-number checks should FAIL at margin=7 (and margin=0/±7 neighborhood) given the known flat-7 lump. After F17-fix-1 lands, re-run: the key-number checks should PASS within a stated tolerance (e.g. +/-1.5 percentage points versus margin-distribution.js's fitted mass).

candidates.candidate: Give simulateRemainder() a halftime break and real overtime handling
candidates.fixes_finding: the season-remainder simulator has no halftime or overtime at all
candidates.mechanism: simulateRemainder() (nfl-drive-sim.js:773-869) runs a single `while (clock > 0)` loop treating the game clock as one uninterrupted countdown from whatever `secondsLeft` the live state provides, with no reset/kickoff logic at the halftime boundary and no branch at all for a tied score at clock<=0 (contrast simulateGame's explicit two-half loop plus dedicated OT block at lines 540-558). Any live win-probability query made before halftime is therefore simulating a continuous single 'half' that runs straight through what should be a clock stoppage, possession change, and (if tied) a genuinely different sudden-death rule set.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Add a halftime boundary check inside simulateRemainder()'s main loop (mirroring simulateGame's `for (const half of [1,2])` structure, entered at the correct `state.secondsLeft`/`state.half` starting point) that resets timeouts to 3/3 and re-assigns kickoff possession at the 1800s mark, and append the same (or the fixed, see F17-new-6) overtime block used in simulateGame when `clock<=0 && h===a`.
candidates.expected_value: In-game win probabilities computed for any live state in the first half currently have no representation of the halftime stoppage or of tied games at the end of regulation at all -- this is a live-facing correctness gap, not just an offline-calibration one, and fixing it makes simulateRemainder() structurally consistent with simulateGame() rather than a separate, less-correct code path.
candidates.exit_test: Feed simulateRemainder() a state exactly at 2nd-quarter 0:05 remaining, tied score: verify the simulated trials show a possession change and reset timeouts at the 1800s boundary (spot-check via collectLog-style instrumentation or a unit test asserting clock never goes negative across the boundary without a reset event) and that tied-at-zero trials are routed into an explicit OT resolution rather than silently returning finalHome===finalAway with no OT scoring applied.

candidates.candidate: Replace nfl-team-strength.js's hand-tuned preseason/in-season blend with a Glickman-Stern-style AR(1) state-space update
candidates.fixes_finding: Team-strength ratings (nfl-team-strength.js) mix stale preseason priors with in-season data via a hand-tuned blend, not a principled state-space/Bayesian update.
candidates.mechanism: Glickman & Stern (1998) fit team strengths as a first-order autoregressive state-space process with two SEPARATE evolution variances -- between-week (sigma_w, posterior mean ~0.88, i.e. small week-to-week drift) and between-season (sigma_s, posterior mean ~2.35, i.e. much larger season-to-season drift from personnel/coaching changes) -- fit jointly by MCMC with genuine posterior uncertainty, rather than a single fixed blend weight applied the same way regardless of how much in-season data has accumulated.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: In nfl-team-strength.js, replace the current fixed blend-weight logic with a Kalman-filter-style update: prior team-strength (preseason) as the week-0 state, updated each week by a linear shrinkage toward that week's observed scoring margin, with the shrinkage factor itself governed by two tunable evolution variances (within-season vs. between-season) fit by walk-forward CV the same way margin-distribution.js already validates its own smoothing parameter (season-blocked 5-fold CV) -- reusing that CV harness pattern rather than building a new one from scratch.
candidates.expected_value: Team-strength ratings feed directly into the drive simulator's per-team scoring/allowing rates, so a principled, uncertainty-quantified update (vs. a fixed blend) should reduce systematic mis-calibration of the simulator's margin center especially early-season when preseason priors dominate but the current blend may over- or under-weight them.
candidates.exit_test: Walk-forward backtest (mirroring nfl-drive-sim.js's own backtest()/edgeHunt() pattern): compare weekly log-loss of game outcomes predicted from state-space team strengths vs. the current hand-tuned-blend strengths, on identical held-out seasons; the state-space version should not be worse, and should show measurably better calibration specifically in weeks 1-4 where the preseason-vs-in-season weighting matters most.

candidates.candidate: Held-out log-loss/Brier calibration harness for the drive simulator's FULL margin distribution shape
candidates.mechanism: Nothing in the repo today scores the drive simulator's simulated margin distribution against reality using a proper scoring rule (log-loss/Brier) across the full support -- calibrationReport() checks 3 summary moments (mean total, mean margin, margin SD) and margin-distribution.js's outOfSampleCalibration()/crossBothReproduction() score only the STANDALONE empirical teaser model, never the drive simulator's own output. A proper distributional scoring rule would catch shape errors (over/under-dispersion, wrong skew, missed key numbers) that moment-matching cannot.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New function alongside calibrationReport() in nfl-drive-sim.js: for each of N held-out historical games, run simulateMatchup() to get an empirical margin PMF from trials, compute log-loss/Brier of that PMF against the realized margin, and walk-forward across seasons the same way margin-distribution.js's outOfSampleCalibration() already does (train-through/test-from split, same scoring functions scoreLeg()-style) -- directly reusing that module's tested pattern rather than inventing a new one.
candidates.expected_value: Gives a single, trustworthy number (log-loss per game) that would have caught the flat-7 HFA bug, the missing-halftime bug, and any future drive-sim regression in the distribution's SHAPE, not just its first two moments -- a capability that currently exists only for the unrelated standalone teaser model.
candidates.exit_test: Run the new harness on the current (pre-F01-fix) simulator and confirm its log-loss is measurably worse than margin-distribution.js's own fitted-model log-loss on the same held-out games (establishing the harness actually discriminates); after F01's bugs and F17-fix-1 land, confirm the gap narrows.

candidates.candidate: Dirichlet/categorical overtime-outcome model calibrated to the empirical 2015-2023 NFL OT score-pair table
candidates.mechanism: Moyer et al. (2024) Table 2 gives the exact empirical distribution of NFL overtime score pairs for 2015-2023 (n=145): {3-0: 74, 6-0: 49, 6-3: 13, 0-0: 7, 3-3: 2, 2-0: 0}. This is a small, sudden-death-specific outcome space that current OT logic (both simulateGame's `had<8` loop and, once fixed, simulateRemainder's new OT branch) tries to reproduce by resimulating full drives under regulation-time policies never validated for sudden-death incentives (e.g., a team already assured a tie by kicking a FG plays very differently than mid-regulation).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Add a lightweight categorical/Dirichlet-multinomial OT-outcome model (fit on Gridiron's own game_lines OT rows if available, with Moyer et al.'s table as an informative prior given the likely small n in-house) as an alternative or cross-check path callable from simulateGame's OT block, returning a directly-drawn (home_pts, away_pts) pair with proper posterior uncertainty instead of resimulating possessions.
candidates.expected_value: Replaces an untested structural assumption (symmetric regulation-style OT drives) with a statistically grounded, easily-updated small model; cheap to build and interpret, and gives an explicit uncertainty interval on OT outcome frequencies that nothing in the repo currently has.
candidates.exit_test: Chi-square goodness-of-fit test comparing the new categorical model's implied OT outcome distribution (or, for the resimulated version, a large sample of simulated OT drives) against Moyer et al.'s Table 2 frequencies; should not reject at p<0.05 on a reasonably sized simulated sample.

candidates.candidate: Cheap closed-form margin CDF (normal baseline x fitted key-number multipliers) as a near-zero-cost consistency check
candidates.mechanism: Sides, Harvill & Sides (2022) show a normal(spread, SD) baseline can be corrected to match key-number mass by multiplying each cell's probability by an empirically-fit ratio (historical/normal frequency) and renormalizing -- an O(1) closed-form calculation, versus the drive simulator's O(trials x plays) cost per query. Nothing in Gridiron currently offers a sub-millisecond margin CDF; every current path (drive-sim trials, or margin-distribution.js's Newton-fitted conditional logit) costs meaningfully more than a closed-form lookup.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New small module (or a fast-path export on margin-distribution.js) precomputing, for each integer spread in the range the book posts, a vector of normal(spread, SD)-times-multiplier probabilities calibrated once against margin-distribution.js's own fitted key-number masses (reusing that module's numbers rather than re-deriving Sides et al.'s CFB-specific multipliers) -- callable anywhere code currently pays for a full simulateMatchup() run just to get P(margin > x), e.g. inner loops of edgeHunt()/backtest() in nfl-drive-sim.js.
candidates.expected_value: Near-zero marginal cost per call; useful as a cheap sanity bound/screen inside expensive loops (edgeHunt, backtest) that currently re-run full drive simulations for every candidate line, without pretending to replace the full simulator's fidelity for anything that needs play-level detail.
candidates.exit_test: Compare the closed-form CDF's P(cover) at each of the 8 cross-both teaser lines against both margin-distribution.js's crossBothReproduction() empirical targets and the drive simulator's own trial-based estimate; the closed-form version should track margin-distribution.js closely (it is calibrated to it) and should run at least 100x faster per call in a microbenchmark.

candidates.candidate: Independent, cheap compound-Poisson TOTAL-POINTS engine as an ensemble member / fast sanity check
candidates.mechanism: Moyer et al. (2024)'s non-stationary, state-dependent Poisson process model (separate 6/7/8-pt TD, FG, safety scoring-rate processes, reweighted by live score differential and 6 in-game time segments) cut joint-score-PMF RMSE by 7.8% versus a naive independent-Poisson baseline and matched the true 2015-2023 mean margin (11.25 vs 11.11) at a fraction of the computational cost of full play-by-play drive simulation -- it needs only team-level scoring-event rates, not down/distance/EP modeling.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New standalone module implementing the 6-segment piecewise-constant compound-Poisson process from the paper, parameterized off Gridiron's own historical scoring-event rates (available via the same nflverse/play-by-play tables the drive simulator already reads), producing a fast total-points and margin distribution usable as (a) an independent ensemble input to nfl-ensemble.js's total/margin blend, or (b) a fast pre-screen before committing to an expensive simulateMatchup() run.
candidates.expected_value: Gives a second, structurally-independent model of the total-points distribution (useful precisely because nfl-ensemble.js's 20 components already collapse to ~3 independent signals -- a genuinely different model family adds real diversity rather than another shrinkage-toward-market variant), at much lower per-call cost than the full drive simulator.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest the new engine's total-points predictions (mean and P(over/under) at posted totals) walk-forward against realized totals on held-out seasons, using the same log-loss/Brier scoring as F17-new-5; it should beat a naive independent-Poisson baseline by a measurable margin (targeting the paper's own ~7.8% RMSE improvement as a rough bar) before being wired into any live ensemble.

do_not_do: Do not port Karlis & Ntzoufras (2003)-style bivariate/diagonal-inflated Poisson goal models literally to NFL scores -- they are built for soccer's raw goal counts (0-5 range, draws matter); NFL scores are compound sums of 3/6/7/8-point events, and Moyer et al. (2024) show even a properly-separated multi-event independent-Poisson NFL model still underpredicts key-number mass by roughly 2x. Note: the Karlis & Ntzoufras paper itself could not be fetched (its host was unreachable both attempts), so this is based on two independent secondary summaries of its method, not a full read -- treat 'diagonal inflation' as a reference pointer only, not a validated recipe to implement.

Do not treat Stern (1991)'s N(spread, 13.86^2) -- or any single fixed-SD normal -- as sufficient for anything beyond win/cover probability at one point. It is provably wrong for key-number mass and for any teaser/alternate-line question, which is exactly why margin-distribution.js already exists in this repo; do not rebuild what it already does correctly.

Do not fold the HFA fix (F17-fix-1) into calibrationReport's existing +/-3 / +/-3.5 point tolerances without adding the explicit key-number check (F17-fix-2) -- a mean/SD-only calibration can and did pass while this exact distortion shipped silently.

Do not declare the overtime fix (F17-fix-3) complete once halftime/clock logic is mechanically correct -- separately validate the simulated OT score-pair distribution against Moyer et al.'s Table 2 via a chi-square/multinomial test; a clock-correct OT loop can still have the wrong FG-vs-TD mix.

Do not recalibrate margin SD using a single fixed constant taken from one era (pre-2015 Stern's 13.86, Football Perspective's 2002-2013 12.1, or Glickman-Stern's 1988-93 12.78) -- these visibly differ by era and by how explicitly team strength is modeled. margin-distribution.js already has the right machinery (a walk-forward-validated exponential season half-life of 6) for this; reuse it rather than hard-coding one literature number.

Do not spend build budget on the new totals engine (F17-new-8) or the fast closed-form CDF (F17-new-7) before F01's 6 known drive-simulator physics bugs are actually fixed -- calibrating distribution shape on top of broken mechanics (wrong-team turnovers, inverted kneel rule, non-decrementing timeouts, home-spread used for away win probability) will just calibrate around the bugs and produce a confidently-wrong shape.

result.label: F16-dfp-devig-favorite-longshot
result.summary: Traced the call graph and read four primary FLB/devig papers to answer: Gridiron's dog/over pick bias is NOT a devig artifact. In nfl-ensemble.js and nfl-auto-picks.js, marketMargin comes straight from -g.home_spread (raw points) and the pick's side is fixed by edge=projectedMargin-marketMargin BEFORE any devig call runs; Shin's method (already implemented tonight in nfl-devig.js, correctly grounded in Shin 1992/fixed-odds theory per Ottaviani & Sørensen) only touches confidence/CLV scoring downstream of side selection, and even pushes fair probability toward favorites, not dogs -- the opposite sign from the observed bias. Hegarty & Whelan (2025, read in full: soccer N=151,683, tennis N=131,283) additionally show the naive-vs-real loss-rate gap that drives FLB does NOT appear in Asian-Handicap-style markets, which are structurally the closest real-world analogue to NFL point spreads -- so FLB is plausibly near-moot on the exact surface (spreads) where the bias was measured, and more likely to matter on moneylines/rare-event props where Gridiron's own test file shows Shin and proportional devig actually diverge. Conclusion: the -2.28 CLV / 78%-adverse-move pattern is a mechanical attenuation bug in the point-margin blend (0.68+0.632*market), not a devig-explainable signal.

sources.title: Explaining the Favorite–Long Shot Bias: Is it Risk-Love or Misperceptions?
sources.sample: All 6,403,712 US horse-race starts 1992-2001 (Jockey Club data); 1,485,112-start exacta/quinella/trifecta subsample; plus Australia (2.725M starts) and UK (380K starts) data
sources.key_result: Rate of return ~-5.5% betting every favorite vs -23% betting randomly vs -61% at 100/1+ odds; using compound-bet (exacta/quinella/trifecta) prices to discriminate theories, the misperceptions/prospect-theory class fits better than risk-love

sources.title: Noise, Information, and the Favorite-Longshot Bias in Parimutuel Predictions
sources.venue: American Economic Journal: Microeconomics 2(1), 58-85 (draft read: Jan 2009 WP)
sources.sample: Theoretical model paper, no proprietary dataset; comparative statics checked against existing FLB literature
sources.key_result: FLB emerges from informed-vs-noise betting in parimutuel markets; explicitly distinguishes this from Shin's (1991/1992) fixed-odds bookmaker mechanism, noting more informed money STRENGTHENS FLB in fixed-odds markets (adverse selection) but the opposite in parimutuel markets -- the key citation for why Shin, not a parimutuel model, is the right frame for Gridiron's bookmaker-priced NFL lines

sources.title: The Timing of Bets and the Favorite-Longshot Bias
sources.sample: Theoretical model, no dataset (purely a Cournot-style timing model of parimutuel betting)
sources.key_result: Models early vs late informed betting as competing strategic incentives; explains early-betting, late-informed-betting and FLB as one mechanism; explicitly parimutuel-only, fixed-odds timing left out of scope

sources.title: Estimating Expected Loss Rates in Betting Markets: Theory and Evidence
sources.venue: University College Dublin working paper (revised draft)
sources.sample: Soccer: N=151,683 matches, 2005/06-2025/26 seasons, 10 bookmakers; Tennis: N=131,283 matches, 2010-2024, 5 bookmakers (Buchdahl odds data)
sources.key_result: Normalized/overround-implied loss rates understate realized losses because bookmakers set higher margins on lower-probability outcomes: soccer 7.1% predicted vs 8.7% realized (+20%), tennis 5.4% vs 7.5% (+40%), holding even at Pinnacle; but this gap does NOT appear in Asian Handicap (point-spread-style) betting -- the market structurally closest to NFL spreads

candidates.candidate: Consolidate the remaining zero/raw-vig 'market probability' surfaces (staking.js's stakeFor, line-shopping.js's edge_vs_worst) onto Shin's method already unified in nfl-devig.js, and empirically compare Shin vs proportional against Gridiron's own realized bet outcomes (Brier/log-loss), not just internal-consistency unit tests.
candidates.fixes_finding: No real devig method comparison exists; probabilities are extracted with one ad hoc approach / Five independent, disagreeing CLV implementations exist over four different tables
candidates.mechanism: server/services/staking.js:91-92,119 computes marketProb via a single-sided americanToProb with NO devig at all (worse than the 'one ad hoc method' finding describes) and is live behind GET /nfl/stake (server/routes/nfl-betting.js:949); line-shopping.js:24,157's edge_vs_worst is similarly undevigged. Add an optional opposite-price param routing both through shinNoVig, relabel the raw single-sided case as raw_implied_probability, and add a walk-forward Brier-score comparison of Shin vs proportional fair probabilities against nfl_bet_log outcomes.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/staking.js (stakeFor, marketProb), server/routes/nfl-betting.js:949 (/nfl/stake), server/services/line-shopping.js:24,157 (edge_vs_worst)
candidates.expected_value: Closes the exact defect class FOUND flagged at its worst remaining live surface (zero devig, not just naive); converts 'Shin is right' from borrowed literature authority into a locally-verified fact for Gridiron's own market
candidates.exit_test: New test: stakeFor's market_probability matches shinNoVig bit-for-bit when an opposite price is supplied, and is renamed raw_implied_probability when it is not; a one-off backtest script reports Brier scores of Shin vs proportional fair probabilities against nfl_bet_log, surfaced as a diagnostic (not auto-adopted, per the project's promotion-gate discipline)

candidates.candidate: Add a permanent regression test proving the ensemble's dog/over bias is a margin-blend artifact, not a devig artifact, by re-running the existing blind-audit harness under both Shin's and proportional devig for CLV grading and asserting the pick-direction/adverse-move statistics are unchanged.
candidates.fixes_finding: The raw blend is a shrinkage of the closing line toward zero (model ≈ 0.68 + 0.632·market); 152/153 spread picks and 48/48 total picks were dogs/overs -- and the five-disagreeing-CLV-implementations finding, by making the devig-sensitivity of the CLV number an explicit, tested quantity instead of an assumed one
candidates.mechanism: nfl-ensemble.js's marketMargin/edge computation never calls any devig function (confirmed by grep -- no noVig/shinNoVig import in the file); nfl-auto-picks.js fixes the pick's side via edge=projectedMargin-marketMargin at line 104-107, a full call BEFORE noVigProbability is invoked at line 114. Re-run blind-audit runs 27/31 (545 bets each) with nfl-clv.js's gradeClosingLineValue parameterized to Shin vs proportional and assert mean CLV, adverse-move rate, and dog/favorite split are statistically indistinguishable between the two.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-ensemble.js (marketMargin/edge), server/services/nfl-auto-picks.js:99-116 (side selection precedes devig call), server/services/nfl-clv.js (gradeClosingLineValue), server/services/nfl-blind-audit.js / nfl-replay.js (rerun harness)
candidates.expected_value: Prevents a future contributor from 'fixing' the dog-bias by swapping devig methods (which cannot work, per the call graph) and documents precisely where the real fix belongs (the 0.632 attenuation slope in the margin blend)
candidates.exit_test: The new comparison test should show near-identical CLV/dog-split under Shin vs proportional; if it ever diverges materially, that itself flags a regression where devig got wired into side-selection

candidates.candidate: Extend Shin-consistent devig to props' one-sided rare-event (anytime-TD) markets, where genuine longshot odds (+400 to +1200) put Gridiron squarely in the region the FLB literature says the naive-vig gap is largest.
candidates.fixes_finding: Player props are point-estimate projections, not distributions... under-measured against real prices / No real devig method comparison exists
candidates.mechanism: nfl-props.js:658-665's anytime-TD marketP is americanToProb(m.over) -- raw, one-sided, no devig -- because the feed has no real 'No' price to pair against, unlike every two-sided market on the same board which correctly calls noVig. Impute an effective opposite price from the same book's own typical overround (already observable from its two-sided markets that week) and route the imputed pair through shinDevig instead of reporting the raw vig-inclusive number.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-props.js:658-665 (anytime-TD marketP), server/services/nfl-prop-calibration.js (calibrateAnytimeTd, where the walk-forward check must run)
candidates.expected_value: Could materially change measured anytime-TD Brier skill (the module's one area of real measured edge, currently 2+ TD +27.3%, any-type TD +20.6%) by correcting a market baseline biased in exactly the direction the literature predicts -- but only ship if it improves calibration out of sample

candidates.candidate: Add a Snowberg-Wolfers-style prospect-theory (Prelec) probability-weighting term as a second, distinct calibration hypothesis alongside the existing logistic-offset shrinkage in nfl-cover-calibration.js.
candidates.mechanism: Snowberg & Wolfers (2010) found a nonlinear probability-WEIGHTING function -- not a linear-in-logit shrinkage -- is what actually rationalizes real bettors' revealed preferences across win bets AND compound bets jointly. Gridiron's fitLogisticOffset (sigmoid(logit(market)+b0+b1*edge/7)) is a different, purely Bayesian-shrinkage functional form and has never been tested against a behavioral/misperceptions-style curvature term.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-cover-calibration.js's fitLogisticOffset/calibratedCoverProbability -- add a Prelec-shaped term fit the same walk-forward, training-seasons-only way selectLambda already is
candidates.expected_value: A genuinely new (behavioral, not Bayesian-shrinkage) lens on the market-vs-model gap; if the fitted curvature is near zero, that's a clean, useful negative result ruling out FLB-style misperception in NFL spreads specifically, consistent with the Asian-Handicap finding
candidates.exit_test: Ship only if it improves held-out log-loss/Brier over the existing logistic-offset model in the same walk-forward, Holm-corrected discipline the rest of the calibration module already uses; otherwise document as a dead end

candidates.candidate: Persist and use Shin's fitted informed-money-share parameter z as a new per-quote diagnostic signal, distinct from Gridiron's existing cross-book steam detection.
candidates.mechanism: Shin (1992) and O&S give z a real economic meaning: the modeled share of wagers from bettors with genuine informational edge. nfl-devig.js's shinDevig already computes z for every two-sided price pair, but every caller (nfl-market.js, nfl-auto-picks.js, nfl-clv.js, nfl-cover-calibration.js, nfl-props.js) destructures out only probA/probB and discards it -- a free, already-computed signal, information-theoretically distinct from nfl-sharp.js's inter-book/inter-time steam detector since z is intra-quote (one book, one moment).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-devig.js (shinDevig's discarded z), persisted alongside captured quotes (line-shopping.js's line_snapshots or game_lines), correlated against server/services/nfl-sharp.js's steamMoves() output
candidates.expected_value: A leading indicator that costs nothing to compute (it already is computed and thrown away); per O&S's fixed-odds prediction, rising z should precede sharp moves -- if confirmed, a second independent early-warning signal Gridiron's sharp-money detection currently lacks entirely
candidates.exit_test: Does pre-move z Granger-cause/lead documented steam events in the existing steamMoves() dataset; must clear the same promotion-gate/Holm-correction bar (nfl-candidate-findings.js) as any other candidate finding before touching live picks

candidates.candidate: Build a Gridiron-native, odds-bucketed favorite-longshot curve (replicating Snowberg-Wolfers Fig.1 / Hegarty-Whelan Fig.1) for both Gridiron's own picks and the raw market it trades in.
candidates.mechanism: Every paper read bucketed realized outcomes by odds/probability decile and plotted realized-vs-implied to measure FLB's actual size. Gridiron has an aggregate CLV mean (-2.28) but no odds-bucketed curve for either its own picks or the underlying market, so it cannot see at a glance whether FLB has room to matter in its specific narrow-odds spread universe (which Hegarty & Whelan's Asian-Handicap result suggests may show little to none) versus its moneyline/props universe (where it likely does).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: new module (e.g. server/services/nfl-flb-curve.js) reading nfl_bet_log + game_lines/nfl_odds_archive, bucketing by devigged probability decile, feeding a chart into the existing betting-hub UI (server/routes/betting-hub.js)
candidates.expected_value: Directly and quantitatively scopes how much the whole devig-choice question matters for each of Gridiron's market types, replacing a general literature-borrowed assumption with a Gridiron-specific measurement
candidates.exit_test: Report the 90th-percentile |Shin - proportional| divergence and the realized-vs-implied gap by decile across Gridiron's actual quote history, separately for spreads, moneylines, and props; use this to prioritize (or deprioritize) further devig work by market

do_not_do: Do not conclude the dog/over bias is a hidden real FLB-exploitable edge and size bets on it -- the call graph shows devig math is strictly downstream of side selection, so it structurally cannot be the cause, and Shin's own correction runs the opposite direction (toward favorites, not dogs) from the observed bias.

Do not switch away from or 're-derive' Shin's method in nfl-devig.js on general literature authority alone without first running a Gridiron-native Brier/log-loss comparison -- Hegarty & Whelan (2025) show the naive-vs-real FLB gap does not appear in Asian-Handicap-style (point-spread) markets, so 'Shin beats proportional' is not automatically true for NFL spreads even though it is well supported for moneylines and horse racing.

Do not touch the ensemble's margin blend coefficients (0.68 + 0.632*market) as part of any devig-related fix -- that shrinkage lives entirely in point-margin space, upstream of and untouched by any devig call; conflating the two wastes effort and risks mislabeling a real bug as a devig nuance.

Do not wire any new signal from this research (Prelec calibration, persisted z, the FLB curve) into nfl-execution-edge.js's real gated stakeFor path without going through nfl-candidate-findings.js's promotion gate -- per the project's own 'shrink-only, never boost' rule and the fact that 0 of 21 spread models have ever earned proven CLV.

Do not touch the fantasy-football-dashboard database, run its tests/builds/migrations, or interact with its live process while acting on any of this -- per the hard rule, and because Week 1 2026 games are still being captured through Sunday.

result.label: Time-series foundation models (Chronos/TimesFM/Moirai/Lag-Llama) for short weekly NFL panels
result.summary: Read all four core zero-shot time-series foundation model papers in full (Chronos TMLR'24, TimesFM ICML'24/Google, Moirai ICML'24 oral/Salesforce, Lag-Llama NeurIPS-W'24). Honest verdict: none of the four benchmarks evaluates anything close to a 17-point series — TimesFM's own authors had to shrink context to 256 for weekly data because their multi-year weekly panels were "not sufficiently long," and Lag-Llama's lag-based tokenization requires a context window at least as long as its largest lag index (up to 52 weeks), which structurally disqualifies a single team's single-season series. Zero-shot performance across all four is "comparable, occasionally superior" at best (Chronos), "within significance" not clearly better (TimesFM on Darts), or worse than several from-scratch supervised baselines (Lag-Llama zero-shot rank 6.7/13, only reaching rank 2.8 after fine-tuning). The one exploitable structural fact: Moirai trains with per-variate windows as short as 2 steps because it pools many short series cross-sectionally rather than relying on long individual context — exactly the shape of Gridiron's existing `nfl_team_week_features`/`nfl_player_week_features` tables (32 teams x 5-6 seasons x 17 weeks = 150-190 short series per stat). That pooled-panel framing, not naive single-team zero-shotting, is the honest pilot design. Six candidates specified against grepped real files/tables, three explicitly fixing FOUND defects (hand-tuned team-strength blend, fantasy cold-start no-op, missing conformal/point-estimate-only uncertainty) and three pure new-capability (pooled fine-tuned team/player forecaster, PBP sequence-model feature extraction, TSFM-vs-hand-fit significance harness), each with a concrete exit test using the repo's own `pairedBootstrapDiff` (n>=10 requirement) and `model-governance.js` contract-gating pattern.

sources.title: Chronos: Learning the Language of Time Series
sources.authors: Ansari, Stella, Turkmen, Zhang, Mercado, Shen, Shchur, Rangapuram, Pineda Arango, Kapoor, Zschiegner, Maddix, Wang, Mahoney, Torkkola, Wilson, Bohlke-Schneider, Wang (AWS AI Labs et al.)
sources.sample: 28 pretraining datasets, ~890K series, ~84B tokens; zero-shot Benchmark II = 27 held-out datasets / 190,674 series spanning 5-min to yearly frequency across energy/retail/web/finance/healthcare/transport
sources.key_result: T5-based 20M-710M models tokenize scaled/quantized values and train via plain cross-entropy (classification, not regression); on the 27-dataset zero-shot benchmark, Chronos has 'comparable and occasionally superior' performance vs methods trained specifically on those datasets — not uniformly better, and decisively better only on in-training-corpus (Benchmark I) sets. No series anywhere near 17 points is evaluated.

sources.title: A decoder-only foundation model for time-series forecasting (TimesFM)
sources.sample: O(100B) real pretraining time points, mostly 22k Google Trends queries (2007-2022) and Wikipedia pageviews (2012-2023), plus M4/Electricity/Traffic/Weather and 3M synthetic 2048-point series; zero-shot eval on Monash (18 datasets), Darts (8 single-series datasets), and Informer/ETT (4 datasets x 2 horizons)
sources.key_result: 200M-param decoder-only patch transformer is top model on Monash (beats N-BEATS 'within significance'), only 'within significance' of ARIMA/llmtime on Darts (not clearly better, authors note error bars aren't sharp with only 8 series), and best/near-best on ETT long-horizon. Critically, the paper states weekly-granularity pretraining series were judged 'not sufficiently long,' forcing context length down from 512 to 256 for that frequency — direct evidence these models are built and tested for regimes far longer than a 17-week season.

sources.title: Unified Training of Universal Time Series Forecasting Transformers (Moirai)
sources.authors: Woo, Liu, Kumar, Xiong, Savarese, Sahoo (Salesforce AI Research)
sources.sample: LOTSA pretraining corpus: 27.6B observations, 9 domains (Energy 59%, Transport 18%, Climate 15%, plus CloudOps/Web/Sales/Nature/Econ-Fin/Healthcare); weekly frequency is only 0.067% of LOTSA (18.5M obs); zero-shot probabilistic eval on 6 datasets (Electricity, Solar, Walmart, Weather, Istanbul Traffic, Turkey Power)
sources.key_result: 14M/91M/311M masked-encoder models with Any-variate Attention and a 4-component mixture output (Student-t/neg-binomial/log-normal/normal) get best-or-second-best zero-shot CRPS on 4/6 datasets, 'still close to best' on the other 2, versus baselines trained specifically on each target set. Structurally important: pretraining task sampling allows per-variate windows as short as 2 time-steps, because the model pools many short series cross-sectionally rather than depending on long individual context — this is the mechanism a Gridiron pilot can actually exploit.

sources.title: Lag-Llama: Towards Foundation Models for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
sources.authors: Rasul, Ashok, Williams, Ghonia, Bhagwatkar, Khorasani, Darvishi Bayazi, Adamopoulos, Riachi, Hassen, Biloš, Garg, Schneider, Chapados, Drouin, Zantedeschi, Nevmyvaka, Rish (ServiceNow/Mila et al.)
sources.sample: 27 datasets, 7,965 univariate series, ~352M training windows across energy/transportation/economics/nature/air-quality/cloud-ops; zero-shot + fine-tune + few-shot (20/40/60/80% of history) eval on 7 held-out datasets
sources.key_result: LLaMA-backbone decoder-only model tokenizes each timestep as a vector of lagged values (up to 52-week lag for weekly frequency) plus calendar covariates, requiring a context window at least as long as the largest lag used — structurally incompatible with a single 17-point season. Zero-shot average rank is 6.714 of 13 methods (worse than several from-scratch supervised baselines: PatchTST 5.643, N-BEATS/TFT 5.0); only after fine-tuning does it reach best average rank (2.786). Zero-shot claims for this model class do not reliably beat simple dataset-specific baselines without adaptation data.

candidates.candidate: Pooled cross-sectional TSFM challenger to the hand-tuned team-strength blend
candidates.fixes_finding: Team-strength ratings (nfl-team-strength.js) mix stale preseason priors with in-season data via a hand-tuned blend, not a principled state-space/Bayesian update.
candidates.mechanism: Stack every team's weekly stat (e.g. scoring margin, off_epa) across 32 teams x 5-6 seasons (2021-2026) from nfl_team_week_features into ~150-190 short (17-point) series and run zero-shot Chronos-Bolt-small / Moirai-Small over that pooled panel (exactly the 'many short series pooled' regime Moirai's own training uses per-variate windows as short as 2 steps for) to produce an independent forecast + calibrated quantile band for the same target the hand-tuned blend predicts, in-season, updated weekly instead of blended once from priors.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New service alongside server/services/nfl-team-strength.js; read nfl_team_week_features (server/db/schema/nfl-n-to-z.js:154), write a parallel `ts_foundation_team_signal` column, gate it in model-governance.js as a new blocked contract (mirroring the 'NFL/spread/team_efficiency' row already there) before it ever reaches nfl-gbm.js.
candidates.expected_value: Likely a wash-to-small-improvement on MAE for the earliest weeks (1-4) where the current hand-tuned blend leans hardest on stale priors and has the least in-season data — matches the exact regime (very short current-season history) TSFM zero-shot is built for; unlikely to help mid/late season once the current model has 8+ weeks of real data.
candidates.exit_test: pairedBootstrapDiff (server/services/backtest-significance.js:57, n>=10 paired weeks) on |TSFM forecast - actual| vs |current blend - actual| across weeks 1-4 of 2022-2025 held out; ship only if the bootstrap CI on the mean difference excludes zero in TSFM's favor and it survives the same no-look-ahead audit nfl-team-strength.js already requires.

candidates.candidate: TSFM predictive quantiles as an honest uncertainty check on player-props point estimates
candidates.fixes_finding: No conformal or otherwise honestly-calibrated uncertainty interval exists anywhere in the pipeline — margins/totals are point forecasts with an assumed-normal SD.
candidates.mechanism: Moirai's native mixture-distribution head (Student-t / negative-binomial / log-normal / normal) and Chronos's sample-path forecasting both produce full predictive distributions without hand-picking a dispersion parameter. Run either zero-shot on the pooled player_week_usage panel for a target stat (e.g. receiving yards) and compare its quantile spread against player-week-engine.js's current fixed/fit dispersion constants (e.g. TEAM_PASS_ATTEMPT_DISPERSION=47) via coverage (what % of actual outcomes fall inside the model's 80% interval).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/player-week-engine.js (heads/candidate_heads path) and server/services/nfl-props.js; compare against player_week_usage (server/db/schema/mlb-model-misc.js:257).
candidates.expected_value: A calibration diagnostic, not a pricing signal on its own — value is in exposing whether the current hand-fit dispersion under- or over-covers actual outcomes, which the project has never measured with an independent method.
candidates.exit_test: Empirical coverage of TSFM 80%/50% intervals on held-out weeks must be within +/-5 points of nominal to be usable at all; if it beats the current NB-dispersion coverage by a bootstrap-significant margin, register as a calibration-only feature under model-governance.js (never priced directly, per the sportsbook_quote contract's 'model-only; never report edge or ROI' precedent).

candidates.candidate: Zero-shot TSFM forecast as the real cold-start strategy for the fantasy weekly-learning loop
candidates.fixes_finding: The fantasy weekly-learning loop has never captured one forward snapshot in its life (cold-start: player_week_engine.heads is null week 1) — it needs a real cold-start/transfer strategy, not a silent no-op.
