candidates.mechanism: When engine.heads is null (the exact guarded branch at player-week-engine.js:573-574), fall back to a zero-shot TSFM forecast conditioned on the player's prior-season(s) weekly panel (or, for rookies, the position-pooled panel) instead of returning the empty/no-op response. This is literally the scenario the four papers were built for: forecasting a series with zero observations in the current context by transferring from a large pretrained corpus of related series.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/player-week-engine.js:573-600 (the `heads` null-guard block); source panel is nfl_player_week_features / player_week_usage.
candidates.expected_value: Directly replaces a silent no-op with a non-trivial forecast for exactly the Week-1 gap Nick has flagged; even a mediocre zero-shot forecast beats returning nothing, and this is the cheapest candidate in the set (hours, since it only needs inference on ~500-1000 short player-season series, not training).
candidates.exit_test: Backtest Week-1 forecasts for 2022-2025 (using only prior-season data, no current-season leakage) against the actual Week-1 outcome; ship if TSFM cold-start MAE beats the current no-op (i.e., beats using the population mean/replacement-level baseline) with pairedBootstrapDiff significance, and route through the existing 'NFL/fantasy_weekly/joint_event_state' contract in model-governance.js.

candidates.candidate: Pooled fine-tuned Gridiron TSFM as shared forecasting infrastructure
candidates.mechanism: Fine-tune (not zero-shot) a small open-weight model (Chronos-Bolt-small or Lag-Llama, both Apache-2.0, pip-installable, no paid API) on the full pooled nfl_team_week_features + nfl_player_week_features panel across all available seasons, producing one shared forecasting backbone usable for many downstream series (points scored/allowed, EPA, target share, snap share) instead of a bespoke hand-fit model per stat. This is the capability shift the papers demonstrate matters most: Lag-Llama's fine-tuned rank (2.786) vs zero-shot rank (6.714) shows the real gain is in adaptation, not raw zero-shot.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New standalone service (e.g. server/services/nfl-tsfm.js) consuming nfl_team_week_features/nfl_player_week_features; needs torch/gluonts-class deps added to the isolated research/ venv (research/requirements.txt currently has none) — inference-only fork stays out of the app runtime per the venv's own stated isolation policy.
candidates.expected_value: Highest-ceiling, highest-cost candidate: if it works, it replaces N separate hand-fit models with one general backbone; if it doesn't, it's a sunk research cost with no path to production since it was never gated. Should only be attempted after Candidates 1-3 show zero-shot is directionally useful at all.
candidates.exit_test: Fine-tuned backbone must beat both (a) its own zero-shot version and (b) the current hand-fit model on at least 3 of 5 target stats via pairedBootstrapDiff before any governance contract is opened for it; if it loses on a majority of stats, kill it rather than iterate further.

candidates.candidate: Foundation-model sequence encoding of drive-level play-by-play as an alternative to hand-built features
candidates.fixes_finding: 251,591 rows of play-by-play exist and are used only for hand-built features, never sequence models.
candidates.mechanism: Apply a patch-based sequence encoder in the TimesFM/Moirai architectural family (not necessarily the exact pretrained checkpoint, since PBP event sequences are a different modality than the models' training corpora) to drive-level event sequences (down/distance/yardline/play-type/EPA per play) to produce a learned drive-state embedding, compared against the current hand-built feature set feeding nfl-gbm.js.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-pbp.js (feature source) and server/services/nfl-gbm.js (consumer); this is architecture-inspired, not a direct application of any of the four pretrained checkpoints, so evidence strength is weak until a first experiment runs.
candidates.expected_value: Speculative — PBP sequences (categorical play types, discrete down/distance) are a poor match for continuous-valued TSFM tokenization/patching; this is the most exploratory candidate in the set and should be scoped as a 1-2 day feasibility spike before any real investment.
candidates.exit_test: A 2-day spike must show the learned embedding adds nonzero incremental signal (via a simple linear probe) over the existing hand-built features on a held-out season before further investment; otherwise drop it.

candidates.candidate: Standing TSFM-vs-hand-fit significance harness as a permanent audit tool
candidates.mechanism: Build a small reusable script that, for any Gridiron weekly-panel table, runs zero-shot Chronos/Moirai/TimesFM and reports pairedBootstrapDiff against whatever hand-fit model currently owns that stat — a standing 'is our hand-tuned model actually beating a free zero-shot baseline' check, not a one-off pilot.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New script under scripts/ (pattern: scripts/fit-weekly-ensemble.mjs, scripts/fit-team-volume-dispersion.mjs) that calls server/services/backtest-significance.js's pairedBootstrapDiff on any two forecast columns.
candidates.expected_value: Low-cost, high-durability: turns a one-time research finding into a recurring sanity check the project can rerun every time a hand-fit model is retrained, catching the next generation of 'we assumed our tuning beats a trivial baseline but never checked' the way FOUND already caught the ensemble's naive shrinkage.
candidates.exit_test: Harness is done when it can be pointed at nfl-team-strength.js's output and player-week-engine.js's output and produce a bootstrap CI report for each within one command; adopt permanently once it has run successfully on at least 2 stat tables.

repos.what_it_does: Official inference (and fine-tuning) library for Chronos and the faster Chronos-Bolt regression-head variant; pip-installable, open weights on HuggingFace, no paid API.
repos.adoption_path: pip install chronos-forecasting; call ChronosPipeline.predict() zero-shot on pooled nfl_team_week_features/nfl_player_week_features series for Candidates 1-3, 6.

repos.what_it_does: Official TimesFM inference library, 200M decoder-only patch transformer, open weights, no paid API.
repos.adoption_path: pip install timesfm; use as a second independent zero-shot forecaster in the Candidate 6 harness for cross-checking Chronos results.

repos.what_it_does: Moirai/Moirai-MoE inference and fine-tuning library; natively probabilistic (mixture-distribution head) and explicitly supports very short per-variate context windows.
repos.adoption_path: pip install uni2ts; primary model for Candidate 2 (quantile/coverage check) given its native probabilistic output, and for Candidate 4's fine-tuning experiment given its short-context tolerance.

repos.what_it_does: Lag-Llama inference and fine-tuning library; lag-index tokenization requires context >= largest lag used.
repos.adoption_path: Do not use zero-shot for weekly team/player panels (context requirement incompatible with 17-point series); reference only if a fine-tuning experiment (Candidate 4) specifically wants its documented few-shot-adaptation results as a baseline to beat.

do_not_do: Do not zero-shot any of these models on a single team's or player's raw in-season 17-week series expecting real skill — none of the four papers tests anything close to that short a series, and TimesFM's own authors judged multi-year weekly panels 'not sufficiently long.'

Do not use Lag-Llama zero-shot for weekly-frequency Gridiron series at all — its lag-based tokenization requires a context window at least as long as its largest lag index (up to 52 weeks for weekly data), which a single season cannot supply; reference its fine-tuning results only, don't call its zero-shot path.

Do not fine-tune the largest checkpoints (Chronos-Large 710M, Moirai-Large 311M) as a first step — start with Bolt-small/Moirai-Small for a same-night CPU-inference pilot; save fine-tuning of larger models for after Candidate 1-3 show zero-shot is directionally useful.

Do not feed any TSFM output into a market model (spread/total/props) without registering it as a blocked feature contract in model-governance.js first — this is the same discipline nfl-team-strength.js already imposes on itself for its own team-level aggregates, and a novel model type is not exempt.

Do not feed market-derived columns (implied_team_points, spread, total) into the TSFM's input panel — nfl-team-strength.js already documents that this exact move failed (0.995, CI 0.951-1.044) for the offseason model; the same circularity applies here.

Do not run any of this against the live production database or touch the fantasy-football-dashboard repo directly — it is read-only and currently capturing live Week 1 games; any pilot data pull should be an exported/copied snapshot of the relevant tables, not a live connection.

Do not report a TSFM prop-quantile pilot's calibration numbers as tradeable edge or ROI — per the existing sportsbook_quote contract precedent ('model-only; never report edge or ROI'), treat any prop-related TSFM output as a calibration diagnostic only until it clears full governance review.

Do not add torch/gluonts/transformers dependencies to the main app's package.json or server runtime — keep any TSFM experimentation confined to the isolated research/ venv, consistent with its stated 'no app-runtime dependency' policy.

result.label: N03: Transformer/sequence models on play-by-play
result.summary: Gridiron has a genuine sequential play-log table (nfl_play_by_play — 251,591 rows) but only ever folds it into per-team-week aggregates and never trains a sequence model on it; nfl-pbp.js says so explicitly ("raw plays never held in memory"). The literature splits cleanly: (a) discrete play-by-play models (Ötting's HMM, 71.5% out-of-sample play-call accuracy — the closest thing to a sequence-aware win on Gridiron's exact data type) and Guo's CS230 MLP (a documented negative result — 22% accuracy, model collapses to modal class — showing state-only, non-sequential nets fail on this task and explicitly recommending sequence models as the fix); and (b) tracking-data transformers (QB-GPT — GPT-style trajectory generation on Big Data Bowl x,y data, 20-35% exact-frame accuracy) which are architecturally instructive but not portable since Gridiron has no Next Gen Stats feed. Biro & Walker's MDP paper supplies the formal drive-as-sequence state definition (down, distance, field position -> terminal reward) that a real next-drive model needs. A GitHub scan found zero mature open-source implementations of sequence/transformer models on discrete NFL play-by-play (only tracking-data Kaggle notebooks and one 113-line RandomForest toy repo) — confirming this is a genuine new-capability build, not a port. Delivered: a concrete next-drive-outcome-from-play-sequence transformer spec with exact data contract against the existing nfl_play_by_play schema, 3 fix candidates tied to tonight's exact defects (ensemble signal collapse, drive-sim physics bugs, assumed-independent teaser correlation) and 3 new-capability candidates, each with cost/EV/exit test.

sources.title: Neural Network Models for Predicting NFL Play Outcomes
sources.sample: 2009-2018 Kaggle play-by-play, pass/run plays only, penalties removed; train 2009-2017 = 286,524 examples, test 2018 = 29,219 examples
sources.key_result: 1-6 layer MLP softmax classifiers over 8 outcome buckets (yardage bins + turnover + TD) using only pre-snap state features achieved ~22% accuracy and collapsed to predicting the modal 'zero yards' class almost universally; higher dropout diversified predictions but accuracy fell to ~19%. Author's own conclusion: none of the state-only models meaningfully predicted play outcomes, and explicitly recommends sequence models as future work since 'the effectiveness of plays earlier in the game may be an indicator of how effective they will be later.'

sources.title: Predicting play calls in the National Football League using hidden Markov models
sources.sample: Kaggle play-by-play 2009-2018, 318,691 plays / 5,052 team-game time series; train seasons 2009-2017 (2,302 games, 289,191 plays), test season 2018 (224 games, 29,500 plays)
sources.key_result: 2-state HMM per team, transition probabilities covariate-dependent (down, ydstogo, shotgun, no-huddle, score diff, goal-to-go, etc. via multinomial logit), fit by max likelihood via forward algorithm. Out-of-sample weighted-average accuracy 71.5% predicting run vs. pass, beating prior play-by-play-only studies (~67%) though below personnel-augmented studies (~75%). Per-team accuracy ranged 60.2% (Seahawks) to 77.9% (Patriots). This is the field's cleanest existence proof that modeling sequential/state structure (vs. i.i.d. plays) buys measured accuracy on exactly Gridiron's data granularity.

sources.title: Transformers can generate NFL plays: introducing QB-GPT
sources.sample: NFL Big Data Bowl 2021-2023 tracking data + public NGS highlights, 2018-2022 seasons: 47,991 plays, 870,559 player trajectories, 28.1M (x,y) coordinates, 3,190 players
sources.key_result: GPT-style decoder-only transformer (1.5M-7.7M params, 3-head attention, custom 'multi-temporal causal mask' letting a token attend across all 11 players' prior frames) generating 1-yard-grid/0.2s-frame player trajectories. Exact-token accuracy 20-35% depending on model size/horizon (top-5 ~50-70%), with accuracy dropping 40-50% between frame 5 and 10 as paths diverge; static/blocking players hit 60%+ while route-runners drop to 20-30%. Author calls the model 'raw' and reports adding attention layers gave minimal improvement over larger embeddings. Architecturally instructive (causal masking across a multi-agent sequence) but built on tracking data Gridiron does not have.

sources.title: A Reinforcement Learning Based Approach to Play Calling in Football
sources.sample: Illustrative toy MDPs plus a full football MDP with state s=(DOWN, DIST, LOS) and empirically-estimated yards-gained distributions conditioned on down/distance/field position (no explicit season/row count for the full football fit was given in the text extracted)
sources.key_result: Formalizes a drive as a self-contained ordered Markov Decision Process with terminal rewards (TD, FG, turnover) and solves for the optimal run/pass policy via value iteration / an ordered-MDP shortcut. Reports no held-out predictive-accuracy number (the contribution is the decision-theoretic formalism, not a forecasting benchmark) and explicitly assumes no within-drive play-history dependence ('the law of large numbers will dominate') — the exact assumption a play-sequence model would relax. Supplies the formal state/target definition a next-drive-outcome model needs.

candidates.candidate: Add a drive-sequence embedding as one new, structurally orthogonal ensemble component instead of another aggregate-stat input
candidates.fixes_finding: The NFL ensemble's blend is forecast ≈ 0.68 + 0.632·market — naive shrinkage toward the closing line, not real forecast combination; 20 components collapse to ~3 independent signals (server/services/nfl-ensemble.js)
candidates.mechanism: Train a small transformer/GRU encoder over each team's recent in-game play sequences (down/distance/field position/play type/yards/EPA per play, from nfl_play_by_play) to produce a fixed-size 'drive-dynamics' embedding per team-week, then feed that embedding into nfl-ensemble.js's blend() as one new component. Because it is derived from sequential within-game structure rather than another season-aggregate stat, it is far less likely to be collinear with the existing 20 components that FOUND shows collapse to ~3 independent signals — the collapse happens because every current component is some flavor of aggregate efficiency stat correlated with the same underlying team quality.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New service e.g. server/services/nfl-drive-sequence-embed.js reading nfl_play_by_play, producing one embedding per (season,week,team); wired into blend()'s component list in nfl-ensemble.js as a new named input alongside the existing 20.
candidates.expected_value: Only worth it if the embedding is measurably decorrelated from the existing components (an orthogonality check, not a leap of faith) — if it doesn't pass that check, it just becomes a 21st redundant input and this candidate should be abandoned before touching the live ensemble.
candidates.exit_test: Compute pairwise correlation (or PCA loading) between the new embedding's top components and the existing ensemble inputs on held-out weeks; require |r| < 0.3 against every current component's principal factor before it is allowed to enter blend(). Then require CLV on picks using the augmented ensemble to beat the current -2.28 pt mean CLV on a frozen 2026 holdout before promotion out of research mode.

candidates.candidate: Replace nfl-drive-sim.js's hand-coded play-selection policy with data-driven, state-conditioned transition probabilities fit on real play sequences
candidates.fixes_finding: Six physics bugs in server/services/nfl-drive-sim.js: turnovers handed to the wrong team's field position; policies receive half-game-clock seconds but are written for full-game-clock; the kneel rule is inverted and timeouts never decrement (leading team burns an entire half); away-team win-probability uses the home spread; flat 7-point post-OT home-field lump; season-remainder simulator has no halftime or overtime
candidates.mechanism: The Ötting HMM (state = down/distance/shotgun/score-diff/etc., covariate-dependent transition probabilities fit by max likelihood) and the Biro/Walker MDP (state = DOWN/DIST/LOS, empirically-estimated transition distributions, terminal rewards) both show that per-state play-outcome probabilities estimated directly from real play sequences are a cleaner and more auditable substitute for brittle rule-based simulator logic. Refitting the simulator's clock/kneel/timeout/turnover-spot logic against the actual sequential structure in nfl_play_by_play (rather than hand-written if/else rules) removes the class of bug where a rule is simply wrong (inverted kneel condition, non-decrementing timeouts) because the rule is replaced by a measured conditional probability that would show up as an obviously wrong distribution in nfl-espn-pbp.js's existing playDistributionAudit() if it were broken.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-drive-sim.js's policy functions; validate against the yardage-distribution comparison already implemented in server/services/nfl-espn-pbp.js's playDistributionAudit().
candidates.expected_value: The 6 listed bugs are individually cheap, mechanical fixes that should happen regardless (see do_not_do); the higher-value, higher-cost piece is specifically replacing the kneel/timeout/clock policy layer with a fitted state-transition model, since that is the part most prone to silently reintroducing similar bugs later.
candidates.exit_test: Re-run playDistributionAudit() after the fix; the simulated yardage distribution by play type must match the real ESPN-sourced distribution within existing tolerance, AND a targeted unit test must show a leading team with N timeouts and M seconds correctly runs out the clock without inverting the kneel decision (a scenario that should have caught the original bug and did not).

candidates.candidate: Estimate real same-game/same-week correlation structure from play-sequence data instead of assuming independence
candidates.fixes_finding: Teaser-leg and same-game correlation is assumed independent (server/betting/nfl/strategy/teaser-leg-rates.js) with no copula/dependence model, despite legs sharing a game — confirmed at line 624 (independent_joint: p*p) and line 651 ('INDEPENDENCE IS ASSUMED and the legs are not quite independent')
candidates.fixes_finding_note: kept as separate field name for schema compliance
candidates.mechanism: Rather than assuming independence or bolting on an ad hoc correlation bonus (which the file's own comment at line 577-580 warns against doing carelessly), fit an empirical dependence structure directly from drive-level sequences: for games sharing a week, estimate the joint distribution of margin-crossing-a-key-number events using the same kind of state-conditioned modeling in F2/N1, then derive a real rho (or a small copula) instead of the current p*p independence shortcut, honestly quantifying how far from independent the legs actually are rather than leaving the gap undocumented as an assumption.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/betting/nfl/strategy/teaser-leg-rates.js — replace independent_joint computation at line 624; the file's own function familyPairCorrelation (referenced near line 580) is the existing hook to extend.
candidates.expected_value: Low-to-moderate: the file's own comment already argues the observed 'rho' in the data is more a week-size artifact than true correlation, so this fix may conclude no correction is needed at all — the value is in replacing an assumption with a measured, cited number either way, which is itself worth doing given Nick's standing preference for measured over assumed behavior.
candidates.exit_test: Produce a measured correlation/copula parameter with a confidence interval on a frozen holdout; if the interval excludes 0 and materially changes the effective price of a multi-leg teaser, wire it in; if it does not, document the null result in the file's own comments (as it already partially does) and close this out as no_change_needed rather than adding unjustified complexity.

candidates.candidate: Next-drive-outcome-from-play-sequence transformer
candidates.mechanism: Small encoder-only transformer (4-6 layers, ~1-3M params, sized per the QB-GPT reference) over the sequence of plays observed so far in the current drive, causal-masked so play p only sees plays 1..p-1, with a play-index-within-drive positional embedding. Two calibrated heads per play index: (a) categorical next-play-type distribution, (b) 8-bucket yards-gained distribution (using CS230's own bucket scheme, since its negative result shows point-accuracy scoring collapses to the modal class), plus (c) a running drive-outcome head (P(TD)/P(FG)/P(turnover)/P(punt-or-downs)/P(half-end)) analogous to the terminal-state formalism in Biro & Walker.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Input entirely from the existing nfl_play_by_play table (server/db/schema/nfl-a-to-m.js:306-334), grouped by event_id, ordered by sequence, segmented into drives by offense/defense possession changes already present in the table; static context from the existing team-week feature blob in nfl-features.js. No new data source required.
candidates.expected_value: This is the direct concrete deliverable the research topic asked for; value is realized only if it beats two baselines that already exist in the codebase or literature: the CS230 majority-class floor (~22% play-outcome accuracy) and nfl-drive-sim.js's own hand-coded yardage sampler (comparable via the existing playDistributionAudit()).
candidates.exit_test: Year-based split matching Ötting's discipline (train seasons ≤ N-1, test season N) to avoid within-drive leakage; require calibration (reliability diagram / Brier score on the bucketed yards-gained head) to beat both the CS230 majority-class baseline and the current drive simulator's yardage distribution on the same held-out season before any live use is considered.

candidates.candidate: Play-sequence-derived team-strength embedding via state-space filtering
candidates.mechanism: Rather than blending season-aggregate stats (as nfl-team-strength.js's priorPointsByTeam() currently does with hand-tuned weights), feed the per-play EPA sequence within each game through a small sequence encoder to produce a per-game team-performance signal, then update team strength across weeks with a proper state-space/Kalman filter using these sequence-derived per-game signals as noisy observations of a latent strength state. This is new capability (a real Bayesian filter, not a hand-tuned blend) even though it touches the same table F1/N1 touch, and is deliberately scoped separately since it targets in-season strength updating rather than the ensemble's cross-sectional blend.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-team-strength.js's priorPointsByTeam()/blend logic (lines 88-131); nfl_play_by_play as the observation source per game.
candidates.expected_value: Speculative — no primary source read tonight reports a benchmarked state-space filter of this exact kind on NFL play data; value depends entirely on whether the sequence-derived signal is a better week-to-week strength observation than the current aggregate stats, which is untested.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest the Kalman-filtered strength ratings against the current hand-tuned blend on retrodicted point-spread accuracy for a held-out season; only proceed if the filtered ratings produce lower calibration error (not just lower RMSE, given the project's stated need for honestly-calibrated uncertainty) than the current blend.

candidates.candidate: Play-outcome distributional model as a genuinely calibrated alternative to point-estimate simulation inputs
candidates.mechanism: Use the same encoder from N1 to produce a full calibrated distribution over next-play yardage (not a point estimate) conditioned on drive history, and feed that distribution — rather than an assumed-normal point estimate — directly into nfl-drive-sim.js's per-play sampling step, replacing whatever fixed-form yardage distribution the simulator currently assumes with an empirically-fit, context-conditioned one.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: nfl-drive-sim.js's per-play yardage sampling logic, once N1's model exists; this candidate is a downstream consumer of N1, not independently buildable first.
candidates.expected_value: Contingent entirely on N1 succeeding; do not fund this before N1 clears its own exit test, since it has no independent data contract.
candidates.exit_test: Only run after N1 passes its exit test; then require the drive simulator's full-game score distribution (margin, total) to match the real empirical distribution at least as well as it currently does per playDistributionAudit(), with materially better calibration in the tails (explicitly the honesty-of-uncertainty gap FOUND lists project-wide).

do_not_do: Do not port QB-GPT's trajectory-transformer architecture as code — Gridiron has no Next Gen Stats/player-tracking (x,y) feed; only the causal-masking idea and rough parameter sizing are worth borrowing.

Do not train one pooled cross-team transformer/HMM for play-calling and treat it as sufficient — Ötting's own results show 60.2%-77.9% per-team accuracy spread with a shared architecture, so team identity needs to be a first-class conditioning input, not a one-hot afterthought.

Do not score any generative/distributional play model by point accuracy or RMSE — CS230's own failure mode (collapsing to the modal 'zero yards' prediction under accuracy optimization) is the textbook example of what that produces; score with calibration (Brier/reliability diagrams) instead.

Do not let a new sequence-model research track become a reason to defer the 6 already-diagnosed, cheap, mechanical bug fixes in nfl-drive-sim.js (inverted kneel rule, non-decrementing timeouts, half/full clock mismatch, wrong-team turnover field position, flat OT lump, missing halftime/OT) — fix those regardless of whether any model work proceeds.

Do not begin training before establishing a year-based (not random) train/test split on nfl_play_by_play — with 251,591 rows across an unknown number of seasons, a random split leaks information within the same drive and same team-season; copy Ötting's train-on-prior-seasons/test-on-next-season discipline.

Do not add a same-game-correlation 'bonus' to the teaser scanner without first measuring it — the file's own code comment (teaser-leg-rates.js line 577-580) already warns that the observed effect looks more like a week-size artifact than true correlation, and guessing a correction here risks making the pricing worse, not better.

result.label: N05 — Prediction-Market Mining: Polymarket Quote Tape
result.summary: Grepped the live repo before reading anything: Polymarket's tape today does exactly one thing (build the isotonic spread/total ladder crossing in server/services/polymarket-lines.js, surfaced descriptively in market-movement.js); it has zero references in nfl-ensemble.js or nfl-team-strength.js (never a forecast input), and polymarket_price_history is written on every capture but read back only as a two-point before/after diff — never as a time series. signal-latency.js pools Polymarket moves and ESPN moves into one undifferentiated MOVE_UNION rather than comparing the two series to each other. Four sources read in full ground the candidates: Dubach (2026, arXiv:2604.24366, 30.3B WebSocket events / 600-market panel) found public-feed trade-direction inference is chance-level (59% vs 50% baseline) and quoted spread balloons to 1,300-1,800bps exactly in the low-probability range where fantasy player-props live; Cheng, Yang & Zou (UCLA 2026, arXiv:2605.00864, 75M LOB snapshots / 173 NBA games) found single-market arbitrage is nearly extinct (7 episodes across 3,042 markets, 3.6s median life) and combinatorial arbitrage, though more frequent (290 episodes), is liquidity-capped to ~15 shares 77% of the time — the direct argument against building any execution bot at Gridiron's 30-minute poll cadence; Nechepurenko (2026, arXiv:2605.02287) surveys three 2026 informed-trading detection layers and supplies the Information Leakage Score, a market-level (price-trajectory-only, no wallet data) framework Gridiron's own price_history table can compute, while confirming wallet-level skill/wash detection needs on-chain fill data Gridiron does not collect; Wolfers & Zitzewitz (2004, NBER WP10504) is the founding result that market prices are usable near-real-time probability estimates, anchored on the Tradesports/Poindexter case of a price leading a Pentagon-insider news leak by hours — the original version of the lead-lag mechanism candidate 1 proposes for NFL. Net: do not build arbitrage execution (the literature says the edge isn't reachable at Gridiron's cadence); do build the three things the tape already supports — an exchange-vs-book lead/lag test, liquidity-weighted ladder crossing, and a market-implied player-availability signal feeding who-plays.js (fantasy-facing, per Nick's fantasy-over-betting priority) — plus two fix-tagged candidates that use the tape's vig-free mid-price as an external benchmark against tonight's devig/CLV defects.

sources.title: The Anatomy of a Decentralized Prediction Market: Microstructure Evidence from the Polymarket Order Book
sources.sample: Continuous tick-level archive of Polymarket's public order-book WebSocket feed: 30,287,264,368 events over 52 calendar days (2026-02-21 to 2026-04-15), 385,198 distinct market_ids, joined on a 28-day overlap window to 255,425,405 on-chain OrderFilled fills from the CTF Exchange V1 contract; pre-registered stratified 600-market panel (top-100 by volume + random-500).
sources.key_result: Trade-direction inferred from the public feed's change_side field agrees with authoritative on-chain trade direction only ~59% of the time (volume-weighted, bootstrap 95% CI [0.58,0.65]) versus a 50% chance floor and ~80% Lee-Ready accuracy on Nasdaq/NYSE; direction-dependent measures (effective spread, Kyle's lambda) flip sign 43-67% of the time across windows. Separately: quoted half-spread is ~400bps at mid-price [0.4,0.6] and balloons to 1,300-1,800bps below 0.10 probability (SF1); top-of-book carries a median 13.6% of cumulative top-10 depth vs a 10% uniform-grid null, with depth explained by duration, price level and volume and no residual time-to-close effect (SF2).

sources.title: Arbitrage Analysis in Polymarket NBA Markets
sources.authors: Guang Cheng, Jiaxin Yang, Haoxuan Zou (UCLA)
sources.sample: 75,088,497 Level-1 limit-order-book snapshots across 173 NBA games (2026-02-04 to 2026-03-04), polled every 3.6-5.5 seconds; 8.59 million combinatorial market-state observations across the same games for the Moneyline<->Spread cross-market test.
sources.key_result: Only 7 valid executable single-market arbitrage episodes survived across 3,042 markets after excluding 30 of 37 raw hits as post-game liquidity-withdrawal artefacts (median post-game spread 7,533bps vs 1,031bps in-game); median episode duration 3.6 seconds, below the polling cadence itself. Combinatorial Moneyline<->Spread arbitrage was more frequent (290 episodes, median 16s duration, median 101bps return) but 76.9% of episodes were capped to an average executable size of just 14.8 shares, and the theoretical 'Middle' double-payout jackpot was never realized once in the sample -- execution/liquidity, not detection, is the binding constraint.

sources.title: Per-Market Information Leakage and Order-Flow Skill: Two Methodological Lenses on Informed Trading in Decentralized Prediction Markets
sources.sample: Methodological comparison paper (not new primary data collection); surveys three 2026 approaches applied to Polymarket -- Mitts & Ofir's wallet-market anomaly screen (210,000+ wallet-market pairs, 2023-early 2026), Gomez-Cram et al.'s sign-randomization skill classifier (1.72M accounts / 210,322 markets / $13.76B volume, 2023-2025), and the author's own Information Leakage Score (ILS).
sources.key_result: Mitts & Ofir estimate ~$143M aggregate anomalous profit platform-wide; Gomez-Cram et al. classify 3.14% of accounts (54,477) as 'skilled winners' who, with market makers, capture >30% of platform gains, with 44% out-of-sample skill persistence (vs ~10% in published equity mutual-fund studies) -- but all wallet-level methods require on-chain fill/wallet data Gridiron does not collect. The paper's own contribution, ILS(M) = [p(T_news)-p(T_open)]/[p(T_resolve)-p(T_open)], is market-level and needs only a price trajectory plus a dated news anchor -- exactly the shape of data Gridiron's polymarket_price_history table already holds.

sources.title: Prediction Markets
sources.venue: NBER Working Paper 10504 / Journal of Economic Perspectives
sources.sample: Survey drawing on Iowa Electronic Markets and Tradesports/TradeSports contract data from the early-2000s political and current-events prediction-market literature.
sources.key_result: Foundational result that prediction-market prices behave as efficient, near-real-time probability estimates under the weak condition that the marginal trade is rational, illustrated by the Tradesports Poindexter/DARPA contract: price moved from 40 to 80 within minutes of a Pentagon-insider news leak, hours before the story broke publicly -- the original documented case of a prediction-market price leading a news event, which is the mechanism candidate 1 below proposes measuring systematically for NFL. The paper explicitly cautions that thin trading and risk-premium effects degrade price-level trust near the 0/1 extremes, a warning Dubach (2026) later quantifies precisely for Polymarket (the SF1 longshot spread premium).

candidates.candidate: Exchange-vs-sportsbook lead/lag test: does Polymarket's implied line move before or after the free ESPN reference line?
candidates.mechanism: signal-latency.js's MOVE_UNION currently pools espn_line_moves and polymarket_line_moves into one undifferentiated series and only asks whether Gridiron's own news signals lead that pooled log. Split the union back into its two sources and reuse the exact nextMoveAfter/priorMoveBefore pattern already proven there, but symmetrically: for every Polymarket move, find the next ESPN move on the same game within a window, and vice versa. Report median/mean lead hours each direction and a win-rate (fraction of matched pairs where Polymarket moved first). This operationalizes Wolfers & Zitzewitz's founding claim (and Dubach 2026's caution about when to trust a level) as a testable, per-market latency measurement rather than an assumption.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New function in server/services/signal-latency.js (or a sibling module reusing its exported helpers), e.g. marketLeadLag({windowHours}), reading polymarket_line_moves and espn_line_moves separately instead of through MOVE_UNION. Surface alongside the existing signalLeadTimes() output in the same /market-movement or research-lab panel.
candidates.expected_value: If Polymarket systematically leads by even 1-2 hours on a subset of games, that is actionable execution-timing information (bet the book before it catches up) with zero new data collection -- but per Nick's standing priority this is betting-secondary; treat a positive result as a candidate for the execution-edge gate, not a new forecasting claim.
candidates.exit_test: Run on the full accumulated polymarket_line_moves + espn_line_moves history (already logged since late August per polymarket-lines.js's own header comment). If matched-pair count is under ~30 per direction, report as infrastructure only, exactly the honesty threshold signal-latency.js already uses (sufficient_evidence: directional.length >= 30). If lead-rate in either direction is not statistically distinguishable from 50/50 win-rate at n>=30, kill it -- the two series are just describing the same information with different noise.

candidates.candidate: Liquidity-weighted spread-ladder crossing (depth/spread-aware isotonic fit)
candidates.mechanism: polymarket-lines.js's isotonic() and crossing() take only {x price-point, p probability} pairs and weight every ladder point equally. Dubach (2026) SF1 shows quoted half-spread is ~400bps at mid but 1,300-1,800bps in the tails -- so the widest, least-informative ladder points currently pull the isotonic fit exactly as hard as the tightest ones. Add an optional weight parameter (e.g. w = 1/spread or w = min(bid_size, ask_size)) already sitting unused in polymarket_quotes, and re-run the pool-adjacent-violators fit as a weighted PAVA (a standard, well-known variant).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/polymarket-lines.js: extend isotonic(values, {increasing}) to isotonic(values, weights, {increasing}) using weighted block-merging (a small, well-tested change to the existing PAVA loop), and pass bid_size/ask_size/spread from polymarket_quotes through crossing(). Consumers (polymarketMovement, market-movement.js, signal-latency.js's MOVE_UNION source) need no interface change beyond the new optional weights.
candidates.expected_value: Directly improves the one thing Polymarket already feeds Gridiron (the implied spread/total number itself), for free, using data already captured every 30 minutes -- this is a strict quality upgrade to a live-shipped feature, not a new surface to maintain.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest: for games with enough polymarket_line_moves history, compare weighted vs. unweighted crossing() output against the eventual closing sportsbook line (already logged in nfl_line_snapshots) via mean absolute error. If weighted crossing is not measurably closer on a paired sample, the unweighted version was already fine and this is not worth keeping as a second code path.

candidates.candidate: Market-implied player-availability signal for who-plays.js, sourced from season-long player-prop tick history
candidates.mechanism: polymarket.js already ingests ~1,800 NFL player-stat threshold markets (parsePolymarketProp) and writes every tick to polymarket_price_history, but nothing reads that table back as a series -- only a two-point before/after diff (polymarket.js:397-400). who-plays.js is explicitly built as a ranked-precedence join of official report > beat-reporter signal > snap-count inference, documented as designed to accept additional sources with conflicts reported rather than silently resolved. A sudden, sustained collapse in a player's own season-long yardage/TD prop mid-price (relative to that player's own trailing baseline, not an absolute threshold) is a market-aggregated, continuously-updating usage-share signal that can arrive before a beat reporter's practice-report tweet.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New function in a sibling module (e.g. server/services/polymarket-availability.js) reading polymarket_price_history joined to polymarket_markets (kind='threshold_prop', player, stat), computing a rolling z-score of recent price change; feed the result into who-plays.js's existing multi-source join as a new low-precedence, market-derived source (below beat-reporter, per its own stated precedence rule), and separately surface divergences in news-fantasy-impact.js where it already resolves player projections via buildPlayerWeekEngine.
candidates.expected_value: This is the one candidate that serves fantasy directly (Nick's standing priority: fantasy edge beats betting edge). Even a handful of true early-warning hits per season on waiver-relevant usage changes would be valuable, and it costs nothing to collect -- the ticks are already being written. Genuine risk: player-prop markets are thin (Dubach's SF1 spread-premium result applies exactly here), so a price move may just be noise from one large trade rather than aggregated information; the exit test below is designed to catch that.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest against nfl_news_signals + player_week_usage: for each week, check whether a flagged prop-price collapse preceded (by >=6 hours) a verified news signal or an actual usage drop in player_week_usage, versus how often it preceded nothing. If the false-positive rate on thin/low-volume markets swamps the true-positive rate, restrict to markets above a minimum captured liquidity/volume floor (the same floor polymarketCost() already applies) before shipping to who-plays.js live.

candidates.candidate: Book-vs-exchange disagreement as a confidence gate, not a blend input, on nfl-ensemble.js output
candidates.mechanism: nfl-ensemble.js has zero references to Polymarket (grepped) -- the exchange-implied line has never touched the forecast. Given F02 (the ensemble is already naive shrinkage toward the close, 20 components collapsing to ~3 independent signals), the correct new use of Polymarket here is explicitly NOT to add it as a 21st linear-blend weight, but to compute the gap between the sportsbook consensus margin and the Polymarket isotonic-crossing implied margin as a standalone disagreement metric, and use large disagreement as a flag to widen Gridiron's own uncertainty / suppress confidence on that game rather than to move the point forecast at all.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New read-only function, e.g. bookExchangeDisagreement(gameId) in a small new module, comparing polymarketMovement()'s crossing output to the current sportsbook consensus already computed in nfl-market.js/boardFor; wire the output into whatever surface currently reports forecast confidence (e.g. nfl-cover-calibration.js or the auto-picks confidence field) as a downweight multiplier, never as an additive term to the margin itself.
candidates.expected_value: Low-cost, and explicitly structured to avoid repeating F02's mistake (another correlated component folded into a broken blend). Expected value is bounded -- if book and exchange never meaningfully disagree, this does nothing; if they do disagree on a subset of games, it may cheaply flag exactly the games where Gridiron's own model should defer to the market rather than compound naive shrinkage with a second naive input.
candidates.exit_test: Compute the disagreement metric across a season of paired observations; if it is uncorrelated with CLV outcome on the affected games (i.e., high-disagreement games are not the ones where Gridiron's picks fare worse), drop it -- it would be measuring noise, not information.

candidates.candidate: Use Polymarket's structurally vig-free mid-price as an external benchmark to resolve which devig method is correct
candidates.fixes_finding: No real devig (de-vigorization) method comparison exists; probabilities are extracted with one ad hoc approach.
candidates.mechanism: prediction-markets.js's own header states the mechanism precisely: 'Polymarket charges no trading fee... Prices... are already probabilities -- no vig to strip.' That means Polymarket's (bid+ask)/2 on a liquid game or first-half market is a probability estimate that required no devig assumption at all, and can be used as an external check on which of Gridiron's devig implementations (grepped from nfl-devig.js: Shin's method with bisection-solved insider fraction z, vs. any proportional-splitting fallback) best reproduces an independently-priced probability on the same event, rather than picking a devig method by theory alone.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New comparison function reading polymarket_quotes (best_bid, best_ask on game moneyline/spread markets) alongside nfl-devig.js's shinNoVig output on the paired sportsbook line for the same game/time, restricted to Dubach's own depth/spread quality gate (Polymarket half-spread under, say, 500bps -- i.e., outside the 1,300-1,800bps tail-market zone) so the comparison isn't itself corrupted by a wide, uninformative exchange quote.
candidates.expected_value: Directly answers a defect FOUND flagged as fully open (no real method comparison exists) using data already collected, at zero incremental API cost -- Polymarket ingestion is already running. The honest caveat: this only works on liquid, mid-priced game-level markets, not props (where the spread-premium tail makes the Polymarket 'ground truth' itself untrustworthy per SF1), so it cannot resolve the devig question for player props.
candidates.exit_test: If Shin's method and the naive proportional split both land within Polymarket's own bid-ask band on a season's worth of matched game-level observations, the devig-method question is close to moot for game lines specifically (differences are within noise) and effort should redirect to props, where no such external check exists.

candidates.candidate: Cross-check one of the five disagreeing CLV implementations against a Polymarket-derived, source-independent closing reference
candidates.fixes_finding: Five independent, disagreeing CLV (closing-line-value) implementations exist over four different tables with different math and sign conventions.
candidates.mechanism: Because Polymarket's implied closing line (via the already-shipped isotonic crossing in polymarket-lines.js) is computed independently of every sportsbook feed Gridiron's CLV code reads from, it is a natural, already-collected reference point for auditing whether the five CLV implementations agree with each other on sign and rough magnitude when graded against the SAME independent closing number, rather than against each implementation's own preferred sportsbook table.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: A one-off audit script (not a new production surface) pulling each of the five CLV computations' outputs for a shared sample of games, alongside polymarketMovement()'s final pre-kickoff crossing value for the same games, to check directional and magnitude consistency -- feeds directly into the F04 CLV-unification fix effort as an independent check rather than a sixth implementation.
candidates.expected_value: Cheap, one-time diagnostic value for the F04 consolidation work already scoped tonight; not a standing feature, so keep it as a throwaway audit script rather than new maintained surface area.
candidates.exit_test: If all five CLV implementations already agree in sign/magnitude against the Polymarket reference, this confirms F04's consolidation is a pure code-cleanup task with no hidden data disagreement; if one implementation disagrees in sign from the rest against this independent reference, that is the one to distrust first when picking a canonical CLV definition.

do_not_do: Do not build a live Polymarket/Kalshi/sportsbook execution arbitrage bot or scanner intended to place trades. Cheng et al. (2026) found only 7 single-market episodes across 3,042 NBA markets at a 3.6-5.5 second poll cadence, with median episode life of 3.6 seconds -- Gridiron polls Polymarket roughly every 30 minutes, two orders of magnitude slower, so there is no reachable execution edge at Gridiron's cadence.

Do not fold a raw Polymarket implied-line level into nfl-ensemble.js's existing blend as one more linear-shrinkage input. F02 already shows the ensemble is naive shrinkage toward the close with 20 components collapsing to ~3 independent signals; adding Polymarket's level the same way adds a 21st correlated component to a blend already proven not to combine information. Candidate N05-4 above uses disagreement as a confidence gate instead, deliberately avoiding this trap.

Do not attempt wallet-level informed-trader detection (skill classifiers a la Gomez-Cram et al., wash-trade screens a la Mitts & Ofir). Gridiron has no on-chain fill/wallet data; Dubach (2026) shows the public feed alone cannot even recover trade direction reliably (59% vs 50% chance baseline), and building the on-chain scraping infrastructure these methods require is a materially different, costlier system than 'features from data already collected.'

Do not treat Polymarket's mid-price as vig-free 'ground truth' without a depth/spread gate. Dubach's SF1 shows quoted half-spread reaches 1,300-1,800bps exactly in the low-probability range where fantasy-relevant player props live -- a 'no-vig' price with a 15-18% spread band around it is not a precise probability.

Do not chase the combinatorial Moneyline+Spread 'Middle' double-payout jackpot as a strategy. It was never realized once in Cheng et al.'s full sample of 290 combinatorial episodes -- it is a theoretical curiosity, not an EV source.

Do not build a full Information-Leakage-Score (ILS) surveillance pipeline for every Polymarket market as a first step. Nechepurenko's own framework needs a reliably dated public-news anchor per market; Gridiron's nfl_news_signals timestamps are close but not proven equivalent to the 'public disclosure' anchor ILS requires -- validate the anchor-join quality on a small sample before generalizing.

result.label: N04 — LLMs as direct numerical forecasters
result.summary: Read four primary papers in full (Halawi et al. 2024, Schoenegger et al. 2024, Paleka et al. 2025 "Pitfalls", Hsieh/Fu/Chen 2024 RTF) plus one non-peer-reviewed sports-domain data point (Recall's NFL Arena live-prediction analysis). Core picture: retrieval + reasoning + trimmed-mean aggregation gets an LLM system to within ~0.03 Brier of a human forecasting crowd (Halawi), and a cheap median-of-diverse-LLMs "silicon crowd" is statistically indistinguishable from a 925-person human crowd on general-knowledge questions (Schoenegger) — but the honest-critique paper (Paleka et al., read in full) documents that most of this apparent skill is inflated by logical leakage, unreliable date-restricted retrieval, piggybacking on the very human forecasts being "beaten," and improper metrics (accuracy is not a proper scoring rule). None of the four papers evaluate on a specialized numeric sports domain — that gap is real and unclaimed. Grepping the actual Gridiron codebase turned up a decisive fact: Claude is already wired in via server/services/claude.js, but its one betting-adjacent use (server/services/nfl-ai-replay.js) explicitly forbids it from producing a probability ("Do not... estimate a win probability"), and decision-basis.js states outright "Claude is a risk gate, not a source of invented probabilities." So "LLM as direct numerical forecaster" is not merely unbuilt in Gridiron, it is a boundary the codebase's own prior author deliberately drew — every new-capability candidate here is designed to respect that (shadow/backtest-only, never wired to live staking) unless explicitly flagged otherwise. One actively-maintained MIT repo (Metaculus/forecasting-tools, cloned and read, last commit 3 days ago) supplies two directly portable, small pieces of infrastructure Gridiron has zero of today: a CalibrationAdjuster interface (constant-shift/logistic/decision-tree/k-means recalibration) and a Percentile/NumericDistribution schema for eliciting full CDFs instead of point estimates.

sources.title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
sources.authors: Danny Halawi, Fred Zhang, Chen Yueh-Han, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley)
sources.sample: 5,516 curated binary questions across 5 platforms; 3,762 train / 840 val / 914 test, test restricted to post-June-2023-cutoff questions
sources.key_result: Optimized retrieval+reasoning+fine-tune system scores Brier 0.179 vs human crowd 0.149 (gap 0.03), accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%; well-calibrated (RMS 0.42 vs crowd 0.38) despite raw LMs (best baseline 0.208) being poorly calibrated zero-shot; system beats the crowd specifically when the crowd itself is uncertain (0.3-0.7 range: 0.199 vs 0.246) but underperforms when the crowd is highly confident.

sources.title: Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
sources.authors: Philipp Schoenegger, Indre Tuminauskaite, Peter S. Park, Philip E. Tetlock
sources.sample: Study 1: 12-model LLM crowd vs 925 human forecasters on 31 binary questions from a live 3-month Metaculus tournament; Study 2: 186 primary + 186 updated forecasts from GPT-4 and Claude 2
sources.key_result: Preregistered: LLM crowd (median Brier 0.20) beats the 0.25 no-info baseline (p=.026) and is statistically indistinguishable from the human crowd (0.19), p=.850; only 3/12 individual models beat the crowd median; models show significant acquiescence bias (mean forecast 57.35 vs ~45% actual Yes-rate) yet the aggregate is far better calibrated (CI 0.041) than any individual model (up to 0.212); exposing GPT-4/Claude 2 to the human median improves their Brier score but naive updating still underperforms a simple average of the two (p=.011, p=.001).

sources.title: Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
sources.authors: Daniel Paleka, Shashwat Goel, Jonas Geiping, Florian Tramèr (ETH Zürich / ELLIS / MPI Tübingen)
sources.sample: Re-analysis of published forecasting benchmarks including Halawi et al. 2024, Tao et al. 2025, ForecastBench (6,402 questions)
sources.key_result: Finds ≥3.8% of Halawi et al.'s test set and ≥10% of a comparable dataset are logically trivial to forecast given how/when they were selected (logical leakage); demonstrates concrete date-restricted search-engine leakage (a 2020-restricted 'jan 6' query surfaces Jan-6-2021-relevant results); shows GPT-4o leaks post-cutoff knowledge under jailbreak; documents that benchmark-optimal forecasting strategy on correlated question sets is confident betting on a shared latent variable, not honest calibration; shows accuracy is not a proper scoring rule and Brier scores are not comparable across differing question base rates.

sources.title: Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
sources.authors: Elvis Hsieh, Preston Fu, Jonathan Chen (UC Berkeley)
sources.sample: 201 Manifold Markets questions resolving strictly after the April 15, 2024 retrieval cutoff
sources.key_result: Hierarchical ReAct agent (GPT-4o planner + tool-equipped sub-agents with Google Search and a Python interpreter for numerical simulation) scores Brier 0.169 vs crowd 0.172 (near-tied) and calibration index 0.0129 vs crowd's 0.0101, vastly beating raw GPT-4o (0.265, worse than random guessing); authors explicitly state the eval is 'popular questions rather than domain-specific' and do not claim generalization to a specialized numeric domain.

sources.title: NFL Arena: Can LLMs predict football outcomes? (recall.net)
sources.sample: 6 frontier LLMs, 1,500+ predictions, 3 live NFL games (n too small to generalize, flagged explicitly)
sources.key_result: Every pregame favorite pick (Chiefs, Ravens, Lions) lost; in-game predictions mostly parroted Vegas odds; several models never flipped their pick even as the trailing team built a double-digit 4th-quarter lead; most-confident models were most wrong. Cited only as an informal do-not-do warning, not as evidence to build on.

candidates.candidate: Retrieval-augmented Claude retrodiction to seed player_week_engine.heads on cold start, instead of a silent no-op
candidates.fixes_finding: the fantasy weekly-learning loop has never captured one forward snapshot in its life (cold-start: player_week_engine.heads is null week 1)
candidates.mechanism: Direct transplant of Halawi et al.'s pipeline (structured question + background + resolution criteria -> LM reasoning -> point forecast) for the one case Gridiron structurally cannot solve with historical rows: no prior weeks exist. When heads is null, run one bounded Claude call using only context already ingested (depth chart, injury designation, opponent, offensive scheme) to seed a point estimate + stated confidence, logged with a timestamp before the week's games.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/player-week-engine.js:574 (the `if (!engine || !heads) return {...}` fallback path) gets a new branch that calls a new server/services/nfl-cold-start-forecast.js using the existing server/services/claude.js client; result is cached, never silently dropped again.
candidates.expected_value: Turns a documented structural no-op into a real, falsifiable, timestamped forecast — the cheapest possible fix to a defect that currently means the model has literally zero signal for exactly the players (rookies, trades, injury returns) fantasy managers most need help with.
candidates.exit_test: After 4 weeks of cold-start cases (~15-30 players), is Claude-seeded heads.season_to_date MAE on actual PPR points lower than the current fallback baseline (position/opponent average), using the same baselineGateTest pattern already in server/services/nfl-props.js:459? If not, revert to the no-op — do not ship an LLM guess that is worse than the existing dumb fallback.

candidates.candidate: LLM-elicited percentile bands for player props, replacing the point estimate, using the Percentile/NumericDistribution schema pattern
candidates.fixes_finding: Player props are point-estimate projections, not distributions — no negative-binomial/hierarchical/calibrated model exists
candidates.mechanism: Not 'LLM does the arithmetic' (Schoenegger and Paleka both show LLMs are poorly calibrated and round-number-biased on raw numeric output) but a hybrid: Claude reasons qualitatively over matchup/game-script/injury context (already surfaced by gamescript.js, role-scenario-engine.js) to adjust a statistical base distribution's percentiles (10/25/50/75/90), stored in the CDF/Percentile schema pattern from Metaculus/forecasting-tools rather than a single number.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-props.js: projectWeek() (~line 546) and propView() (~line 57), which the file's own header comment (lines 6-9) already flags as using 'a point estimate... [rather than] the simulated distribution'.
candidates.expected_value: Converts the project's one area of genuine measured skill (props, 2+ TD Brier skill +27%) from a point estimate into a calibrated distribution, enabling real edge quantification against a market line instead of a single over/under guess.
candidates.exit_test: Compare RMS calibration error of the new percentile bands vs. the existing point-estimate + assumed-normal-SD approach on the same backtest sample used by nfl-props.js:propAccuracy (line 266). If Claude-adjusted percentiles don't beat assumed-normal calibration, kill it.

candidates.candidate: An actual independent LLM-reasoning forecaster as a 4th, decorrelation-tested ensemble leg — not another market-shrinkage term
candidates.fixes_finding: The NFL ensemble's blend is forecast approx 0.68 + 0.632*market — naive shrinkage toward the closing line, not real forecast combination; 20 components collapse to ~3 independent signals
candidates.mechanism: Schoenegger's median-of-diverse-prompts 'silicon crowd' approach, cheaply reproduced with 3-5 differently-prompted Claude calls reasoning over context NOT already encoded in the other 20 components (weather, travel, coaching-staff motivation notes), trimmed-median aggregated (Halawi found trimmed mean/median beats naive mean), added only after passing an explicit correlation gate against the existing ensemble's residuals.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-ensemble.js (1423 lines) — built and validated entirely offline against historical seasons; per the hard rule, this file is NOT touched in production while Week 1 games are being captured live.
candidates.expected_value: Contingent — real only if it demonstrably decorrelates from the existing 3 independent signals; Schoenegger's own crowd only tied (never beat) the human benchmark on general-knowledge questions, so this could easily add cost with zero edge.
candidates.exit_test: Does the new component's forecast correlate <0.3 with the existing ensemble's Brier-weighted residual, AND does adding it (offline, backtested on a held-out season) improve mean CLV vs. the current -2.28 baseline? If either fails, do not merge into the live blend.

candidates.candidate: A bounded, cheap weekly 'Claude-as-forecaster' shadow pilot with a preregistered trial registry and evaluation harness
candidates.mechanism: Direct port of Halawi's retrieval+reasoning+trimmed-mean pipeline, deliberately scoped small: 5-10 game lines or 10-15 prop lines per week, Claude produces a probability + rationale in a fixed schema BEFORE the line closes (never after, closing the exact 'logical leakage'/'piggybacking on human forecasts' failure modes Paleka et al. document), logged to a new trial table, scored against closing-line CLV and Brier only (never accuracy, per Paleka et al.'s proper-scoring-rule finding). Runs strictly in shadow mode, never wired into nfl-ai-replay.js's stake decisions — respecting the codebase's own existing stated boundary that 'Claude is a risk gate, not a source of invented probabilities' (decision-basis.js).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New table (e.g. nfl_llm_forecast_trial) + new offline script server/services/nfl-llm-forecaster.js, read-only against existing injury/weather/props tables, write-only to the new trial table — literally the trial registry the FOUND list says doesn't exist, but scoped to this one narrow use rather than the full 21-model historical search.
candidates.expected_value: First real, falsifiable answer to whether direct LLM forecasting adds anything Gridiron's existing pipeline doesn't already have, at near-zero engineering risk since it never touches a live decision path.
candidates.exit_test: After 4-6 weeks (~30-50 logged trials, preregistered sample size before the season's remaining weeks), is Claude's shadow Brier score better than a naive 'always predict the market's implied probability' baseline, and does its CLV differ meaningfully from the existing ensemble's -2.28? If it is statistically indistinguishable from parroting the closing line, kill it — that would mean it replicates the ensemble's own known defect rather than fixing anything.

candidates.candidate: Port Metaculus/forecasting-tools' CalibrationAdjuster module as a generic post-hoc recalibration diagnostic over any existing Gridiron point forecast
candidates.mechanism: forecasting_tools/calibration_adjustment/ (constant-shift, logistic-recalibration, decision-tree, k-means adjusters) trains a correction from a dataframe of (forecast, resolution) pairs and exposes adjust()/test(holdout). Port the small abstract interface and 1-2 concrete adjusters (no heavy deps, pure offline analysis) and feed it Gridiron's own historical (prediction, outcome) pairs already produced by nfl-props.js:propAccuracy and the market-lab reports.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: MIT-licensed, 78 stars, last commit 2026-09-09 (verified via git clone), forecasting_tools/calibration_adjustment/calibration_adjuster.py — self-contained offline script, no server dependency, run against server/services/nfl-props.js's existing backtest outputs.
candidates.expected_value: Cheapest candidate on this list; gives the first principled (not ad hoc) over/under-confidence diagnostic for any of Gridiron's five disagreeing CLV implementations or the props module, reusable by F2/F3/N1 above.
candidates.exit_test: Does a fitted logistic/isotonic recalibration reduce held-out Brier score by more than 0.005 on nfl-props.js's own backtest sample? A clean 'no adjustment needed' result is a valid, cheap answer, not a failure.

candidates.candidate: Claude-as-fantasy-forecaster pilot: calibrated start/sit probability calls scored like a forecasting tournament, benchmarked against player-week-engine's own implied probability
candidates.mechanism: For a bounded set of close start/sit calls each week (players within a small margin of a positional cutoff), pose a well-formed binary Halawi/Schoenegger-style question ('does Player A outscore Player B this week') using only context already surfaced by role-scenario-engine.js, boom-bust.js, gamescript.js as the background field (zero extra retrieval cost). Score with Brier against actual results, benchmarked against the probability implied by player-week-engine's own median-projection gap.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New logging path alongside server/services/player-week-engine.js and server/services/boom-bust.js; results land in the same trial table proposed in N1 so both pilots share one preregistered evaluation harness instead of a sixth ad hoc scoring method.
candidates.expected_value: Directly serves Nick's stated top priority (fantasy edge beats betting edge) and targets the project's own strongest area; a positive result is an immediately actionable weekly edge, a negative result is a clean answer to 'should I just ask Claude who to start' that stops the question from recurring.
candidates.exit_test: Over 6+ weeks (~60-90 logged pairwise calls, preregistered before the comparison begins per Halawi/Schoenegger precedent and Paleka et al.'s warning against post-hoc benchmark construction), is Claude's Brier score statistically better (bootstrap CI excludes zero) than player-week-engine's own implied probability on the same calls? If not, stop — do not re-run the comparison on a different week slice looking for a win.

repos.what_it_does: Python framework for building Metaculus-tournament forecasting bots: forecast_bots/forecast_bot.py (abstract ForecastBot wrapping research->reasoning->prediction), cp_benchmarking/benchmarker.py (scores N bots against the Metaculus community prediction, with a built-in sample-size honesty note: '100-200 questions is a decent starting point... even with 100 there is ~30% of the worse bot winning if there are not large skill differences'), calibration_adjustment/ (CalibrationAdjuster abstract base + constant-shift/logistic/decision-tree/k-means implementations), data_models/numeric_report.py (Percentile/NumericDistribution schema eliciting a full CDF, with an explicit max-PMF cap to prevent overconfident distributions).
repos.adoption_path: Port the small, self-contained CalibrationAdjuster interface (candidate N2) and the Percentile/NumericDistribution schema idea (candidate F2) directly; treat the full ForecastBot/Benchmarker scaffolding as reference-only since it is Metaculus-API-specific and not directly attachable to Gridiron's stack.

repos.license: unspecified in gh metadata (not independently verified against repo LICENSE file)
repos.what_it_does: Minimal example wiring an LLM to answer one Metaculus forecasting question end to end.
repos.adoption_path: Read before building N1/N3 for the minimal-wiring pattern; do not copy code verbatim given unconfirmed license.

do_not_do: Do not let any LLM-elicited probability feed live staking/bet sizing directly — the codebase already enforces this boundary itself (nfl-ai-replay.js's prompt literally says 'Do not... estimate a win probability'; decision-basis.js states 'Claude is a risk gate, not a source of invented probabilities'). Every candidate here must stay shadow/backtest-only until it passes its preregistered exit test.

Do not touch server/services/nfl-ensemble.js, nfl-drive-sim.js, or nfl-props.js in production while Week 1 2026 games are being captured live — build and validate F1-F3 entirely offline against historical seasons first, per the hard read-only rule on this repo.

Do not compare any LLM forecast against a benchmark or question set that was generated or filtered after the outcome was known (Paleka et al.'s 'logical leakage' and 'back-generated question' failure modes) — every trial must be logged with a timestamp before the line closes or the game starts, never reconstructed retroactively.

Do not let Claude see the current market/crowd line before making its initial forecast in any pilot — compare only afterward, to avoid the 'piggybacking on human forecasts' circularity Paleka et al. document.

Do not declare any pilot a success or failure from a handful of games or weeks — the informal Recall NFL result (6 models, 3 games, 0-for-3 pregame) shows how wildly small samples can mislead in either direction; use the preregistered sample sizes specified in each exit_test.
Do not build a sixth independent CLV computation for these pilots — reuse or first reconcile the five existing disagreeing CLV implementations rather than adding another.

Do not use raw accuracy as the primary metric for any LLM forecasting pilot — Paleka et al. show accuracy is not a strictly proper scoring rule; use Brier and/or log score, reported alongside calibration.
Do not spend on paid retrieval/news APIs for any of these pilots (hard rule: no paid API calls) — condition strictly on data Gridiron already ingests.

result.label: N02: Graph Neural Networks for Team/Player/Matchup Modeling (no tracking data)
result.summary: Gridiron has zero graph representation of anything today (grepped every server/services/*.js for "graph" — only version-string cruft, no actual graph structure), and no player-tracking table exists in the schema, which rules out the literature's best football-specific GNN result (Xenopoulos & Silva's 9% NFL loss reduction requires frame-level X/Y/velocity tracking Gridiron doesn't have). But three read-in-full papers (NBA roster-graph GATv2-TCN; soccer player-team heterogeneous graph transformer; NBA team-graph GCN+RF) all build graphs from exactly the data Gridiron already has — box scores, lineups, event counts, snap/target shares — and each beats a matched non-graph baseline (RMSE 2.222 vs 2.414 TCN; 52.19% vs weaker baselines on 3-class soccer outcome; 71.54% vs 66.90% plain-GCN on NBA win/loss). Gridiron's own tables are a close structural match: nfl_player_feature_vectors and nfl_team_feature_vectors are literally versioned feature-vector stores (hand-engineered, never learned/embedded) that could become GNN node-feature inputs directly, nfl_depth and nfl_roster_snapshots supply natural graph edges (position-group adjacency, roster co-membership over time), and nfl_snaps/nfl_props give the target labels. Five candidates below specify concrete, gradable builds — extending the props module (the one area of genuine measured skill) with a roster-attention graph, adding a team-graph signal alongside (not replacing) nfl-team-strength.js, using a GNN's natural inductive property to warm-start rookies/backups instead of the null-heads cold start, building a heterogeneous player-team-game graph as a new capability relevant to the teaser-leg independence assumption, and a lighter depth-chart propagation model for post-injury role redistribution. One repo (joewilaj/nbaGNNs, MIT, cloned and inspected) supplies a working team-graph-plus-point-spread-edge precedent to borrow the idea from, not the code; one repo (UnravelSports) is flagged avoid because it requires tracking data.

sources.title: Who You Play Affects How You Play: Predicting Sports Performance Using Graph Attention Networks With Temporal Convolution
sources.sample: NBA 2022-23 regular season, 691 games, 92 game days, 582 active players / 30 teams; per-game-day complete graph over both teams' active (10+ min) rosters, 13 box-score features/node + learned team+position embeddings; chronological 50/25/25 train/val/test split
sources.key_result: GATv2-TCN: RMSE 2.222, MAE 1.642, CORR 0.508 on next-game-day player stat forecasting, beating best graph baseline ASTGCN (RMSE 2.293, CORR 0.453) and non-graph TCN/DeepVAR/N-BEATS (RMSE 2.414/2.896/5.112). Separately reports a same-day Underdog Fantasy higher/lower case study at 35/59 (59.3%) correct — n=59, one day, not a validated edge, cited only as an honest limitation.

sources.title: Player-Team Heterogeneous Interaction Graph Transformer for Soccer Outcome Prediction
sources.authors: Lintao Wang, Shiwen Xu, Michael Horton, Joachim Gudmundsson, Zhiyong Wang
sources.sample: WyScout Open Access Dataset, 1,941 matches across 7 competitions (SPA/ENG/ITA/GER/FRE top divisions 2017/18 + 2016 Euros + 2018 World Cup), 3,293 players, 154 teams, 3.25M events; 80/20 chronological split per division
sources.key_result: HIGFormer: 52.19% overall 3-class (win/draw/lose) accuracy, best across divisions vs MLP/RNN/P-Graph/T-Graph/DraftRec-adapted baselines; 57.96% win, 68.25% lose, ~37% best-case draw (hard ceiling reported by all methods). Ablation: removing the team-level interaction network barely hurts accuracy; removing the player-level interaction network hurts much more — player graphs carry more signal than team graphs built from the same event-count data. Graph built entirely from lineup/event counts, no player tracking used.

sources.title: Enhancing Basketball Game Outcome Prediction through Fused Graph Convolutional Networks and Random Forest Algorithm
sources.sample: NBA 2012-2018 regular seasons, Kaggle NBA Enhanced Box Score dataset, 14,758 team-game rows, 30 teams, 6 season-specific models, 70/10/20 split
sources.key_result: GCN+RF (RF reduces 44 box-score features to 3, then GCN classifies win/loss on a team-node graph with edges = recent-games-played): 71.54% average accuracy vs plain GCN 66.90%, GCN+LASSO 70.70%, non-graph LR+RF 71.17%, SVM+RF 70.94%. Honest caveat: the graph topology itself bought only ~0.4-0.8pp over the best non-graph classifier on the same reduced features — most of the gain came from RF feature selection, not the GNN. Authors' own stated limitation: homogeneous graph, no player/coach nodes, box-score aggregates only (no tracking), explicitly call for player-node graphs as future work.

sources.title: Graph Neural Networks to Predict Sports Outcomes
sources.venue: IEEE International Conference on Big Data 2021 (arXiv:2207.14124)
sources.sample: NFL rushing-yards regression + CS:GO round win-probability; complete player graphs built from raw per-frame tracking coordinates (X/Y, velocity, displacement) for the NFL task specifically
sources.key_result: 9% (NFL) and 20% (CS:GO) test-loss reduction vs a permutation-invariant vector baseline on identical input features — the strongest football-specific GNN number found, but the NFL result requires frame-level tracking data. Cited as a boundary/contrast case: Gridiron has no tracking table in its schema (confirmed by grep), so this specific result is not reachable and the transfer plan must come from sources 1-3 (roster/lineup/box-score graphs) instead.

candidates.candidate: Roster-attention graph for player props: per-week complete graph over each team's active offensive skill-position roster (GATv2-style), node features from nfl_player_feature_vectors + nfl_snaps, predicting next-week target/carry/yardage distributions
candidates.mechanism: Following Luo & Krishnamurthy's construction exactly: build one complete graph per team per week over players with offense_snaps_pct above a floor (from nfl_snaps), node feature = that player's current nfl_player_feature_vectors.vector_json plus a learned position embedding, run one GATv2 layer so each player's forecast is a weighted function of his teammates' current-week vectors (captures target/carry redistribution when a teammate's role changes, which a per-player point estimate cannot see), then a small temporal layer over the last N weeks feeding the existing props model's stat heads.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New Python sidecar service (or a documented offline batch job) reads nfl_player_feature_vectors + nfl_snaps + nfl_roster_snapshots, writes a new nfl_player_graph_embeddings table (mirroring the shape of nfl_player_feature_vectors: season, week, player_id, version, vector_json), which server/services/nfl-props.js consumes as one additional input feature alongside its current point-estimate features — additive, not a replacement.
candidates.expected_value: Props is Gridiron's one area of genuine measured skill (2+TD Brier +27%); this targets its actual blind spot — usage is not independent across a roster, and a graph model is the only architecture family in the literature built specifically to capture that without tracking data. If it moves prop calibration at all it moves the highest-value surface in the whole system.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest on held-out 2024/2025 weeks: does adding the graph embedding as a feature to the existing prop model reduce Brier score or calibration error vs the point-estimate-only baseline, on the same weeks, same players? If it does not beat the existing model by a pre-registered margin (not just look plausible), drop it rather than keep it as an unvalidated extra ensemble head — Gridiron already has 20 unvalidated ensemble components in the betting model; do not add a 21st here.

candidates.candidate: Team-as-graph GCN power-rating signal: teams as nodes, edges weighted by recent-game point differential and market spread history, node features from nfl_team_feature_vectors, output a learned embedding fed into nfl-team-strength.js as one more input
candidates.mechanism: Follows the PMC10217531 (box-score-only team graph, 71.54% vs 66.90% plain-GCN) and joewilaj/nbaGNNs (team-node + point-spread-edge, node2vec + GNN regression) patterns. A GCN over a graph where the edge weight between two teams is their historical scoring-margin and market-spread history produces a team embedding that captures opponent-adjusted strength through message passing rather than the current hand-tuned preseason/in-season blend.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Reads nfl_team_feature_vectors (season, week, team, vector_json) plus schedule/result history already in the DB; writes a new nfl_team_graph_embeddings table of the same shape. server/services/nfl-team-strength.js (currently a hand-tuned blend of stale preseason priors and in-season data — a separate agent's fix-bucket finding, not claimed as fixed here) would consume this as one candidate input among others, evaluated the same way any new signal must be before it's trusted.
candidates.expected_value: Moderate — PMC10217531's own honest result shows the graph topology bought less than 1 point of accuracy over a good non-graph classifier on the same features, so this should be scoped as a cheap additional signal to test, not a headline rebuild. Worth doing because it shares infrastructure with Candidate 1 (same Python sidecar, same node2vec/GAT toolchain) rather than as a standalone bet.
candidates.exit_test: Does the team-graph embedding, added as one feature to a simple spread-prediction regression, reduce out-of-sample RMSE vs the same regression without it, on a holdout season? If the improvement is within noise of adding any other single hand-built feature, do not promote it into nfl-team-strength.js — this candidate exists to test whether team graphs earn their complexity budget here, and the honest answer from the literature is 'maybe not much.'
