candidates.candidate: Inductive graph warm-start for rookies/backups: use a GNN's inductive property (embedding a brand-new node by aggregating its graph neighbors) to generate a non-null initial feature vector for players with zero games played
candidates.mechanism: GNNs (GAT/GCN) naturally embed a node with no training history by message-passing from its neighbors at inference time — this is a structural property none of Gridiron's current point-estimate models have, since they all require the player's own history. Build the roster graph (edges: nfl_depth pos_rank adjacency + nfl_player_roster_events transitions) so a rookie or new backup's initial embedding is a weighted function of (a) the departing/injured starter's own recent feature vector and (b) the rest of the position group's current vectors, instead of a null/default.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/player-week-engine.js currently leaves engine.heads null at cold start (a fix-bucket finding from tonight — noted here only as the surface this candidate is relevant to, not claimed as fixed by this agent, since fixing the never-snapshot no-op is a different, cheaper task). This candidate is the architectural answer to 'what should fill that null on day one' once the underlying snapshot bug is fixed by whoever owns it: nfl_depth + nfl_player_roster_events supply the edges, nfl_player_feature_vectors of the departing player and position-mates supply the neighbor features.
candidates.expected_value: High leverage relative to cost — this does not need a full deep-learning training run; a single fixed or lightly-fit attention formula (weighted average by depth-chart proximity and recency, following GATv2's scoring function directly) over existing tables can be implemented and tested in JS without a new Python dependency, unlike Candidates 1/2/4.
candidates.exit_test: For every rookie/backup's first 3 games in a held-out season, compare the graph warm-start estimate against (a) a null/league-average default and (b) the eventual actual performance. If the graph warm-start is not closer to actual than the league-average default on a meaningful fraction of cases, it is not worth the added table and code path — fall back to the simple default.

candidates.candidate: Heterogeneous player-team-game graph for same-game joint modeling (DFS stacking / teaser-leg dependence), following HIGFormer's player+team node types
candidates.mechanism: A heterogeneous graph with player nodes, team nodes, and a shared game-context node lets message passing propagate game-environment effects (pace, script, weather) jointly to every player in that game, producing correlated (not independent) output distributions as a byproduct of the architecture rather than a fitted correlation coefficient. This is a different mechanism from the existing pairwise fits in server/services/correlation.js (which is a real, working pairwise model, not the defect) — it is new infrastructure relevant background for whoever eventually addresses the explicit 'INDEPENDENCE IS ASSUMED' comment in server/betting/nfl/strategy/teaser-leg-rates.js, but this candidate does not itself touch or claim to fix that file.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Would read nfl_player_feature_vectors, nfl_team_feature_vectors, and game context (weather/pace tables already in schema) to build per-game heterogeneous graphs; output would be a joint sample or correlation matrix stored analogously to prop_correlation_estimates, for consumption by DFS/simulation code, not a direct edit to teaser-leg-rates.js.
candidates.expected_value: Weak/speculative on current evidence — HIGFormer's own ablation (source 2) shows team-level interaction modeling adds little once player-level interaction is present, and this candidate is the most architecturally complex of the five. Sequence it last, after Candidate 1 (player-level graph) is validated, per the do-not-do list.
candidates.exit_test: Compare the graph-implied same-game correlation for a handful of well-known pairs (e.g. a team's RB1 and its own defense/total, a game's two starting RBs) against the actual historical joint rates already computed in teaser-leg-rates.js (rho ≈ -0.044 reported there). If the graph model's implied correlations are not directionally consistent with those already-measured historical rates, the model is not ready to inform anything — this is a sanity check before any staking or correlation-modeling decision uses it.

candidates.candidate: Depth-chart propagation graph for post-injury role redistribution, as a learned alternative/companion to the hand-built conservation rules in role-scenario-engine.js
candidates.mechanism: Build a graph per team-week from nfl_depth (pos_rank, pos_slot) where edges connect adjacent depth-chart slots within a position group and cross-position edges connect RB/WR/TE within the same offense (since target volume redistributes across position groups, not just within one). When a nfl_player_roster_events or nfl_injuries entry marks a player out, propagate a share of his last-known nfl_player_feature_vectors volume to his graph neighbors weighted by depth-chart proximity, rather than the current fixed conservation-of-volume split rule.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/role-scenario-engine.js already implements a hand-built version of this idea (conservedTeamVolume, buildPlayerScenarios) without any graph structure or learned weights — this candidate proposes an alternative redistribution model to run side-by-side and compare, not a rewrite of that file. Reads nfl_depth + nfl_injuries + nfl_player_feature_vectors.
candidates.expected_value: Moderate — like Candidate 3, this can be built as a fixed-weight graph propagation formula in plain JS (no new Python/PyTorch dependency needed) and directly A/B tested against role-scenario-engine.js's existing conservation rule on real historical injury events, which are already logged in nfl_injuries.
candidates.exit_test: For every season/week where a starter's nfl_injuries report_status went to 'Out', compare the graph-propagation redistribution prediction against role-scenario-engine.js's current conservedTeamVolume output and against the actual following-week snap/target shares. If the graph version is not closer to actual on a clear majority of cases, do not merge it — keep the existing hand-built rule.

do_not_do: Do not chase tracking-data-dependent GNN architectures (Big Data Bowl player-trajectory style, or the specific NFL task in Xenopoulos & Silva 2021 that needs per-frame X/Y/velocity) — Gridiron has no player-tracking table anywhere in its schema (grepped and confirmed), so that entire sub-literature, and repos built on it (UnravelSports, kyota-Masu/nfl_gnn_pretrain, krishnaura45/nfl-player-movement-prediction, any NFL Big Data Bowl Kaggle GNN notebook), is not reachable and should not be adopted or ported.

Do not stand up a separate ad hoc Python/PyTorch environment per candidate — Candidates 1, 2, and 4 all need the same graph-learning toolchain; build one shared sidecar service and share it, rather than letting this become three more one-off dependencies for a codebase that already has an ensemble collapsing 20 components to 3 independent signals.

Do not use any of these candidates, or their proximity to player-week-engine.js or teaser-leg-rates.js, as cover for closing out the actual FOUND defects in those files (the null-heads cold-start no-op, the assumed-independence teaser math) — those are fix-bucket work for a different agent; nothing here repairs them, it only builds adjacent new capability.

Do not treat the Luo & Krishnamurthy Underdog Fantasy case study (35/59, 59.3%, one day) as evidence a graph-based props model would print money — it is a single-day demo with no significance test and should not be cited as a strategy result, only as a proof that the pipeline runs end to end.

Do not build the heterogeneous player-team-game graph (Candidate 4) before the simpler player-only roster graph (Candidate 1) has been validated — HIGFormer's own ablation shows the team-level interaction component adds little once player-level interaction is modeled; building the complex version first risks spending weeks on the part of the architecture the literature says matters least.

Do not let a graph model's output enter nfl-team-strength.js, the props module, or any staking decision without the same pre-registered backtest discipline the 21-model historical search never got tonight — each candidate has an explicit exit test above; treat 'looks plausible on a few examples' as a fail, not a pass.

repos.what_it_does: Verified by cloning and reading the file tree/README (not just the description): builds an offense/defense node graph (edges = Four Factors box-score interaction stats from basketball-reference) and a separate Vegas point-spread graph (teams as nodes, spread history as edges), runs node2vec for initial embeddings, then feeds both into one of four GNN layer types (DCNN, GIN, ARMA, GAT via Keras/spektral) to regress NBA/NCAA score differential, backtested against-the-spread. No aggregate accuracy number is committed to the repo (predictions are per-game-day .xls files) — do not repeat any 'beats the spread' claim about it without independently verifying.
repos.adoption_path: Do not depend on the code (2021-era Keras/spektral/node2vec stack is stale). Borrow the graph-construction pattern — team-as-node, point-spread-history-as-edge-weight, box-score-derived node features — as the template for Candidate 2 (team-graph GCN), built fresh against nfl_team_feature_vectors and Gridiron's existing odds/spread tables in a current toolchain (e.g. PyTorch Geometric).

repos.what_it_does: Verified via its own README: converts player positional/tracking data (Kloppy-format soccer providers — Sportec, SkillCorner, PFF, Metrica, StatsPerform, Tracab, SecondSpectrum, HawkEye, Signality — and NFL Big Data Bowl tracking datasets for American football) into PyTorch Geometric / Spektral graph representations for GNN pressing-intensity and formation-identification models.
repos.adoption_path: Not adoptable for this topic — every graph construction in the library is built from player tracking/positional data, which Gridiron does not have and this research explicitly excludes. Listed only so it is not independently rediscovered and pursued later without this note.

result.label: RL for Drive-Sim Play-Calling and Bet-Sizing/Portfolio
result.summary: Read 4 primary sources in full plus 2 supporting sources on RL for play-calling and bet-sizing. Honest finding: what academic papers call "RL for football" is almost always exact tabular value iteration/dynamic programming over small MDPs (Biro & Walker; the fourth-down risk-preference paper), not deep RL — and it works precisely because it doesn't need function approximation. Deep RL genuinely works in finance (Zhang/Zohren, 50 futures contracts 2011-2019, beats a momentum baseline under realistic costs) but only in continuously-rebalanceable, liquid, multi-instrument, years-of-data settings that are nearly the opposite of NFL betting's ~15-33 decisions/season. Real sports-betting Kelly data (Beggy et al., Wharton 2023) shows Full Kelly bankrupts 100% of realistic backtest scenarios even capped at 20%, while a static quarter/half-Kelly plus a strict EV threshold already captures most of the achievable value at low bet volume — bounding how much an adaptive/RL staking layer can realistically add. Codebase recon (read-only) found Gridiron's existing staking math (teaser-staking.js closed-form Kelly) is already rigorous — the gap is a static fraction and no overfitting-detection gate, not a broken Kelly formula — and found a ready-made OPE data source (server/migrations/027_decision_tape.js's append-only decision tape) that no current code uses for off-policy evaluation. 6 candidates delivered: 3 "fix" (drive-sim physics prerequisite, CLV consolidation before using it as a reward signal, same-game correlation measurement before any portfolio treatment) and 3 "new" (value-iteration play-calling policy replacing hand-tuned curves in nfl-sim-policy.js, a tightly bounded contextual-bandit Kelly-fraction pilot capped at 0.5x with a shadow-mode exit test, and — the highest-leverage item — an offline off-policy-evaluation/PBO-style overfitting-check harness built on the existing decision tape, required to gate BOTH other new candidates before either can go live). 8-item do-not-do list, grounded throughout in why RL overfits in this domain (multiple testing, reward/cost leakage, sample-size mismatch, action-space mismatch, backtest-only validation).

sources.title: A Reinforcement Learning Based Approach to Play Calling in Football
sources.venue: arXiv / Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports
sources.sample: NFL play-by-play, 2017-2018 training / 2019 validation (exact play/game counts not disclosed)
sources.key_result: Exact tabular value iteration (not deep RL) over an MDP with state=(down,dist,LOS[,score,time]) and terminal-only rewards; utilities correlate 0.95 with Yurko et al.'s Expected Points model; a value-iteration play-caller beats historically-observed coaching in 1,000 simulated drives. Authors' own honest caveats: assumes league-average offense/defense ("obviously a false assumption"), ignores play-to-play dependence, late-game values "not trained to convergence," explicitly wrong for run-heavy teams (names Tennessee/SF/Baltimore).

sources.title: Learning Risk Preferences in Markov Decision Processes: an Application to the Fourth Down Decision in the National Football League
sources.sample: NFL play-by-play 2014-2022 (9 seasons) via nflfastR/nfl4th
sources.key_result: Inverse optimization infers a risk-preference quantile τ per coach; real coaches are significantly more risk-averse than the nfl4th win-probability-optimal bot, more so in their own territory, with league risk tolerance rising 2014→2022 and correlating positively with team performance. Honest limitations: state space drops score/timeouts/time for tractability, no team-specific transitions (data too sparse), selection bias in rarely-observed 'go for it' states.

sources.title: An Investigation of Sports Betting Selection and Sizing
sources.authors: Beggy, J., Kim, D., Mucaj, K., Nordell, J. (advisor Wyner)
sources.venue: Wharton Sports Analytics Student Research Journal
sources.sample: 121,507 candidate soccer betting lines (top-5 European leagues), 10,275 selected bets at 5% EV threshold, 369 at 10% threshold, 79,860 at 2.5% threshold
sources.key_result: Full Kelly (even capped at 20% of bankroll) went bankrupt in 100% of realistic scenarios; Half Kelly also ruined at the 5% baseline threshold. Quarter Kelly at 5% threshold profited +$40,374/10,275 bets; Half Kelly at the stricter 10% threshold profited +$115,097/369 bets (~80% annualized over 11 years). At the loosest 2.5% threshold every strategy, including all Kelly fractions, went bankrupt. Uses naive average-of-books devig, no formal devig comparison.

sources.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Trading
sources.authors: Zhang, Z., Zohren, S., Roberts, S.
sources.venue: Journal of Financial Data Science / arXiv (Oxford-Man Institute)
sources.sample: 50 most liquid futures contracts (25 commodity, 11 equity index, 5 fixed income, 9 FX), daily data 2011-2019, Pinnacle Data Corp CLC database
sources.key_result: DQN/Policy-Gradient/A2C with volatility-scaled continuous position sizing beat a classical time-series-momentum baseline in aggregate under realistic transaction costs up to 25bp (~$3.5/contract). But results are asset-class dependent (their Fig. 3): equity-index and fixed-income Sharpe ratios solidly positive, commodity and FX Sharpe ratios straddle zero with wide variance — RL works, but not uniformly, and only in a continuously-rebalanceable, liquid, multi-instrument, years-of-daily-data regime very unlike NFL betting.

sources.title: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting
sources.authors: Bailey, D., Borwein, J., López de Prado, M., Zhu, Q.J.
sources.sample: Methodology paper (combinatorially symmetric cross-validation), simulation-based demonstration
sources.key_result: Introduces PBO via CSCV: repeatedly split backtest trials into in/out-of-sample halves and measure how often the in-sample-best strategy ranks poorly out-of-sample; PBO rises sharply as the number of strategy variants tested on the same data grows. Full PDF blocked (403); summarized from a secondary hosted copy plus standard citation record — flagged as not read in full.

sources.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Cryptocurrency Trading: Practical Approach to Address Backtest Overfitting
sources.sample: 10 cryptocurrencies, out-of-sample window 2022-05-01 to 2022-06-27 (~2 months spanning two crypto crashes)
sources.key_result: Formulates backtest-overfitting detection as a hypothesis test on trained DRL agents and rejects agents that fail it. Quoted result: "less overfitted deep reinforcement learning agents have a higher return than that of more overfitted agents, an equal weight strategy, and the S&P DBM Index." Only abstract/landing text recovered (PDF unparseable), so not counted as read in full despite a real quoted result.

candidates.candidate: Freeze all RL/value-iteration training against nfl-drive-sim.js until its 6 physics bugs are fixed and regression-tested
candidates.fixes_finding: The drive simulator has 6 real physics bugs: turnovers handed to the wrong team's field position; policies receive half-game-clock seconds but are written for full-game-clock; the kneel rule is inverted and timeouts never decrement; away-team win-probability uses the home spread; a flat 7-point post-OT HFA lump distorts the key-number distribution; the season-remainder simulator has no halftime or overtime.
candidates.mechanism: Any RL/DP agent trained against a buggy transition model learns to exploit the bugs (e.g. an inverted kneel rule that runs the clock the wrong way, or turnovers that land at the wrong yard line) rather than real football strategy. This launders bad physics into a policy that LOOKS learned/sophisticated while being worse than the current hand-tuned curves it would replace.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-drive-sim.js and server/services/nfl-sim-policy.js (kneelDecision line 291, timeoutPolicy line 316) — add a regression suite asserting kneel/timeout/turnover-position/clock-unit correctness against 2023-2025 real drives before nfl-sim-learn.js's expectedPointsSurface or any value-iteration module is allowed to read from the engine.
candidates.expected_value: Not separately quantifiable — this is a gate, not an edge. Without it, candidate N1 below has negative expected value.
candidates.exit_test: Replay 500 real 2023-2025 drives through the corrected engine; kneel/timeout/turnover-position error rate must be 0% (previously silently wrong on all four), and simulated season-length OT rate must fall within the real NFL's ~5-6% OT rate, which the season-remainder simulator currently cannot produce at all.

candidates.candidate: Consolidate the 5 disagreeing CLV implementations into one canonical, sign-consistent computation before using CLV as any RL/bandit reward signal
candidates.fixes_finding: Five independent, disagreeing CLV (closing-line-value) implementations exist over four different tables with different math and sign conventions.
candidates.mechanism: Any bet-sizing RL/bandit needs one unambiguous scalar reward per settled bet. Feeding it five disagreeing CLV definitions means a staking policy could show 'positive CLV' under one convention and negative under another — the reward signal itself would be unfalsifiable, so no online learning or off-policy evaluation could distinguish a genuinely improving policy from noise.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: grep hits across server/betting/nfl/strategy/spread-probabilities.js, margin-distribution.js, and related CLV call sites — consolidate into one server/betting/nfl/clv.js used everywhere before N2's bandit reward is wired to it.
candidates.expected_value: Prevents any staking-RL pilot from reporting a fake edge; itself has no direct betting EV.
candidates.exit_test: Run the same 100 historical settled bets through all 5 existing CLV computations; if they disagree in sign on more than a small fraction of bets, staking-RL work is blocked until the consolidation ships and re-passes this test at 0% sign disagreement.

candidates.candidate: Measure real same-week/same-game leg correlation before attempting any multi-bet portfolio-allocation RL
candidates.fixes_finding: Teaser-leg and same-game correlation is assumed independent (server/betting/nfl/strategy/teaser-leg-rates.js) with no copula/dependence model, despite legs sharing a game.
candidates.mechanism: Portfolio-level bet sizing (RL or classical Markowitz-style) needs a real covariance/dependence structure across the week's positions; optimizing against an assumed-zero correlation when legs actually share a game computes a fictitious diversification benefit, so any resulting allocator will systematically overbet correlated same-week combinations.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/betting/nfl/strategy/teaser-leg-rates.js already has a same-game pair-count check (familyPairCorrelation, finds 0 same-FAMILY pairs) but that is not the same measurement as correlation between two DIFFERENT legs bet in the same week — extend margin-distribution.js's joint-outcome output to estimate realized same-week leg correlation from history.
candidates.expected_value: May legitimately come back near zero given current bet volume (15-33/season) — this fix could correctly conclude the portfolio-RL idea (not itself proposed here) isn't worth building yet, which is itself valuable information.
candidates.exit_test: Compute realized correlation among same-week decided legs from history; if statistically indistinguishable from 0 at current volume, document that and do not build any portfolio-level optimizer on top of it.

candidates.candidate: Replace nfl-sim-policy.js's hand-tuned fourth-down/two-point/kneel/timeout curves with a policy solved by exact value iteration over the corrected simulator's own transition model
candidates.mechanism: Biro & Walker (2021, read in full) show that exact tabular value iteration over an MDP with a directly-estimable transition model correlates 0.95 with a published Expected Points model and beats historical coaching in simulated drives, using only (down,dist,yard,score,time) state — no deep network needed. Gridiron's nfl-sim-learn.js already computes expectedPointsSurface() from Monte Carlo trials of the (once-fixed) simulator itself; that is the exact ingredient backward induction needs. This replaces logistic-curve heuristics that are informed by published results but never solved against Gridiron's own model.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/nfl-sim-value-iteration.js consuming nfl-sim-learn.js's expectedPointsSurface and nfl-drive-sim.js's (post-F1-fix) transition dynamics; backward-induction results replace the hand-set thresholds in nfl-sim-policy.js's fourthDownByWinProbability, twoPointDecision, kneelDecision, and timeoutPolicy.
candidates.expected_value: Not a betting edge by itself (the drive-sim already disclaims beating the market) — value is a provably-optimal-under-its-own-model decision layer instead of an unverified hand-tuned one, and a Gridiron-native benchmark analogous to nfl4th's finding that real coaches under-go-for-it.
candidates.exit_test: Run both the new value-iteration policy and the existing hand-tuned policy through the SAME corrected simulator on a held-out 2023-2025 sample; the learned policy must weakly dominate the hand-tuned one in expected win probability at matched states — if it does not beat its own predecessor under its own model, the implementation has a bug and does not ship.

candidates.candidate: Bounded contextual-bandit multiplier (not full RL, not full Kelly) on top of teaser-staking.js's existing closed-form Kelly, capped at 0.5x and validated in shadow mode for a full season before any live effect
candidates.mechanism: Beggy et al. (read in full, real data) show Full Kelly bankrupts 100% of realistic backtest scenarios even capped at 20% of bankroll, while a static Quarter/Half-Kelly with a strict EV threshold already captures most of the achievable value at low bet volume. Rather than a full RL policy that could rediscover this the hard way, a Thompson-sampling bandit over a small discrete set of multipliers {0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5}× the existing closedFormKelly output only ever asks 'how much of the already-safe Kelly fraction to use this week,' bounded by nfl-policy.js's existing minExpectedReturn/probabilityHaircut gates.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/betting/nfl/strategy/teaser-staking.js's closedFormKelly/kellyForOutcomes output becomes the bandit's base arm; server/services/nfl-policy.js gains a new frozen policy version gating bandit-selected fractions the same way requireCalibratedAdvantage gates picks today.
candidates.expected_value: Low-to-modest: at only 15-33 tickets/season there are too few decisions per year for online learning to reliably beat the static fractional-Kelly rule the honest literature (Beggy et al.) already shows captures most of the value — flag this explicitly rather than oversell it.
candidates.exit_test: Run the bandit in shadow mode (zero real staking effect) for one full season (>=15 decided tickets); its chosen fraction must beat static Quarter-Kelly's realized log-growth by a margin outside the bootstrap confidence interval before it is allowed to affect a real stake — if it can't clear that bar in shadow mode, retire it.

candidates.candidate: Build an offline off-policy-evaluation (OPE) + PBO-style overfitting-check harness on Gridiron's existing decision tape, required to gate N1 and N2 before either goes live
candidates.mechanism: Every source read for this brief that discusses honest evaluation (Bailey et al.'s PBO/CSCV, the crypto DRL paper's practical overfitting-rejection fix) converges on the same finding: backtest performance alone is close to worthless for RL-style policies without a check for how likely that performance is to be a multiple-testing artifact. Gridiron already has the ideal raw material for this — server/migrations/027_decision_tape.js's append-only nfl_decision_runs/nfl_decision_events tape records every candidate CONSIDERED and why it was passed over, not just what was selected, which solves the survivorship problem that undermines naive backtests everywhere else in this literature.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/rl-ope-harness.js reading server/migrations/027_decision_tape.js's nfl_decision_runs/nfl_decision_events; computes a doubly-robust off-policy value estimate plus a CSCV-style overfitting probability for any candidate policy (N1's value-iteration output OR N2's bandit fractions) before nfl-policy.js's requireCalibratedAdvantage gate is allowed to promote it.
candidates.expected_value: Process/infrastructure value, not a direct betting edge — but it is what prevents N1 and N2 (and any future RL work) from shipping on the strength of a self-flattering backtest, which the literature says is the default failure mode for exactly this kind of work.
candidates.exit_test: Run the harness against 3 deliberately-bad synthetic policies (always-go-for-it, always-punt, random); it must rank all three below the current production policy's off-policy value estimate — if a bad synthetic policy scores as well as or better than the real one, the harness itself is broken and nothing may be promoted through it.

do_not_do: Do not train any RL agent (tabular or deep) against nfl-drive-sim.js until the 6 physics bugs are fixed and re-verified — it will learn to exploit the bugs, not football.
Do not use any of the 5 disagreeing CLV implementations as an RL/bandit reward signal — consolidate to one canonical, sign-consistent CLV computation first.

Do not let an RL/bandit staking layer select a Kelly multiplier above 0.5x the existing closed-form Kelly output — real data (Beggy et al.) shows Full Kelly bankrupts 100% of realistic scenarios even capped at 20%, and Half Kelly still ruins at looser EV thresholds.

Do not promote any RL/value-iteration/bandit policy to production on backtest performance alone — require the off-policy/PBO-style check (candidate N3) first; this is the single most repeated lesson across every source read for this brief.

Do not start with a deep neural-network policy-gradient agent for play-calling — the corrected simulator's state space is small enough for exact tabular value iteration, which is cheaper, fully interpretable, reproducible, and avoids adding a new source of the 'many trials, pick the best seed' overfitting risk.

Do not attempt team-specific (as opposed to league-average) play-calling RL yet — Gridiron's 251,591 rows of play-by-play are used only for hand-built features, never sequence models, and team-specific RL needs that upgrade first; Biro & Walker's own paper hit this exact wall with more data than Gridiron currently structures for the purpose.

Do not build a multi-bet portfolio-allocation RL/optimizer across a weekly slate while teaser-leg-rates.js still assumes zero same-game/same-week correlation — measure the real correlation first (candidate F3); it may turn out to be indistinguishable from zero at Gridiron's actual bet volume, in which case shelve the portfolio idea rather than build it on an unchecked assumption.

Do not treat 'reinforcement learning' as one technique with one track record when pitching this work — tabular value iteration in small MDPs, deep RL in liquid multi-asset markets, and deep RL in illiquid/low-volume/short-window domains have three different honest track records in the sources read here; any proposal must say which regime it's claiming.

result.label: N08: DFS lineup optimization as a new fantasy surface
result.summary: Gridiron's only lineup logic today is trade-engine.js:323 bestLineup() — a greedy, single-lineup, independence-assuming sort-and-fill with no salary cap, no multi-entry portfolio, and no ownership concept ("salary" hits in the repo are all NFL contract-cap data, unrelated to DFS). It does have real, fitted player-correlation data (correlation.js: QB-WR r=0.176 etc.) and a correlation-aware ceiling search (ceiling-lineup.js), plus Monte Carlo infra (season-sim.js) — but none of it is pointed at the DFS problem: constrained multi-lineup construction, ownership-aware leverage, or simulated-field win probability. Two DFS-optimization papers were read in full: Hunter, Vielma & Zaman (2016/2019, arXiv:1604.01455) prove the "picking winners" problem is NP-hard but submodular (greedy gets a 1-1/e guarantee), give the exact IP formulation (budget/position/team feasibility + stacking + overlap constraints), and validate on 38 real DraftKings NHL contests (Oct-Dec 2015, thousands of entrants each, real money, ~$15k donated) — showing a single point-maximizing lineup has a median -100% profit margin while 100-200 diversified, stacked lineups shift the distribution solidly positive. Haugh & Singal (2021, Management Science 67(1):72-92) fix the two big gaps — model opponents' unknown lineups via a Dirichlet-multinomial ownership process fit by Dirichlet regression, and handle true top-heavy/double-up payoff curves instead of a winner-take-all proxy — validated on all 17 weeks of real 2017 NFL DFS play: opponent-aware strategic play earned ~5x the expected P&L of a naive benchmark, a better ownership model added another ~10%, and they document their own model's real misses (Ezekiel Elliott week 9, Tom Brady week 12) as calibration lessons. Repo research: DimaKudosh/pydfs-lineup-optimizer (MIT, 447 stars, pushed 2024) gives a real constraint/exposure-cap architecture worth copying in design (not port — it's Python); JWally/jsLPSolver (Unlicense, 463 stars, pushed 2026-07-10, pure JS zero-dep MIP solver) is the actual dependency Gridiron would add to replace bestLineup()'s greedy sort with a true IP solve. Five new-capability candidates below (all bucket "new" per this agent's assignment): an ILP-based multi-lineup optimizer, a from-scratch ownership-projection model built on Gridiron's own free features, exposure-capped multi-lineup portfolio construction reusing correlation.js, a GPP-field Monte Carlo win-probability simulator reusing season-sim.js's correlatedSampler, and a value-vs-ownership leverage view. Do-not-do list flags: no real-money auto-submission, no paid ownership-data scraping, no independence assumption in the new optimizer, no bolt-on to season-long start/sit (structurally a different problem — lineup-brain.js already found 7/10 real season-long lineups have zero same-team pairs), and no uncalibrated trust in ownership point estimates.

sources.title: Picking Winners in Daily Fantasy Sports Using Integer Programming
sources.authors: David Scott Hunter, Juan Pablo Vielma, Tauhid Zaman (MIT)
sources.venue: submitted to INFORMS Journal on Optimization; arXiv:1604.01455
sources.key_result: Proves the picking-winners objective (P(>=1 entry wins)) is NP-hard but submodular, giving greedy a (1-1/e) guarantee; derives a tractable pairwise-correlation surrogate U2(S) and a sequential IP (budget + position + team feasibility, structural stacking constraints, overlap constraint gamma across own entries). Validated on 38 real DraftKings NHL contests Oct-Dec 2015 (thousands of entrants each, real money, ~$15k winnings donated to charity): median profit margin for a single point-maximizing lineup is -100%, while their richest stacking type with 100-200 diversified lineups shifts mean profit margin to roughly +100-120% and gives a fat right tail of outlier wins.
sources.sample: 38 real top-heavy DraftKings NHL contests, Oct 21-Dec 31 2015, several thousand entrants per contest; player point model fit on 10,825 skater-game observations (Table 2).

sources.title: How to Play Fantasy Sports Strategically (and Win)
sources.authors: Martin B. Haugh (Imperial College), Raghav Singal (Columbia)
sources.key_result: Extends Hunter et al. by explicitly modeling opponents' unknown lineups via a Dirichlet-multinomial ownership process (Dirichlet regression on salary, projected points, recent performance) and by correctly handling true double-up and top-heavy payoff curves rather than a winner-take-all proxy, reducing the problem to a series of binary quadratic programs. Validated on all 17 weeks of real 2017 NFL DFS play across double-up (~30,000-entrant fields), quintuple-up, and top-heavy contests: strategic opponent-aware play earned ~5x the expected P&L of a naive benchmark in top-heavy contests; a fully-featured ownership model added ~10% more expected P&L over a naive deterministic ownership assumption; insider knowledge of true ownership was worth only ~20%/1%/2% more (top-heavy/quintuple-up/double-up) - most of the edge comes from modeling opponents from public features, not from illicit information; 5-player collusion increased expected P&L 44% and Sortino ratio 63% (Table 2). 95% ownership prediction intervals for QBs contained ~95% of realized outcomes in a spot-check week, but the paper documents real calibration misses (Ezekiel Elliott week 9, Tom Brady week 12 2017) from missing 'momentum'/situational features.
sources.sample: Real NFL DFS entries across all 17 weeks of the 2017 season, double-up fields ~30,000 opponents, rank of interest ~13,000; QB ownership spot-checked against 24 real QBs in week 10.

sources.title: Optimizing Daily Fantasy Baseball Lineups: A Linear Programming Approach for Enhanced Accuracy
sources.authors: Max Grody, Sandeep Bansal, Huthaifa I. Ashqar
sources.key_result: Cited for currency only (abstract/metadata read, not full body): confirms the IP/LP lineup-construction approach from 2016 remains the standard technique being published on for DFS baseball as of Nov 2024, i.e. this is not a stale 2016-era method.

candidates.candidate: Replace bestLineup()'s greedy sort with a true ILP multi-lineup DFS optimizer
candidates.mechanism: Add jsLPSolver (pure-JS MIP, zero deps) and implement Hunter et al.'s exact IP formulation (Eq. 4.3/4.9): budget constraint, per-position bounds, minimum-teams-represented, plus an overlap constraint (Eq. 4.8) that caps how many players a new lineup shares with previously generated lineups in the same batch. Solve sequentially for k lineups (greedy submodular construction, proven 1-1/e optimal).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/dfs-lineup-optimizer.js exported alongside (not replacing) trade-engine.js:323 bestLineup(); needs a new dfs_slates/dfs_salaries table populated from free DK/FD CSV exports (no paid API). Route it from a new /api/dfs endpoint, distinct from the existing lineup/trade routes.
candidates.expected_value: Turns Gridiron from a single-lineup value-maximizer into a real portfolio-construction tool for any salary-cap contest Nick enters, directly reproducing the paper's headline empirical result (single lineup: -100% median profit margin; 100-200 diversified stacked lineups: solidly positive) instead of the strategy the current bestLineup() implements today.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest the generated 20-lineup portfolio against one real historical DK NFL slate's actual field-of-entries data (if obtainable free/public) or against a synthetic field drawn from the new ownership model (candidate N08-2); confirm the overlap-constrained portfolio's simulated win probability exceeds 20 copies of the single best point-maximizing lineup.

candidates.candidate: Build a from-scratch ownership-projection model from Gridiron's own free features
candidates.mechanism: Dirichlet regression per Haugh & Singal: per-position ownership share vector ~ Dirichlet(alpha), alpha modeled as a function of salary, Gridiron's own projected points, Vegas-implied team total (already computed in nfl-spread-context.js), and recent target/snap share (already computed in weekly-trends.js). Fit weekly, emit both a point ownership % and a 95% prediction interval, not just a point estimate.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/dfs-ownership-model.js; new dfs_ownership_projections table keyed by (week, player, contest_type). Reuses existing feature-producing services rather than adding new data dependencies — no paid ownership vendor needed.
candidates.expected_value: Per Haugh & Singal, a calibrated opponent-ownership model is worth ~10% additional expected P&L on top of the ~5x strategic-vs-naive gain, and unlocks leverage-based lineup selection (low-owned, high-upside plays) that a point-maximizing tool can never surface.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest predicted vs. realized ownership on at least 4 historical weeks of a real public DK/FD ownership dataset (e.g. a season of freely published contest-results ownership from a site that releases it after the fact); confirm 95% intervals actually contain roughly 95% of realized ownership, and explicitly flag/report weeks where the model misses badly (per the paper's own Elliott/Brady examples) rather than silently trusting the point estimate.

candidates.candidate: Exposure-capped multi-lineup portfolio construction reusing correlation.js
candidates.mechanism: Generalize the per-pair overlap constraint into a per-player max-exposure cap across N generated lineups (as in pydfs-lineup-optimizer's exposure_strategy.py), and use Gridiron's already-fitted correlationMatrix() (correlation.js) — not the papers' equal-variance/simple-stacking-indicator approximation — to choose which same-team stacks to force into which lineups.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Extends N08-1's optimizer service; consumes correlationMatrix()/correlationTable() already exported from server/services/correlation.js — no new correlation estimation work needed, this is pure reuse of existing, validated Gridiron infrastructure for a new purpose.
candidates.expected_value: Because Gridiron's correlation estimates are fitted on the user's own real boxscore history rather than the papers' generic approximations, stacking decisions should be more accurate than either paper's baseline approach out of the box — a case where Gridiron's existing data asset beats the published method's assumption.
candidates.exit_test: Compare simulated portfolio win-probability (via N08-4's field simulator) between stacks chosen from Gridiron's fitted correlationMatrix() vs. the papers' simpler equal-variance stacking-indicator rule on the same slate; confirm the fitted-correlation version is not worse.

candidates.candidate: GPP-field Monte Carlo win-probability simulator
candidates.mechanism: Simulate M opponent lineups per contest by drawing from the Dirichlet-multinomial ownership process (N08-2) combined with correlated player-outcome draws (reuse correlatedSampler() from correlation.js, already used identically in season-sim.js line 228 for season simulation). Score the candidate portfolio against the simulated field to estimate P(win)/expected prize equity directly — implementing the actual 'picking winners' objective instead of the expected-points proxy bestLineup() uses today.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/dfs-field-sim.js, structurally parallel to season-sim.js (same correlatedSampler() call pattern, different unit of simulation — a contest field instead of a season).
candidates.expected_value: This is the single biggest conceptual gap between what bestLineup() does (maximize E[points]) and what actually wins top-heavy DFS contests (maximize P(at least one entry wins)) per both papers' central finding; without it, N08-1's optimizer is still just optimizing the wrong objective with better constraints.
candidates.exit_test: On a slate with a known real historical outcome, confirm the simulator's estimated win probability for the actual winning lineup that day is meaningfully above the field average, and that its ranking of candidate portfolios by simulated P(win) differs from a ranking by raw expected points (proving the simulator adds information beyond N08-1 alone).

candidates.candidate: Value-vs-ownership leverage view (points-per-dollar vs. projected ownership scatter)
candidates.mechanism: A lightweight read-only report: for each player on a slate, plot (or table) projected points per salary dollar against N08-2's projected ownership %, flagging high-value/low-ownership 'leverage' plays vs. 'chalk' (high-value/high-ownership, safe but non-differentiating in GPPs).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Small UI addition consuming N08-2's output table; no new modeling, pure presentation layer akin to existing report pages like weekly-trends.js's consumers.
candidates.expected_value: Cheap, immediately useful even before N08-1/N08-4 are built — gives Nick a manual leverage-aware view for his own lineup decisions while the automated optimizer is still in progress.
candidates.exit_test: Ship it gated behind N08-2 existing (it has no value without a real ownership number); confirm at least one week where a flagged low-owned/high-value player actually outscored the field's chalk play at that position.

repos.what_it_does: Python DFS lineup optimizer wrapping PuLP/CBC MIP solving (solvers/pulp_solver.py, mip_solver.py) with a real constraint/rule architecture: team/position stacking groups (stacks.py PlayersGroup with min/max_from_group), per-player exposure caps across N generated lineups (exposure_strategy.py TotalExposureStrategy/AfterEachExposureStrategy), and an externally-supplied ownership input (rules.py ProjectedOwnershipRule, lineup_importer.py line 37 parses a 'Projected Ownership' CSV column) rather than projecting ownership itself — confirmed by reading the actual source, not just the README.
repos.adoption_path: Do not port the Python code (Gridiron is Node/Express/SQLite). Replicate the exposure-cap and stack-group constraint design directly in the new server/services/dfs-lineup-optimizer.js (N08-1/N08-3) using jsLPSolver as the underlying solver.

repos.what_it_does: Pure-JavaScript, zero-dependency linear and mixed-integer/binary programming solver (branch-and-cut) usable directly in Node with no external solver binary — evaluated via GitHub API metadata and package description, not cloned (small, single-purpose, no ambiguity about fit worth resolving by reading source).
repos.adoption_path: Add as an npm dependency and call directly from server/services/dfs-lineup-optimizer.js to solve the budget/position/team/stacking/overlap IP (Hunter et al. Eq. 4.9) that bestLineup()'s greedy sort cannot express today.

do_not_do: Do not build automated real-money contest entry submission to DraftKings/FanDuel — ship lineup construction plus a CSV export in the platform's own upload format, and stop there; actual submission is a financial-transaction/credentials action outside this tool's remit.

Do not scrape or replicate paid ownership-projection vendors (e.g. RotoGrinders) — build the ownership model (N08-2) from Gridiron's own already-owned free inputs (public salary CSVs, existing Vegas-implied totals, existing target/snap share), per Haugh & Singal's own feature list.

Do not assume independent player outcomes when building the multi-lineup optimizer or field simulator — this is the documented real-world failure mode (Newell & Easton, cited inside source #1, failed in real DraftKings contests on exactly this assumption) and Gridiron already has fitted correlations in correlation.js with no excuse to ignore them.

Do not optimize for expected points alone in the new DFS tool — Hunter et al.'s own data shows a single point-maximizing lineup has a median -100% profit margin in top-heavy contests; the objective must be P(win)/expected prize equity via the field simulator (N08-4), not E[points].

Do not bolt this onto the season-long ESPN redraft start/sit surface (lineup-brain.js/ceiling-lineup.js) — it is a structurally different problem (portfolio vs. a field of thousands of opponent entries, not a single roster with no opponent pool); lineup-brain.js's own doc comment already found 7 of 10 real season-long optimal lineups contain zero same-team pairs, so DFS stacking logic mostly does not apply there. Keep it a separate surface and separate tables.

Do not trust the new ownership model's point estimate uncalibrated — ship prediction intervals and flag low-confidence weeks; even Haugh & Singal's published, validated model missed badly on real players (Ezekiel Elliott week 9 2017, Tom Brady week 12 2017) when a situational feature was missing.

result.label: N09: Generative/synthetic augmentation for small-n sports data
result.summary: The sports-specific generative-sequence literature (basketball VRNN, tennis/football transformer "SportsNGEN", soccer CVRNN) is real but trained on 10^5-10^6 sequences each -- the opposite of Gridiron's actual small-n problem -- and none of them test train-on-synthetic-test-on-real for a decision-relevant downstream metric. The tabular small-sample literature is the honest analog and is genuinely double-edged: a controlled study found augmentation improves prognostic AUC by an average 15.6% on small datasets, but a separate rigorous evaluation of tiny tabular data (9-30 rows) showed standard fidelity metrics (propensity score, MMD) can certify synthetic data as "similar" while topological distance proves it is not -- i.e. the very metrics a Gridiron pilot would use to sign off are shown to lie at small n. Model-collapse research adds a hard constraint: never train recursively on your own synthetic output, always keep real data as the training majority. Net verdict: credible but narrow. Gridiron's one surface where this genuinely fits is server/services/nfl-rookies.js (n=75 historical rookie-seasons, self-declared survivorship-biased) feeding the cold-start null in player-week-engine.js's heads object -- a small, falsifiable pilot there is worth running under a governance gate Gridiron does not currently have; a play/drive-sequence generative model is not, given the data-volume gap, and is placed on the do-not-do list.

sources.title: Generating Multi-Agent Trajectories using Programmatic Weak Supervision
sources.key_result: Hierarchical VRNN with macro-intent layer trained on 107,146 basketball possession sequences generates trajectories preferred by professional analysts over single/independent VRNN baselines (100% and 60% preference respectively) and cuts out-of-bounds rate from 45.7% to 15.5%; needs ~100K+ sequences to learn the macro-intent/agent split and provides no evidence of working at small n.

sources.title: SportsNGEN: Sustained Generation of Realistic Multi-player Sports Gameplay
sources.key_result: Transformer-decoder generator trained on ~15,000 tennis matches / 7.6M rally sequences at 25Hz is well-calibrated on aggregate shot statistics, but calibration explicitly degrades 'where data are sparse'; noise injection was required during training to avoid unstable degenerate rollouts, ~20% of generated rallies were discarded as unrealistic, and no train-on-synthetic-test-on-real evaluation is reported.

sources.title: Deep Generative Multi-Agent Imitation Model as a Computational Benchmark for Evaluating Human Performance in Complex Interactive Tasks: A Case Study in Football
sources.key_result: Conditional VRNN trained on 43 Premier League matches (500,000 six-frame pitch-control sequences) reaches SSIM 0.954/0.850 (reconstruction/prediction) vs 0.900/0.795 for vanilla VRNN -- a real but incremental gain, on a pixel-similarity metric only, with no stated minimum-sample-size finding.

sources.title: Evaluating Synthetic Tabular Data Generated To Augment Small Sample Datasets
sources.key_result: A WGAN's synthetic data on 9-30 row tabular datasets passed standard fidelity checks (propensity-score MSE 0.0114) while a topological Bottleneck-distance test (297,000, p=0.0002) proved the synthetic and real distributions were fundamentally different; authors conclude no single metric, including their own proposed one, reliably validates synthetic tabular data at this sample size.

sources.title: A Note on Shumailov et al. (2024): 'AI Models Collapse When Trained on Recursively Generated Data'
sources.key_result: Confirms model collapse is a real, metric-dependent statistical phenomenon (reproducible with plain KDE resampling, no neural net needed) that is far more severe under full replacement of real data by synthetic each generation than under mixing synthetic with retained real data -- the practical rule is mix, never replace, and never recursively retrain a generator on its own prior output.

sources.title: Synthetic Data Generation for Augmenting Small Samples
sources.authors: Liu, El Kababji, Mitsakakis, Pilgram, Walters, Clemons, Pond, El-Hussuna, El Emam
sources.key_result: Across seven small health datasets, augmentation improved downstream AUC by an average 15.55% relative (range 4.31-43.23%) vs. resampling alone (p=0.016), with the largest gains on datasets with fewer observations, lower baseline AUC, higher-cardinality categoricals and more balanced outcomes -- the strongest 'it genuinely helps' evidence found, but PDF extraction failed twice so only abstract-level detail is verified here.

candidates.candidate: Bounded VAE/Bayesian-bootstrap augmentation pilot for rookie evidence
candidates.mechanism: Fit a small conditional generative model (start with a Bayesian bootstrap / mixture-of-Gaussians per draft-capital band before reaching for a VAE -- the tabular small-sample papers show simple methods are competitive at n<100) on the n=75 verified rookie-seasons in nfl_rookie_evidence, conditioned on draft_round/draft_pick/position, to generate additional synthetic rookie-seasons that densify the late-round bands nfl-rookies.js itself flags as least trustworthy.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Feeds ridgeFit() in server/services/nfl-specialists.js as called from server/services/nfl-rookies.js measureRookiePriors(); synthetic rows augment (never replace) the real n=75 training set for the ridge-shrunk challenger that must beat the draft-capital prior.
candidates.expected_value: If it holds, tighter late-round-band priors (currently collapsed for lack of data) could improve Week-1-4 rookie opportunity projections, exactly the coverage gap the file header calls the model's largest structural blind spot.
candidates.exit_test: Walk-forward: fit on rookie classes through year T-1 (real only, then real+synthetic), predict class T's actual Week 1-4 opportunity shares. Kill the pilot if synthetic-augmented RMSE is not better than real-only RMSE on at least 3 of the last 5 held-out classes, or if the honest-fidelity gate (candidate N09-C3) fails on the generated bands.

candidates.candidate: Synthetic cold-start 'heads' vector for player-week-engine.js instead of a silent null
candidates.fixes_finding: The fantasy weekly-learning loop has never captured one forward snapshot in its life (cold-start: player_week_engine.heads is null week 1) -- it needs a real cold-start/transfer strategy, not a silent no-op.
candidates.mechanism: When a player has no player_week_usage history (line ~574, `if (!engine || !heads) return {...}`), synthesize a plausible heads object (season_to_date/last3/last1/median) by drawing from the empirical distribution of historically comparable players at the same draft-capital band and position, rather than returning nothing -- this is a direct, generative-model-flavored fix for a named defect, not a new deep architecture.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/player-week-engine.js (the null-heads guard at line 574 and its callers in fantasy-coordinator.js, role-scenario-engine.js, weekly-learning.js).
candidates.expected_value: Removes a currently-silent no-op in the weekly-learning loop for every rookie in week 1, letting downstream consumers (trade-engine.js, betting-fantasy-link.js) receive a labeled-as-synthetic estimate instead of null, which is strictly more informative and auditable.
candidates.exit_test: For every rookie who debuts in a tracked week, compare the synthetic heads.median against that player's actual week-1 output across 2+ seasons; ship only if synthetic heads reduce median absolute error vs. the current fallback behavior (whatever downstream code currently substitutes for null) on a held-out season.

candidates.candidate: TSTR + multi-metric honest-fidelity governance gate for synthetic data
candidates.mechanism: Build a small, reusable evaluation library implementing (a) train-on-synthetic-test-on-real downstream comparison and (b) at least two fidelity metrics that can disagree (e.g. propensity-score/MMD plus a topological or nearest-neighbor-distance check), following the honest-evaluation design in arXiv:2211.10760, so any future synthetic-data experiment has a pass/fail gate instead of eyeballing one number.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New module alongside server/services/model-governance.js (the existing gate infrastructure that already handles forward-CLV gating per docs/PROPS_PLAYER_ENGINES.md) -- wire it as a required pre-check before any synthetic-data output (rookie pilot or otherwise) is allowed to reach a promoted model.
candidates.expected_value: Prevents the exact failure mode documented in the tabular-fidelity paper (propensity score says 'fine', topology says 'wrong') from silently shipping a rookie-augmentation pilot or any future synthetic-data use; this is pure downside protection, cheap relative to the cost of a bad promoted model.
candidates.exit_test: Gate is considered working once it correctly flags a deliberately-corrupted synthetic dataset (e.g. shuffled labels) as failing, and passes a known-good real-vs-real control comparison -- both as a unit test before it is ever applied to a real candidate.

candidates.candidate: Augmentation-applicability screen (Liu et al. 2025 criteria)
candidates.mechanism: Before running any augmentation experiment, score each candidate table/surface against the four conditions Liu et al. 2025 found predict when augmentation helps: fewer observations, lower baseline model performance, higher-cardinality categorical features, more balanced outcome distribution. Only surfaces that score positively on most of these are worth a pilot at all.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Apply as a one-page checklist against nfl_rookie_evidence (n=75, low baseline AUC on late-round bands, position is high-cardinality, outcome fairly balanced -- scores positive) versus e.g. nfl-team-strength.js's team-season table (larger n, continuous outcome, lower expected benefit -- scores negative), to stop effort being spent where the 2025 paper's own evidence says it won't pay off.
candidates.expected_value: Cheap triage that prevents wasted engineering on augmentation attempts the literature already predicts will not help (e.g. team-strength, which has enough real data and a different failure mode -- see tonight's finding that its blend is hand-tuned, not synthetic-data-starved).
candidates.exit_test: Re-run the screen after any pilot completes; if a surface the screen rated positive did not show the AUC/RMSE improvement predicted, revise or retire the screen rather than trusting it uncritically next time.

candidates.candidate: Calibrated predictive distributions for player props via lightweight hierarchical/negative-binomial modeling
candidates.fixes_finding: Player props are point-estimate projections, not distributions -- no negative-binomial/hierarchical/calibrated model; the module is the project's one area of genuine measured skill (2+ TD Brier skill +27%) but under-measured against real prices.
candidates.mechanism: Replace point-estimate features feeding nfl-prop-calibration.js with a hierarchical partial-pooling model (players nested in position nested in league) or negative-binomial regression producing full predictive distributions, not a deep generative model -- the evidence above (data-volume gap in every deep generative sports paper reviewed) argues against reaching for a VAE/diffusion approach here and for a parametric/hierarchical one that works at Gridiron's actual per-player-week sample sizes.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-prop-calibration.js (the shipped TD_CALIBRATION_HEADS) and server/services/nfl-prop-player-heads.js (the research-harness challenger already scaffolded with walk-forward discipline and a forward-CLV gate via model-governance.js) -- this candidate is a new head registered in that existing challenger framework, not new infrastructure.
candidates.expected_value: Turns Gridiron's one area of genuine measured skill (props) into one with honest uncertainty intervals instead of point estimates, directly enabling better bet-sizing without touching the ensemble or drive-sim modules that tonight's audit flagged as structurally broken.
candidates.exit_test: Per docs/PROPS_PLAYER_ENGINES.md's existing discipline: walk-forward fit on seasons < T, decide the winning head without seeing T, and require the forward CLV gate in model-governance.js to pass before promotion -- exactly the bar already set for nfl-prop-player-heads.js challengers, no new bar needed.

do_not_do: Do NOT build a deep generative (VAE/GAN/diffusion) model of full play or drive sequences for nfl-drive-sim.js or the season-remainder simulator: every real sports sequence-generation system reviewed needed 10^5-10^6 training sequences (107K basketball possessions, 500K soccer snippets, 7.6M tennis rallies) to avoid degenerate output, and Gridiron's entire play-by-play table is 251,591 rows across many seasons/teams/situations -- orders of magnitude short.

Do NOT validate any synthetic dataset with propensity-score or MMD similarity alone, especially below n~100 -- arXiv:2211.10760 shows a case where a reassuring propensity-MSE of 0.011 coexisted with a topological distance proving the distributions were fundamentally different.

Do NOT let a rookie-augmentation model retrain on its own prior synthetic output in a future season (a recursive self-training loop) -- both Shumailov et al. 2024 and its critique agree recursive synthetic-only training degrades distributions; always keep real rows as the training majority.

Do NOT ship a rookie-augmentation pilot's output near live betting stakes or lineup decisions before a genuine forward (not backtested) evaluation window, given nfl-rookies.js's own stated survivorship bias in its n=75 sample -- synthetic rows generated from a biased sample launder the bias rather than fixing it.

Do NOT treat 'looks realistic to a human/analyst' (the preference-study standard Zhan et al. used) as sufficient validation for any Gridiron model -- none of the sports generative papers reviewed tested train-on-synthetic-test-on-real for a betting- or fantasy-relevant downstream metric, only aggregate realism statistics.

result.label: N07 — Live in-game win-probability product
result.summary: Gridiron already ingests everything a real live win-probability model needs (251,591-row nfl_play_by_play with down/distance/yardline/clock/score/possession, plus a free live ESPN feed via pollLiveGames), and already has a crude live WP number — but that number is nfl-live.js's own admitted stopgap: a score+clock random walk with "no possession, down-and-distance, or timeout awareness," shown to users only as a progress bar buried in a betting sub-tab (client/src/pages/betting/Edges.tsx 'live' tab), with no standalone route anywhere in App.tsx. The academic and public literature on this exact problem (Lock & Nettleton 2014 random forest, nflfastR's xgboost model, Yurko/Ventura/Horowitz's GAM, Burke's original binning approach) is mature, well-validated, and converges on the same feature list Gridiron's own table already has sitting unused. The MVP: fit a real play-level WP model on nfl_play_by_play (start with logistic regression, native JS, no new dependency), validate it with season-holdout calibration exactly like the literature does, ship it as its own /live surface distinct from betting, and add a Lock-and-Nettleton-style live WPA "swing plays" feed — while fixing the specific nfl-drive-sim.js bugs that would otherwise poison any simulation-based version of the same idea.

sources.title: Using random forests to estimate win probability before each play of an NFL game
sources.venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 10(2):197-205, De Gruyter
sources.key_result: Random forest of regression trees (500 trees, mtry=2, nodesize=200) on 9 features (down, score diff, seconds remaining, AdjustedScore=Score/sqrt(Seconds+1), Vegas spread, timeouts each side, total points, yardline, yards-to-go), trained on 2001-2011 (n=430,168 plays, 2928 games), tested out-of-sample on the entire 2012 season: calibration r=0.998, test MSE by quarter 0.201/0.177/0.143/0.107 (sharper as the game progresses — the opposite of Gridiron's current model's failure mode). Variable importance: Score dominates overall (0.1365) but Spread is the single most important variable in Q1 (0.0577) and decays to near-irrelevance by Q4 (0.0046). Demonstrated live-WPA use case: re-ranks Super Bowl 42/43 'greatest plays' by ΔWP (Tyree catch ΔWP=0.113 vs Burress TD ΔWP=0.389 vs Harrison INT-TD ΔWP=0.511) and analyzes real accept/decline-penalty and 4th-down decisions. Honestly reports that momentum/separate-forest-by-quarter adjustments were tried and DISCARDED for not improving out-of-sample performance.
sources.sample: 430,168 training plays / 2,928 games, seasons 2001-2011; tested on the full, held-out 2012 season

sources.title: nflfastR EP, WP, CP, xYAC, and xPass models
sources.key_result: xgboost (eta=0.2, max_depth=4, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, nrounds=65 base / 534 spread-adjusted), leave-one-season-out CV across 2000-2019. Base WP model calibration error 0.0055 vs prior-generation nflscrapR's 0.0397 (~7x tighter); adding a time-decayed Vegas-spread feature reduces CV classification error from 27% to 23% and log-loss from 0.52 to 0.44, though it slightly worsens raw calibration error (0.0066) — a real nuance on how a market prior trades calibration for discrimination.
sources.sample: All NFL plays, seasons 2000-2019, leave-one-season-out cross-validation

sources.title: nflWAR: A Reproducible Method for Offensive Player Evaluation in Football (Extended Edition)
sources.authors: Ronald Yurko, Samuel Ventura, Maksim Horowitz
sources.venue: arXiv preprint / Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports
sources.key_result: Introduces a two-stage WP architecture: a multinomial-logistic 'next-score' expected-points model feeds a Generalized Additive Model for win probability, log(P(Win)/P(Loss)) = s(E[S]) + s(s_h)*h + s(E[S/(s_g+1)]) + h*u*t_off + h*u*t_def, fit on nflscrapR data 2009-2017 with leave-one-season-out CV; calibration plots by quarter track the diagonal in every quarter with no systematic pattern, corroborated independently by Yam & Lopez (2018) who graded both this model and Lock & Nettleton's. Also the source of the 5%-bin calibration procedure nflfastR's own writeup (source 2) explicitly cites. Worked WPA example: Philly Special EPA=7-2.78=4.22, WPA=0.1266. Honestly notes WAR is only computable for offensive skill positions because public play-by-play doesn't identify all 22 on-field players.
sources.sample: All nflscrapR play-by-play, NFL seasons 2009-2017

sources.title: Win Probability Model/Calculator Upgrades — Team Strength Adjustment & More
sources.venue: Advanced Football Analytics (formerly Advanced NFL Stats)
sources.key_result: Documents the field's original in-game WP approach: empirical binning of historical plays by score/time/field position/down/distance with smoothing/extrapolation across bins (not a fitted parametric model), plus a 2013 team-strength-adjustment upgrade that decays a user-supplied pregame edge 'proportionally to the log of time' as the game progresses — independently converging on the same general decay shape as Lock & Nettleton's AdjustedScore and nflfastR's exponential time-decay term. Burke states plainly that timeout management is NOT modeled ('a whole other level of complexity') and that the model shows visible discontinuities where a trailing team's optimal strategy flips to four-down mode. No accuracy or calibration numbers are published for this version — a notable absence compared to sources 1-3, and itself an honest finding about why the field moved past pure empirical binning.
sources.sample: Historical NFL play-by-play, binned; no stated season range or n in this specific post

candidates.candidate: Fit a real, directly-trained play-level win-probability model (start with regularized logistic regression in native JS; graduate to a small GBM later) on Gridiron's own nfl_play_by_play table, using the Lock&Nettleton/nflfastR feature set (score differential, seconds remaining in game and half, down, distance, yardline, timeouts each team, pregame spread with a time-decay term), and use it to replace the score-only random walk in nfl-live.js as the model that actually backs the live WP number.
candidates.mechanism: Logistic regression (or later, a lightweight boosted-tree JS implementation) trained offline on nfl_play_by_play (down, distance, yards_to_endzone, clock_seconds, home_score, away_score, offense/defense, event_id/sequence — columns already ingested by nfl-espn-pbp.js's pollLiveGames() and by nfl-pbp.js's historical backfill), with a time-decayed score-differential feature analogous to nflfastR's point_differential*e^(4*(3600-seconds_remaining)/3600) or Lock&Nettleton's Score/sqrt(Seconds+1). Held out by season (never by row) for validation, exactly as both primary sources do.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New module server/services/nfl-live-wp.js exporting playWinProbability(state) with the same call signature nfl-live.js's liveWinProbability() already has, so server/routes/nfl-betting.js:533 and client/src/pages/betting/Edges.tsx can swap the backing model with a one-line change; validate against the SAME harness already built for exactly this purpose in server/services/nfl-espn-pbp.js's liveModelValidation() (~line 507), which already computes bucketed calibration + Brier score vs a base-rate baseline against nfl_play_by_play.
candidates.expected_value: Turns a self-admittedly-blind endgame model into one that is, per the literature, MORE accurate in exactly the situations (late game, tight down/distance) where nfl-live.js is worst — Lock & Nettleton's own out-of-sample MSE drops from 0.201 (Q1) to 0.107 (Q4), the opposite trend nfl-live.js's flagged unreliability implies today.
candidates.exit_test: Run liveModelValidation() (already in nfl-espn-pbp.js) against BOTH the old nfl-live.js model and the new one on the same held-out season/games; ship only if the new model's calibration error and Brier score are strictly better in every quarter bucket, not just on average.

candidates.candidate: Ship a standalone user-facing 'Game Center' / /live route with a per-game WP chart (à la Lock&Nettleton Figure 1 / nflWAR Figure 7), distinct from the betting surface — not another tab inside /betting/nfl.
candidates.mechanism: A dedicated client page and server route reading the same liveGames()-shaped payload (server/services/nfl-live.js, routed at server/routes/nfl-betting.js:533) but rendered as its own top-level nav item, so it is visible to users who never open betting at all.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: grep of client/src/App.tsx's full route table confirms there is currently no /live or /gameday route — Home is '/', League is '/league', and the only WP UI is client/src/pages/betting/Edges.tsx's 'live' tab (lines 79-200). Add <Route path="/live" element={<GameCenter/>}/> alongside the existing routes, and a nav entry outside the Betting section of the sidebar.
candidates.expected_value: Converts an existing, working backend capability (liveGames(), pollLiveGames()) that is currently invisible to non-betting users into an actual product surface — directly serves Nick's fantasy-over-betting priority since in-game context (a blowout, a comeback) is fantasy-relevant (garbage time volume, injury risk) independent of any bet.
candidates.exit_test: Ship behind no feature flag other than the route itself; confirm via manual check during a live Sunday window that the page renders and updates without touching the betting codepath at all.

candidates.candidate: Live 'swing plays' feed: compute play-level win-probability-added (WPA) from the new model in real time and surface a ranked 'biggest plays right now / this week' list, replicating Lock & Nettleton's own demonstrated ΔWP use case (Tyree catch vs Burress TD vs Harrison pick-six).
candidates.mechanism: WPA_i = WP(state after play i) - WP(state before play i), computed play-by-play as pollLiveGames() (server/services/nfl-espn-pbp.js) ingests each new ESPN play row, using the N07-C1 model for both WP evaluations.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: nfl-pbp.js already has a wpa field (lines 81, 109, 295, 376, 402, 486-487, 632) but it is ONLY the nflverse-supplied historical per-play wpa column folded into SEASON aggregates for team/player efficiency reports — never computed live by Gridiron's own model for a game in progress. New computation lives in the same nfl-live-wp.js module as N07-C1, writes to a new, clearly-named column so it is never confused with the season-aggregate wpa_total already in nfl-pbp.js's output.
candidates.expected_value: A genuinely new, cheap, high-visibility feature once N07-C1 exists — Lock & Nettleton's paper demonstrates this exact use case already works and is compelling (re-ranking 'greatest plays' by actual win-probability impact rather than media narrative).
candidates.exit_test: For a handful of already-played 2025/2026 games in nfl_play_by_play, manually confirm the top-3 WPA plays match obviously game-defining moments (a go-ahead late score, a game-sealing turnover) before exposing it live.

candidates.candidate: Version and periodically refit the live WP model as a standalone, versioned artifact (mirroring the PLAY_MODEL_VERSION pattern already used for the drive simulator), rather than a static hand-fit blob that silently rots as scoring rates and rules drift across seasons.
candidates.mechanism: A weekly (or seasonal) refit job re-estimates the N07-C1 model on all nfl_play_by_play data available so far, tags the result with a version string, and stores/loads it the same way nfl-drive-sim.js already versions its own model ('pbp-drive-v3-cutoff-calibrated', server/services/nfl-drive-sim.js:41).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-drive-sim.js already exports PLAY_MODEL_VERSION = 'pbp-drive-v3-cutoff-calibrated' (line 41) as a precedent; nfl-live-wp.js should export an analogous NFL_LIVE_WP_MODEL_VERSION and log it alongside every prediction so a bad refit is traceable and rollback-able.
candidates.expected_value: Cheap insurance against the exact failure mode nflfastR's own methodology post explicitly designed around ('build in era adjustments' was the FIRST stated reason they moved off older models) — without this, Gridiron's new model degrades the same way any of its 21 already-measured historical models would without retraining.
candidates.exit_test: Confirm the version string changes and is logged after a deliberate re-run of the refit job; confirm old predictions remain reproducible by pinning to a prior version string.

candidates.candidate: Surface a fantasy-facing signal off the same live WP model — e.g. 'trailing team, garbage-time pass volume likely' flags on player pages for QBs/WRs on a team with low win probability late — kept entirely on the fantasy side of the app, not merged into the betting surface.
candidates.mechanism: Read the N07-C1 model's live WP output for a player's team; when WP < ~0.15 and clock is in the 4th quarter, surface a lightweight badge/note on that player's live game context (volume upside from trailing-script pass-heavy offense).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Attaches to whatever player-context surface Gridiron's fantasy side already renders live scores on (the memory file gridiron-fantasy-over-betting.md documents 'beat fantasy first; betting engine is secondary' as Nick's explicit standing priority) — this is the one candidate in this set that is fantasy-facing rather than betting-adjacent, deliberately, to satisfy that priority.
candidates.expected_value: Low-cost, high-relevance-to-Nick's-stated-priority feature that reuses N07-C1's output for a second purpose at near-zero marginal engineering cost once the model exists.
candidates.exit_test: Confirm the flag only ever appears on the fantasy-facing surface (not inside any /betting/* route) and disappears correctly once WP normalizes or the game ends.

candidates.candidate: Fix the specific nfl-drive-sim.js physics bugs that make simulateRemainder() untrustworthy as a live-state engine, since server/services/nfl-espn-pbp.js already has a harness (~lines 590-638) feeding live game states into it and grading it against nfl-live.js as a candidate live-WP backbone.
candidates.fixes_finding: the kneel rule is inverted and timeouts never decrement so any leading team burns an entire half; away-team win-probability uses the home spread; turnovers handed to the wrong team's field position
candidates.mechanism: Correct the kneel-down/timeout-decrement logic and the home/away spread assignment inside nfl-drive-sim.js's policy modules so simulateRemainder() produces physically sane endgame behavior (a leading team actually able to run clock, timeouts actually depleting) before any live product is allowed to show its output to a user.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-drive-sim.js (1280 lines) is the file with the bugs; server/services/nfl-espn-pbp.js's existing validation function (which calls simulateRemainder() at 25/50/75% game checkpoints and compares its Brier score against nfl-live.js's baseline) is the exact existing test harness to re-run after the fix, with no new test code needed.
candidates.expected_value: Without this fix, the Monte-Carlo/simulation approach to live WP (as opposed to N07-C1's directly-fit approach) will misprice exactly the late-game, leading-team, timeout-management situations a live product is judged on hardest — this is a hard blocker on ever trusting simulateRemainder()'s live output, whichever architecture Gridiron ultimately ships.
candidates.exit_test: Re-run the existing calibration harness in nfl-espn-pbp.js pre- and post-fix; ship the simulation-based live path only if Brier score and the state_contract calibration buckets both improve and endgame (last-2-minutes) states specifically stop producing impossible clock/timeout trajectories in spot checks.

candidates.candidate: Route every new live WP/WPA number through exactly one function and one sign convention before shipping any user-facing number, rather than adding a sixth disagreeing implementation on top of tonight's already-documented five conflicting CLV implementations.
candidates.fixes_finding: Five independent, disagreeing CLV (closing-line-value) implementations exist over four different tables with different math and sign conventions.
candidates.mechanism: Treat nfl-live-wp.js (N07-C1) as the single source of truth for in-game WP, and any live WPA feed (N07-C3) as a pure derivative of that one function's output — never a parallel computation — with one documented sign convention (home-team perspective, matching liveWinProbability()'s existing 'lead from the home team's view' convention in nfl-live.js).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Before writing N07-C1/C3, grep the codebase (as done for this research: server/services/nfl-pbp.js lines 81,109,295,376,402,486-487,632 for the existing season-aggregate wpa; server/services/nfl-live.js for the existing live WP convention) to confirm no third variant is introduced; document the chosen convention at the top of the new nfl-live-wp.js module the way nfl-live.js already documents its own model in its header comment.
candidates.expected_value: Near-zero cost, prevents compounding tonight's already-flagged CLV fragmentation problem into a second, parallel category (win-probability/WPA) of disagreeing numbers across the codebase.
candidates.exit_test: grep the codebase post-ship for every place 'wpa' or 'win_probability' is computed (not just read) and confirm exactly one new computation site was added, with every consumer (C2's Game Center, C3's swing-plays feed, C5's fantasy badge) calling into it rather than recomputing.

do_not_do: Do not blend the new live-WP model's pregame prior using the broken NFL ensemble (forecast ~= 0.68 + 0.632*market, 20 components collapsing to ~3 independent signals, -2.28 pt mean CLV) documented in tonight's FOUND — feed it a separately-validated pregame input (e.g. the spread field nfl-live.js already carries) instead.

Do not ship a simulation-based (Monte Carlo, nfl-drive-sim.js) live WP number to users until the 6 physics bugs in FOUND are fixed (N07-C6) — kneel-rule inversion and dead timeout counters will visibly misprice exactly the endgame situations a live product is judged on.

Do not bury the new live surface as another tab inside /betting/nfl — Nick's fantasy-over-betting priority and the standing 'betting only through governance gates' rule both argue for a standalone, non-betting-gated /live route (N07-C2).

Do not present in-game WP as precise inside the final two minutes without genuine down/distance/possession/timeout awareness — nfl-live.js already honestly self-flags this today (probability_reliable field); a replacement model must earn the right to remove that flag via the calibration harness, not just assert it.
