sources.key_result: Backup QB passing rating runs about 16 points below the starting QB's passing rating on average; the market (Vegas spread) does not anticipate in-game injuries -- pregame spread differences between injured-starter and control games are statistically indistinguishable. Author states the causal wage=marginal-product claim is not extended beyond QB because only there is backup quality cleanly observable and priced.

sources.title: Opponent-Adjusted Evaluation of NFL Pass Blocking and Pass Rushing Performance
sources.key_result: Bradley-Terry-style opponent-adjusted evaluation of O-line/D-line performance; reviewed via summary only (WebFetch could not extract full body), noted as pairwise-comparison rather than network/systems-level, so not counted as a read-in-full primary source.

candidates.candidate: Build a team-week blocking/protection graph from play-by-play instead of leaving it as hand-built season aggregates
candidates.fixes_finding: 251,591 rows of play-by-play exist and are used only for hand-built features, never sequence models.
candidates.mechanism: Port Paul Ibrahim (2021)'s gap-based O-line responsibility zones as a play-level join key against a richer nflverse PBP pull (which carries passer/rusher ids upstream) to build a per-game, per-lineman 'zone under pressure' signal, then aggregate to team-week to feed pass-catcher/QB efficiency features instead of only season-level rollups.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/db/schema/nfl-a-to-m.js:306 (nfl_play_by_play -- confirmed to carry no player-id columns today, team/down/distance/shotgun only); server/services/nfl-pbp.js (syncPbpSeason, PBP_URL) is the ingestion point needing the richer column set; output would be a new nfl_pass_protection_zone table rolled up into a team-week feature nfl-roster-strength.js and contingency.js can both read.
candidates.expected_value: A real per-lineman degradation signal to attach to 'LT is out' instead of today's zero-signal gap in contingency.js's INHERITS map; feeds F3's proposed state-space team-strength update.
candidates.exit_test: Re-derive Ibrahim's protection-area-vs-expectation metric on Gridiron's PBP+snap data 2016-2025; check whether weeks with a new/backup LT (nfl_depth pos_rank change) show a paired, statistically significant drop vs. that same team's own baseline weeks -- stop before building anything downstream if the signal doesn't move.

candidates.candidate: Pre-register the injury-network pilot itself before it is allowed to touch anything live
candidates.fixes_finding: No trial registry exists with real preregistration + multiplicity correction (Holm/PBO/deflated-Sharpe) for the 21-model historical search that has already been run.
candidates.mechanism: Use model-governance.js's existing CONTRACTS framework (it already has injury_availability and pregame_role_eligibility contract rows) as the registration point: add the injury-network score as a named challenger with its exit test written down before any backtest is run, so it cannot quietly become model #22 in the same undisciplined search flagged tonight.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/model-governance.js (CONTRACTS array -- the existing ['NFL','player_props','pregame_role_eligibility','depth chart + prior usage snapshot',...] row is the template); server/services/nfl-model-growth.js (the publication-driven retrain/challenger pipeline).
candidates.expected_value: Prevents this exact research idea from becoming an uncorrected 22nd entry in the historical model search; near-zero cost, pure process fix.
candidates.exit_test: A written preregistration entry (exit metric, holdout weeks, Holm-adjusted significance threshold) exists dated before any backtest of the injury-network score runs; if the backtest already happened first, treat the finding as exploratory only and re-test on a fresh holdout.

candidates.candidate: Use validated injury-network shocks as the state-space update team-strength is missing, instead of the current hand-tuned blend
candidates.fixes_finding: Team-strength ratings (nfl-team-strength.js) mix stale preseason priors with in-season data via a hand-tuned blend, not a principled state-space/Bayesian update.
candidates.mechanism: Once F1's protection-degradation signal (or N1's simpler depth-chart-graph signal) is validated, treat a starter going down as an observed shock in a real state equation rather than letting the fixed-weight preseason/in-season blend slowly absorb it over several weeks.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-team-strength.js (depthPrior/participation blend logic, ~lines 279-300) is the mechanism to replace; contingency.js's cascades() output is the natural shock-magnitude input.
candidates.expected_value: A team-strength number that reacts to a real injury the week it happens instead of drifting toward it.
candidates.exit_test: On weeks with a confirmed new starter (nfl_injuries OUT + nfl_depth pos_rank change), compare next-week team-total forecast error under the state-space update vs. the current blend; require Holm-significant improvement per F2's registered test before replacing the blend.

candidates.candidate: Two-hop depth-chart cascade graph (position-siloed one-hop -> cross-position, scheme-weighted multi-hop)
candidates.mechanism: Represent each team-week's offense as a directed graph: nodes are depth-chart slots from nfl_depth/off_rosters (including OL positions already carried there but never used for cascades), edges are (a) direct pos_rank succession within a position (today's one-hop INHERITS logic) and (b) cross-position edges weighted by nfl-scheme.js's team scheme profile (e.g. an OT-slot edge into QB weighted by pass rate/PROE). Walk two hops: OL starter out -> protection degradation (F1) -> QB efficiency delta -> pass-catcher value delta, instead of producing zero signal for OL injuries as today.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/contingency.js (cascades(), SKILL=['QB','RB','WR','TE'] and INHERITS map at lines 22-27 -- extend, don't replace); nfl_depth (pos_abb includes OT/G/C), nfl_snaps (offense_pct), off_rosters (depth_chart_position) supply graph nodes; nfl-scheme.js's SCHEME_DIMENSIONS supplies edge weights.
candidates.expected_value: Turns a documented zero (OL injuries currently produce no fantasy-relevant cascade) into a measured, shrinkage-disciplined signal for pass-catchers behind an OL injury.
candidates.exit_test: On holdout weeks with a documented new starting OT/G/C, does the two-hop cascade's predicted pass-catcher delta beat both a 'no change' null and the current one-hop cascades() output (which predicts nothing here) on out-of-sample MAE, Holm-corrected per F2.

candidates.candidate: Backup-specific scheme-fit score, reusing nfl-scheme.js's own methodology on the player instead of the team
candidates.mechanism: Compute nfl-scheme.js's six SCHEME_DIMENSIONS (neutral pass rate, PROE, early-down pass rate, shotgun rate, no-huddle rate, plays/drive) from a backup's own prior-team/prior-season play-calling context, and measure distance to the current team's profile. Use Gregory-Smith's ~-16 rating-point average backup gap as the null to beat: do misfit backups underperform that average and well-fit backups beat it.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-scheme.js (SCHEME_DIMENSIONS, seasonProfiles()) called per-player via player_week_usage instead of per-team; QB1->QB2 transition weeks findable via nfl_injuries (QB OUT) joined to nfl_snaps offense_pct spikes.
candidates.expected_value: Cheap, code-reusing signal that could sharpen the flat 'backup is worse' prior into a fit-dependent one for backup-QB valuation.
candidates.exit_test: On QB1->QB2 forced-start weeks since 2016 (nfl_team_week_features coverage start), does scheme-distance correlate with EPA/play shortfall beyond career EPA alone, Holm-corrected; drop it if not significant.

candidates.candidate: Correlated/simultaneous-injury interaction term (two starters out is not two independent one-hop cascades)
candidates.mechanism: contingency.js's cascades() estimates each starter's inheritance independently. Build a pairwise interaction residual: for team-weeks with 2+ starters OUT/DOUBTFUL at different positions, compare actual backup performance to the sum of the two independently-estimated one-hop cascades, and characterize the sign/size of the residual (additive, sub-additive, or super-additive).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/contingency.js (cascades() output as the two baselines to sum); nfl_injuries table (season/week/gsis_id/report_status) identifies simultaneous-OUT team-weeks.
candidates.expected_value: Either confirms independence is fine (cheap negative result) or surfaces a real correction for the highest-leverage weeks where current handcuff rankings are most likely wrong.
candidates.exit_test: On team-weeks with 2+ simultaneous OUT starters at different positions (target ~30+ league-wide 2016-2025, matching contingency.js's own MIN_MISSED=3/minGames=6 sample discipline), is the actual-vs-summed-independent residual significantly different from zero; if the sample never reaches ~30 qualifying weeks, report that and stop.

candidates.candidate: Replace handcuffValue()'s flat per-position points-per-opportunity with player-specific (nflWAR-style) replacement level
candidates.mechanism: handcuffValue() currently converts every backup's inherited opportunity to points using one league-average ppo[position] constant (same number for every RB2 in football). Port nflWAR's core insight -- replacement level estimated per role via a roster-based approach, not a constant across all players at a position -- by substituting the specific backup's own trailing rate stats for the flat constant.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/contingency.js lines 271-281 (ppo computation) and 296-298 (expected_points calculation); player_week_usage already carries the per-player rate stats needed -- no new table required.
candidates.expected_value: A more honest handcuff ranking that distinguishes a backup merely receiving carries from one efficient with them, which the flat constant cannot do by construction.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest handcuff-value rankings (flat-ppo baseline vs player-specific replacement level) against actual fantasy points in backup-forced-into-starting weeks; require the player-specific version to beat the baseline on out-of-sample rank correlation or MAE, Holm-corrected per F2, before replacing the constant.

do_not_do: Do not let a network/graph model touch any live projection, trade-engine value, or auto-pick before it clears the same forward-shadow discipline every other Gridiron model goes through (model-governance.js CONTRACTS) — an untested graph score is not exempt just because it 'sounds structural.'

Do not build a full player-level graph neural network as a first step. Xenopoulos & Silva's 9% result came from a fully-connected graph over tracking data Gridiron does not have (no Big Data Bowl-grade tracking feed in this stack). Start with the depth-chart/snap-share graph that already exists in nfl_depth/nfl_snaps.

Do not extend contingency.js's INHERITS map to cross positions (e.g. OL -> QB) by hand-picking a multiplier — nfl-scheme.js's own discipline (measure, validate out of sample, only then trust) is the bar; a hand-tuned cross-position coefficient repeats the exact 'hand-tuned blend' mistake already flagged tonight for nfl-team-strength.js.
Do not treat Paul Ibrahim (2021)'s 6-game/310-play spatial framework as validated — the author says so himself. It is a method template, not a result to import as a coefficient.

Do not claim the Gregory-Smith '-16 rating points' figure as fantasy-football truth without re-deriving it on Gridiron's own player_week_usage/nfl_snaps data — it is QB-specific, 2011-2015, wage-motivated economics, not a fantasy-points number.

Do not build the correlated-injury interaction model (N3) on fewer than ~30 team-weeks with 2+ simultaneous starter-out flags — contingency.js already enforces MIN_MISSED=3 and minGames=6 for a single-player split; a two-player joint split needs more, not less, sample discipline.

result.label: N14-alternative-market-arbitrage
result.summary: Gridiron already runs real cross-sportsbook arbitrage/middle detection (nfl-shopping-board.js:229-307, priceMiddle/findMiddles, empirical-PMF-correct, flags true arbitrage), but it is hard-scoped to the spreads market across 5-6 traditional books and has never been joined to the separately-ingested Kalshi/Polymarket data (prediction-markets.js, polymarket.js). The genuinely new capability is cross-venue (exchange vs. sportsbook) and cross-market-type (moneyline vs. spread) arbitrage/middle detection. The best modern, sports-specific, fully-electronic-market evidence (Cheng/Yang/Zou 2026, Polymarket NBA, read in full) shows this mechanism is now almost extinct at scale: $210 total single-market arbitrage profit and $560 total combinatorial-arbitrage profit across an entire NBA month, 76.9% of episodes liquidity-capped to ~15 shares, and the theoretical "Middle jackpot" double-payout never once realized empirically across 290 episodes. The best historical upper bound (Franck/Verbeek/Nüesch 2013, Economica, read in full) — 2,287 bookmaker-vs-exchange arbitrage opportunities across 11,933 soccer matches, 1.4% avg return, arbitrage in >1-in-6 matches — comes from a slower, pre-automated-market-making era that no longer describes Kalshi or Polymarket. Kalshi's own quote quality is separately compromised: Bürgi/Deng/Whelan 2026 (UCD, read in full) find Kalshi's overall average contract return is about -20%, with sub-10c contracts losing takers over 60% of stake — meaning any detector must discount Kalshi legs for adverse selection, not just the mechanical fee already modeled in kalshiFee(). Ramesh et al. 2019 (read in full) independently confirms cross-book (not cross-venue) mispricing is real and bootstrap-significant, grounding the general "shop many venues" mechanism Gridiron already exploits for spreads. GitHub's public repo landscape for this exact topic ("polymarket-kalshi-arbitrage-bot" etc.) is dominated by keyword-stuffed, unlicensed repos consistent with known crypto-bot malware/wallet-drainer spam patterns — none were cloned or should be trusted. Recommendation: build this as honest measurement infrastructure extending existing, correct math (priceMiddle's empirical-PMF approach) across venues and market types, with hard exit tests tied to the NBA paper's tiny realized numbers, not as a revenue plan — and fix three specific existing defects (ad hoc devig, 5 disagreeing CLV implementations, assumed-leg-independence) before trusting any signal the new detector produces.

sources.title: Inter-market Arbitrage in Betting
sources.authors: Egon Franck, Erwin Verbeek, Stephan Nüesch
sources.sample: 11,933 European soccer matches (EPL, Ligue 1, Bundesliga, Serie A, Primera Division), 7 seasons 2004/05-2010/11, 10 bookmakers + Betfair exchange
sources.key_result: 2,287 bookmaker-vs-exchange (inter-market) arbitrage opportunities found, average return 1.4%, available in more than 1 in 6 matches; only 102 bookmaker-vs-bookmaker (intra-market) opportunities. Bookmakers lose money on the arbitraged leg (-11.3% avg), suggesting deliberate customer-acquisition pricing, not random noise.

sources.title: Arbitrage Analysis in Polymarket NBA Markets
sources.authors: Guang Cheng, Jiaxin Yang, Haoxuan Zou
sources.sample: 173 NBA games Feb 4-Mar 4 2026; 75,088,497 order-book snapshots polled every 3.6-5.5s; 3,042 single markets, 8.59M combinatorial states
sources.key_result: Single-market arbitrage: only 7 executable episodes total, median duration 3.6 seconds, capped profit $210.19 across the whole month. Combinatorial (moneyline vs spread) arbitrage: 290 episodes, median yield 101bps, capped profit $559.59 total, 76.9% of episodes bottlenecked to ~14.8 shares by shallow depth. The theoretical double-payout 'Middle jackpot' was mathematically defined but never once empirically realized across all 290 episodes.

sources.title: Makers and Takers: The Economics of the Kalshi Prediction Market
sources.authors: Constantin Burgi, Wanying Deng, Karl Whelan
sources.sample: 46,282 distinct Kalshi contracts, 12,403 events, 2021-April 2025, 300,000+ prices (transaction-level, Maker/Taker side identified directly from Kalshi's own data)
sources.key_result: Clear favorite-longshot bias: contracts priced under 10c lose over 60% of investors' money on average; overall average return across all Kalshi contracts is about -20%. Takers (the side any arbitrage bot would be, accepting a quote) lose more than Makers on both ends of the bias.

sources.title: Beating the House: Identifying Inefficiencies in Sports Betting Markets
sources.authors: Sathya Ramesh, Ragib Mostofa, Marco Bornstein, John Dobelman
sources.venue: arXiv preprint (Federal Reserve Board / Rice / U. Maryland)
sources.sample: 16 Las Vegas sportsbooks, 1990-2017, NFL/NBA/NCAAF(Power Five)/NCAAB/WNBA, line and result data scraped from vegasinsider.com and archive.org
sources.key_result: Random spread betting returns about -4.4% (baseline vig). A non-parametric win-probability model exploiting cross-book price dispersion produces a statistically significant positive optimal ROI in all 5 sports under a 10,000-iteration bootstrap with Bonferroni-corrected 99% CIs excluding zero -- though the optimal hyperparameters are tuned on the same historical sample used to report the result, an overfitting risk the paper does not itself flag.

sources.title: How quickly is temporary market inefficiency removed?
sources.venue: Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance 49(3), 917-930
sources.sample: Internet sports-betting arbitrage opportunities (per published abstract/secondary summary)
sources.key_result: Median arbitrage-opportunity duration approximately 15 minutes; most gone within an hour; harder-to-find opportunities persist longer.

sources.title: Inefficient Forecasts at the Sportsbook: An Analysis of Real-Time Betting Line Movement
sources.sample: 3,681 MLB games, opening-to-close line movement, 4 sportsbooks (per published abstract/secondary summary; full text paywalled)
sources.key_result: Simple strategies exploiting line movement (the mechanism underlying middling) would have yielded significant profit; line changes are significantly negatively autocorrelated (overreaction followed by partial reversion), rejecting weak-form efficiency.

sources.title: Unravelling the Probabilistic Forest: Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
sources.authors: Oriol Saguillo, Vahid Ghafouri, Lucianna Kiffer, Guillermo Suarez-Tangil
sources.venue: arXiv preprint / AFT 2025 (IMDEA Networks, Oxford Internet Institute)
sources.sample: All of Polymarket, ~1 year window, 86M+ trades, 7,000+ markets (per published abstract/secondary summary)
sources.key_result: $40M in realized arbitrage profit extracted platform-wide across intra-market ('Market Rebalancing') and inter-market ('Combinatorial') arbitrage -- but this is dominated by political/crypto/culture markets, not sports, which S2 above shows is a tiny liquidity-starved slice.

candidates.candidate: Replace the assumed-normal spread-to-probability proxy in exchangeVsBook() with a real devig method (Shin's method / power method / multiplicative, compared head-to-head) before treating any Kalshi-vs-book gap as a signal.
candidates.fixes_finding: No real devig method comparison exists; probabilities are extracted with one ad hoc approach.
candidates.mechanism: server/services/prediction-markets.js:173-228 exchangeVsBook() converts a book's posted SPREAD into a win probability via normCdf(-spread/14.16) -- an assumed-normal proxy -- and compares that to Kalshi's real moneyline price. This is not a no-vig book PRICE at all; it is a modeled stand-in. Any divergence it reports could be pure proxy error rather than real cross-venue disagreement, and the function's own docstring already concedes this ('an approximation of a no-vig moneyline rather than a quoted one').
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Implement 2-3 real devig methods (multiplicative, Shin, power) as pure functions, feed them from actual two-sided book moneyline quotes already captured in nfl_line_snapshots (book-feeds.js), and use that -- not the spread proxy -- as the book_probability input to exchangeVsBook(). Backtest calibration (Brier score) of each devig method against real game outcomes before picking one.
candidates.expected_value: No direct revenue; this is a correctness gate. Without it, every downstream cross-venue candidate below inherits an unvalidated proxy and risks manufacturing false-positive 'edges' the same way the failed 22-model NFL ensemble did.
candidates.exit_test: Compare Brier score of (a) the current normCdf(spread/14.16) proxy vs (b) each devig method, against a season of matched book-moneyline/game-outcome pairs. If no devig method improves calibration by a meaningful margin (e.g. Brier improvement > 0.005), document that the proxy is adequate and stop -- do not ship complexity that doesn't earn its keep.

candidates.candidate: Consolidate the 5 disagreeing CLV implementations into one ledger schema before building the cross-venue P&L tracking a new arb/middle detector needs.
candidates.fixes_finding: Five independent, disagreeing CLV (closing-line-value) implementations exist over four different tables with different math and sign conventions.
candidates.mechanism: nfl-clv.js, nfl-prop-clv.js, nfl-execution-clv.js, forward-ledger.js, and the betting-hub CLV route each compute closing-line-value differently. A cross-venue middle/arb detector needs to honestly measure realized vs. theoretical EV over time (exactly what CLV tracking is for) -- building that on top of an already-fractured measurement layer produces a 6th disagreeing implementation, not a fix.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Pick one canonical schema (likely forward-ledger.js's, since it's the one built to snapshot forward-looking state), migrate the other four call sites to write into it, and delete the redundant math rather than layering a sixth on top for the new detector's needs.
candidates.expected_value: Enables honest, comparable measurement of any candidate below; prevents this research from adding to a known-broken pattern the FOUND findings already flagged.
candidates.exit_test: Re-price the same 200+ historical picks through the old and new unified ledger; if the reconciled numbers don't match within noise, do not retire the old implementations until the discrepancy is understood.

candidates.candidate: Fix the same-game leg-independence assumption (root-caused in teaser-leg-rates.js) before pricing any combinatorial (moneyline+spread, same game) middle/arbitrage.
candidates.fixes_finding: Teaser-leg and same-game correlation is assumed independent (server/betting/nfl/strategy/teaser-leg-rates.js) with no copula/dependence model, despite legs sharing a game.
candidates.mechanism: A combinatorial cross-market-type middle (candidate new-combinatorial below) is structurally a same-game, correlated-leg bet -- Spread-cover is a strict subset of Moneyline-win by definition (per S2's own math). Pricing its hit probability by naive independence is not just imprecise, it is provably wrong in the nested case, the exact same failure mode already documented for teasers.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Extend signedMarginDistribution() in nfl-shopping-board.js (already an empirical PMF, already correct for the single-spread case) to a joint empirical distribution over (moneyline outcome, spread outcome) pairs from real historical game results, and use that joint PMF -- not an independence assumption -- inside any new combinatorial pricing function.
candidates.expected_value: Without this fix, a combinatorial detector's reported hit-probability and EV for the new-combinatorial candidate below are wrong by construction (nested events cannot be independent), which would repeat exactly the modeling error this research is grounded to fix.
candidates.exit_test: Compare hit-probability under naive independence vs. the true joint empirical PMF on held-out games for the Spread-implies-Moneyline case; ship only the joint-PMF version regardless of the size of the gap, since independence is mathematically wrong here, not just imprecise.

candidates.candidate: Generalize priceMiddle()/findMiddles() to accept a Kalshi or Polymarket leg alongside a sportsbook leg, producing the first cross-venue (exchange vs. sportsbook) arbitrage/middle signal Gridiron has ever computed.
candidates.mechanism: findMiddles() (nfl-shopping-board.js:267) is hard-scoped to simultaneousQuotes('spreads') across sportsbooks only; prediction-markets.js and polymarket.js are never called by it. Joining Kalshi's/Polymarket's already-captured quotes (captureKalshi, capturePolymarket) as an additional 'book' input to the existing, correct empirical-PMF math would be new, not duplicated, capability.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Add a venue-agnostic quote adapter that normalizes a Kalshi/Polymarket moneyline quote into the same {book, line, american_price} shape simultaneousQuotes() already produces for sportsbooks, feed it into priceMiddle() alongside a sportsbook moneyline leg (not spread, since Kalshi/Polymarket NFL game markets are moneyline-only per venueCostComparison()'s own caveat), and surface results in a new /betting/nfl/cross-venue-arb route.
candidates.expected_value: Realistically small in absolute dollars per S2 (whole-NBA-month total profit of $210-560), but this is the actual new measurement infrastructure the topic asks for, and its value is in the honest signal, not a revenue projection.
candidates.exit_test: After 4 weeks of live NFL-season capture, if fewer than ~5 executable (>$500 notional, matching polymarketCost()'s own 'tradeable' liquidity tier) cross-venue windows appear, retire the live-execution ambition and keep this as measurement-only, exactly the disposition prediction-markets.js already recommends for its own whale-flow module.

candidates.candidate: Build a combinatorial (moneyline vs. spread, cross-market-type) arbitrage/middle detector modeled on the mechanism S2 measures, generalized to any two of {Kalshi, Polymarket, sportsbook}.
candidates.mechanism: S2 shows this specific mechanism (Bid(Spread) > Ask(Moneyline), a mathematical mispricing since Spread-cover implies Moneyline-win) produced 290 episodes and $560 capped profit for one sport in one month -- more frequent than pure single-market arbitrage, but nothing in Gridiron checks Moneyline-vs-Spread consistency across ANY two venues today.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New module (e.g. server/services/nfl-combinatorial-arb.js) that pulls a Kalshi/Polymarket moneyline quote and a sportsbook spread quote for the same game+instant, checks the nested-event pricing inequality, and prices hit probability using the JOINT empirical PMF from the fix-correlation-independence candidate above (a hard dependency, not optional).
candidates.expected_value: Per S2's own numbers (median 101bps yield but $560 total profit, whole NBA month, 76.9% liquidity-capped to ~15 shares) and Gridiron's documented thinner NFL/Polymarket depth, expected value is likely below the NBA case -- frame internally as a research instrument, not a P&L line.
candidates.exit_test: Require the measured NFL combinatorial-episode rate (from real captured data) to be within the same order of magnitude as S2's NBA rate (roughly 2/game) before allocating any execution capital; if episodes run near 0/week for a full month of capture, retire the live version and keep the detector as a passive research/measurement tool only.

candidates.candidate: Build a depth/fill-aware execution simulator that consumes the bid_size/ask_size Polymarket already captures but nothing downstream reads.
candidates.mechanism: polymarket.js's captureOrderBooks() (line 140) stores best_bid, best_ask, bid_size, ask_size for every captured market, but polymarketCost() and every other consumer only ever reads price fields -- size is captured and never used. S2's headline liquidity finding (76.9% of episodes capped to ~14.8 shares) shows that ignoring size turns every theoretical-profit number into fiction.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: A pure function that walks a captured order book's size ladder against a target stake and returns realized-fillable size and realized (not quoted) EV; wire it into any candidate above before reporting a dollar figure to Nick.
candidates.expected_value: Makes every other candidate here trustworthy rather than aspirational; the honest finding may well be 'realistic fillable size is under $50, this is a research instrument, not a revenue stream' -- which is itself valuable output.
candidates.exit_test: Run the simulator retroactively against a week of already-captured order books; if realized fillable notional is consistently below a token stake (e.g. <$50), report that finding plainly rather than building further execution tooling.

candidates.candidate: Build a Kalshi maker/taker adverse-selection cost model, informed by S3's favorite-longshot findings, to haircut any Kalshi leg before it is treated as a clean tradeable price.
candidates.mechanism: kalshiFee() (polymarket.js:292) models only the mechanical 0.07*p*(1-p) trading fee. S3 shows a much larger, systematic cost: sub-10c contracts lose over 60% of stake on average and overall Kalshi contract return is about -20%, worse for Takers (the side any Gridiron detector would be on). No haircut for this exists anywhere in the codebase today.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: A new function alongside kalshiFee() that applies a price-dependent haircut curve fit to S3's reported favorite-longshot pattern, applied to every captured Kalshi quote before it enters exchangeVsBook() or the new cross-venue-middle candidate.
candidates.expected_value: Directly tests whether previously 'positive' cross-venue divergences survive a realistic cost model -- likely deflationary, which is the honest and useful result.
candidates.exit_test: Apply the haircut to a season of captured Kalshi quotes; if the haircut alone flips the majority of previously-detected positive-EV divergences negative, that is the finding to report -- do not suppress or re-tune the haircut to preserve a positive headline number.

do_not_do: Do not clone, install, or run any of the GitHub "polymarket-kalshi-arbitrage-bot" / "polymarket-arbitrage-trading-bot" repos found via gh search -- nearly all have keyword-stuffed descriptions repeating the same phrase 10-20 times, missing/non-standard licenses, and clustered recent-update timestamps, consistent with the well-documented GitHub crypto-trading-bot malware/wallet-drainer spam pattern. Treat as untrustworthy, not as a starting point.

Do not build any live-execution or auto-trading connector to a Kalshi or Polymarket wallet/API key. This is out of scope under the hard rule against executing financial trades, and the evidence (S2: $210-560 total capped profit across an entire NBA month) says the realistic edge is far too small to justify wallet/key custody risk.

Do not treat exchangeVsBook() divergences as a trading signal until the devig fix ships -- today the 'book probability' side is a normal-CDF proxy of a spread, not a real no-vig market price, so a reported gap may be pure model error.

Do not extend findMiddles()/priceMiddle() to include a Kalshi leg by treating Kalshi as just another spread-quoting 'book' -- Kalshi's NFL contracts are moneyline-only (per venueCostComparison()'s own caveat); naively pairing incompatible bet types will silently generate nonsense windows.

Do not present the Polymarket 'Middle jackpot' double-payout mechanism as an expected revenue pathway -- S2 measured zero jackpot realizations across all 290 combinatorial episodes in its sample; it is a mean-101bps-yield mechanism, not a lottery payoff to plan around.

Do not size any live position beyond token/paper-trading scale until a full season of live NFL capture validates episode frequency directly -- the NBA numbers in S2 do not transfer to NFL's much lower game density and Gridiron's own documented thinner Polymarket NFL liquidity.
Do not let this research quietly become a 6th CLV implementation -- unify the ledger (fix-clv-unify) before building any new P&L tracking for cross-venue trades.

result.label: Route/route-tree & man-vs-zone proxies from public PBP + formation data
result.summary: Gridiron already downloads and then discards the exact data this brief asked us to go find a "proxy" for. `nfl-formations.js` fetches nflverse's `pbp_participation_<season>.csv` every season and stores only 9 of its ~26 columns into `nfl_play_formations`. Verified by downloading and CSV-parsing the 2022, 2024, and 2025 release files directly: the file has always carried `route` (the primary receiver's charted route, 13-value domain), `defense_man_zone_type` (MAN_COVERAGE/ZONE_COVERAGE), `defense_coverage_type` (Cover 0/1/2/3/4/6/9, 2-Man, Combo), `was_pressure`, and `time_to_throw` — all FTN human film-charting (not tracking; `ngs_air_yards` is explicitly deprecated/NA from 2024 on per nflreadr's own dictionary, confirming the charting-not-tracking provenance). 2024 has 22,408 dropback plays labeled with a coverage shell (11,369 zone / 11,039 man) and 19,110 plays with a charted route. 2025 (last season) is fully backfillable through the Super Bowl. 2026 (this week's live season) has no file yet (404, confirmed) — this is a historical/backtest asset only until nflverse cuts a 2026 release, so it does not touch or help the live capture the harness is told not to disturb. Separately, the FTN charting table Gridiron *does* ingest is also missing 8 of its 29 published fields (read_thrown, n_blitzers, is_drop, starting_hash, etc.) — same pattern, same fix. `nfl_ngs` already stores real weekly avg_separation/avg_cushion/avg_yac_above_expectation per receiver but today is only ever averaged into one flat modifier scalar (nfl-player-value.js) — never conditioned on the opponent's man/zone rate, which is the actual matchup signal a props/route model needs and which nothing in Gridiron computes today. Literature confirms the general mechanism (situational/pre-snap features carry real coverage signal, and man/zone coverage strongly reshapes target-rate distribution by position: RBs get 12.74% TPRR vs man vs 19.90% vs zone, stable 2022-2025) but every tracking-free classification method in the papers surveyed still requires snap-frame tracking positions, not box-score formation counts — so a pure formation-only man/zone classifier for the live current season is a genuinely new thing to build, not something the literature has already validated.

sources.title: NFL Coverage Funnels & Positional Target Tendencies
sources.key_result: Using charted coverage data across 2022-2025 regular seasons: RB target-rate-per-route-run is 12.74% vs man coverage but 19.90% vs zone (stable each season); WRs see higher target share vs man, TEs/RBs vs zone; slot receivers gain +3.93pp target rate on a blitz vs +2.94pp for outside WRs, and RBs are the only group whose target rate falls on a blitz. States its own limitation: coverage-shell splits (single-high/two-high) are coarser than true coverage-type splits since different coverage types under one shell produce very different target distributions.
sources.sample: Charted plays, 2022-2025 NFL regular seasons (SumerSports charting lineage, same underlying methodology family as FTN's public nflverse release)

sources.title: Integrating Unsupervised and Supervised Learning for the Prediction of Defensive Schemes in American Football
sources.key_result: Elastic-net logistic regression + GBM classify man vs zone coverage on 3,963 plays (2,980 zone / 983 man) from the first 9 weeks of the 2024 NFL Big Data Bowl tracking release. Pre-motion contextual features (down, distance, score, quarter, seconds remaining) plus tracking-derived snap-frame positions form the baseline; adding post-snap trajectory + HMM-derived latent-assignment features improves accuracy/AUC/logloss (reported only as boxplots over 50 cross-fitting runs, no single point estimate given). Authors explicitly flag the sample as 'quite small, constraining both model complexity and generalizability.' Critically, even the paper's 'pre-motion' baseline requires tracking-derived standardized player coordinates at the snap — it is NOT a tracking-free method, despite using only pre-snap timing.
sources.sample: 3,963 offensive plays, weeks 1-9 of the 2024 season, NFL Big Data Bowl 2025 tracking data

sources.title: Unsupervised methods for identifying pass coverage among defensive backs with NFL player tracking data
sources.venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 16(2), pp. 143-161
sources.key_result: Canonical academic reference for coverage identification via hierarchical clustering on full player-tracking trajectories — cited here only as the tracking-based ceiling method, to bound how much signal a charted-label or formation-only proxy necessarily gives up (mid-play rotations, busted assignments) relative to true tracking.

candidates.candidate: Stop discarding it: extend nfl-formations.js ingestFormations() to store route, defense_man_zone_type, defense_coverage_type, was_pressure, time_to_throw into nfl_play_formations (new columns), backfill seasons 2019-2025, and delete the stale 'participation ends after 2023' comment.
candidates.mechanism: The pbp_participation CSV Gridiron already fetches every season has always carried these 6 columns; the parser in ingestFormations() (server/services/nfl-formations.js) only ever mapped 9 of ~26 header fields into the INSERT statement. This is a one-function edit plus an ALTER TABLE, not new data acquisition — verified by downloading and parsing the actual 2019-2025 release files in this session.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-formations.js ingestFormations(); server/db/schema/nfl-a-to-m.js nfl_play_formations CREATE TABLE (add columns via migration, keyed off existing game_id+play_id PK which already matches nflverse pbp's join key)
candidates.expected_value: Ground-truth man/zone coverage shell and targeted-receiver route on ~2.9M play-rows across 7 seasons, for zero new data acquisition cost — the single highest-value/lowest-cost item in this research.
candidates.exit_test: After backfill, SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE defense_man_zone_type IS NOT NULL by season should land near the row counts measured in this session (2024: 22,408 of 45,919; 2025: comparable) — if far lower, the column mapping is wrong, not the data.

candidates.candidate: Backfill the 8 missing FTN charting columns (read_thrown, n_blitzers, is_drop, is_interception_worthy, is_catchable_ball, is_created_reception, starting_hash, is_qb_sneak) into nfl_play_charting.
candidates.mechanism: Same pattern as C1: ingestCharting() in nfl-formations.js already downloads ftn_charting_<season>.csv and only maps 12 of the file's 29 documented fields into the INSERT. read_thrown (which progression read a route was) is directly route-context relevant and currently thrown away.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-formations.js ingestCharting(); nfl_play_charting table (server/db/schema/nfl-a-to-m.js)
candidates.expected_value: Cheap breadth: read_thrown and n_blitzers are usable QB-decision/pressure-design features for prop and matchup models with no new ingestion pipeline.
candidates.exit_test: Row-level spot check that read_thrown values match a small hand-checked sample of known plays (e.g. a documented broken coverage / blown assignment play) before trusting it in any feature.

candidates.candidate: Add a `coverage` feature block to PROP_PLAYER_FEATURE_BLOCKS in nfl-props-player-features.js: per-player pre-week rolling man-rate-faced, zone-rate-faced, and route-mix share, joined from the C1 table via game_id/play_id to the target's gsis_id in pbp.
candidates.mechanism: nfl-props-player-features.js already has the exact pattern for season-level, strictly-pre-Week-1 context blocks (career/preseason/churn) with *_missing indicators; this candidate follows that same contract using play-level coverage data joined to the shared player-week engine, rather than season-aggregated engines.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-props-player-features.js PROP_PLAYER_FEATURE_BLOCKS; join target via nflverse_game_id/play_id from C1's nfl_play_formations to pbp's receiver_player_id
candidates.expected_value: Direct signal for the props module (Gridiron's one area of measured skill, +27% Brier on 2+ TD) using the JJ substack's confirmed effect sizes (RB TPRR 12.74% man vs 19.90% zone) as a prior on expected feature importance.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest 2023-2025: does adding the coverage block improve out-of-sample Brier score on RB/WR reception-prop heads vs. the career/preseason/churn-only baseline already in the file? Ship only if yes on held-out weeks.

candidates.candidate: Defense-level man-rate/zone-rate/blitz-rate splits by team, computed from the C1 table, exposed as a new opponent-matchup surface (e.g. nfl-formations.js formationDistribution()-style endpoint, team-keyed).
candidates.mechanism: Group C1's defense_man_zone_type and n_blitzers (from C2) by defending team and week to produce a rolling 'this defense plays X% man' number — the missing multiplier between a receiver's own avg_separation (already in nfl_ngs) and the specific defense he's about to face.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New function alongside formationDistribution() in server/services/nfl-formations.js, grouped by possession's opponent rather than possession team
candidates.expected_value: Turns the currently-unconditioned nfl_ngs avg_separation number (server/services/nfl-player-value.js:159, flat multi-week average with no opponent context) into an opponent-aware feature.
candidates.exit_test: Sanity-check against 2-3 well-known man-heavy/zone-heavy defenses by public reputation (e.g. teams widely reported as predominantly Cover-1/man in that season) before trusting the numbers for modeling.

candidates.candidate: Same-target-share negative correlation for player-prop parlays: use C1's route/coverage-shell data to estimate how two receivers on the same team/game actually trade targets under a given coverage shell, replacing whatever independence assumption nfl-prop-correlation.js currently uses for cross-player legs.
candidates.mechanism: Two WRs facing the same coverage shell on the same drive are drawing from a shared, shell-constrained target pool; C1's per-play coverage label plus existing target/route data lets this be measured directly rather than assumed independent or estimated purely from historical target-share covariance.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-prop-correlation.js fitPropCorrelations()/samePlayerCorrelation() — add a shell-conditioned cross-player term
candidates.expected_value: Improves same-game-parlay pricing realism for player props specifically (distinct from the game-margin teaser correlation defect, which this does not address — see do_not_do).
candidates.exit_test: Compare shell-conditioned cross-player correlation estimate against the existing empirical historical covariance in fitPropCorrelations() on a held-out season; only ship if it moves in the theoretically expected direction (more negative under heavier man coverage, where one WR's press coverage frees the other) and not just noise.

candidates.candidate: Train a formation-only (no tracking) man/zone probability classifier on 2019-2025 ground truth from C1, using only same-week-available features (offense_formation, personnel, defenders_in_box, down, distance, score differential) — to impute coverage-shell probability for the live current season before nflverse's delayed participation file exists.
candidates.mechanism: Every tracking-free man/zone classification method found in the literature surveyed here (arXiv 2602.10784, and the Big Data Bowl coverage-classification lineage it draws on) still uses tracking-derived snap-frame positions, not box-score formation counts — this specific approach (features from nfl_play_formations/PBP only) has not been validated in the literature reviewed and would be a genuinely novel model, gradeable against real held-out FTN labels from the very data this research surfaced.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New service alongside nfl-formations.js; train/eval using nfl_play_formations (post-C1) as both features and labels, leave-one-season-out
candidates.expected_value: Only candidate here that gives a coverage-shell signal for the live 2026 season (participation file lag confirmed: 404 as of 2026-09-12) — but explicitly speculative; no published baseline exists to compare against, so the exit test is the whole point of doing it.
candidates.exit_test: Leave-one-season-out AUC against real FTN labels (2019-2025) must clear a pre-registered bar (e.g. AUC > 0.65, chosen before looking at results) before this is used for anything beyond an experiment; if it doesn't clear the bar, the honest conclusion is that formation-only proxies don't work and Gridiron should just wait for the delayed nflverse release each season.

candidates.candidate: Use C1's charted route-type outcome distributions (yards/catch-rate per route label, e.g. SCREEN vs GO vs SLANT) as latent mixture components: a player's weekly prop projection becomes a mixture over his own route mix rather than one point forecast, giving the props module its first real distributional structure.
candidates.fixes_finding: Player props are point-estimate projections, not distributions — no negative-binomial/hierarchical/calibrated model; the module is the project's one area of genuine measured skill (2+ TD Brier skill +27%) but under-measured against real prices.
candidates.mechanism: Each of the 13 charted route labels in C1 has its own empirical yards-per-target and catch-probability distribution (directly measurable once C1 is ingested). Weighting those component distributions by a player's own route mix (and, combined with C4, by the upcoming defense's coverage-shell tendency) produces a genuine finite mixture distribution for a reception/yardage prop instead of a single scalar rescaled by a calibration head — a real, if modest, first step toward the negative-binomial/hierarchical structure the finding says is missing.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-props.js (the volume x efficiency point-forecast chain described in nfl-props-player-features.js's own header) — insert the mixture step between the player-week engine output and the calibration head
candidates.expected_value: Directly targets the props module's one confirmed weakness (point estimates, no calibrated interval) using data this research shows is already sitting unused in a file Gridiron downloads every week.
candidates.exit_test: Compare CRPS (continuous ranked probability score) or pinball loss of the mixture-distribution forecast against the current point-estimate + calibration-head forecast on 2023-2025 held-out weeks; ship only if it beats the point-estimate baseline, since a distribution that is no more accurate than the point estimate it's built from is not worth the added complexity.

do_not_do: Do not ingest raw Big Data Bowl player-tracking coordinates (x/y trajectories) to chase a 'better' coverage classifier — it is a large new data-storage and parsing commitment that duplicates what FTN's already-public charted labels (C1) give for free, for the specific years Gridiron actually needs (2019-2025 history).

Do not build or rely on any real-time/live coverage-shell feed during the current season — no free public feed publishes man/zone labels in-week; the 2026 pbp_participation file does not exist yet (confirmed 404 on 2026-09-12) and treating a formation-only proxy (C6) as ground-truth-equivalent for live decisions would be dishonest about its unvalidated accuracy.

Do not touch, query heavily, or run any ingestion job against the live fantasy-football-dashboard database or its running server while it is capturing this week's NFL games — all verification in this research was done by downloading nflverse CSVs directly to a scratch directory, not by touching the read-only repo's live process.

Do not describe the charted `route` field as a full route-tree (every receiver's route on the play) — it is one route per play, for the primary/targeted receiver only; overselling this to the modeling team would produce a feature that silently degrades to null on plays where the target isn't the intended primary read.

Do not present a formation-only man/zone classifier (C6) as validated by the literature — every tracking-free-sounding method found in this search still uses tracking-derived snap-frame positions; C6 is explicitly unvalidated and must clear a pre-registered accuracy bar before use, not be assumed to work by analogy.

result.label: N17-weather-and-venue-causal
result.summary: Gridiron's weather/venue "adjustment" (server/services/nfl-ensemble.js:581-595, component `weather_total`) is three hand-picked constants (dome +1.2, wind>=15 -2.4, cold<32 -1.6) with no controls, no altitude term, and no team-level heterogeneity — applied identically to every team/season. This is not because the data is missing: Gridiron already has game-level archived weather (nfl_game_weather), a 5-lead forecast history (nfl_game_weather_forecast_history, consumed only by line-move-study.js for market-movement study, never for a totals signal), an ingested-but-unused altitude column (nfl_stadiums.altitude, populated by nfelo.js but never joined into features/ensemble), and per-team dome_epa_delta/wind_epa_delta already computed in nfl-features.js but discarded by the flat constant. Read 1 Stanford STATS50 project in full (2009-2015, ~1,800 games, lasso regression interacting weather with team pass/rush strength, MSE 12.5 pts, 67-68.6% win accuracy, and an honestly-stated limitation that they couldn't separate weather effects from unmodeled home-field advantage). Read 1 open-access exercise-physiology review (Frontiers/PMC) in full for the altitude causal mechanism (VO2max decrements starting ~1600m, ~2-week acclimatization, team-sport sprint recovery insufficient even after individual-athlete windows) — Denver sits at 1,609m. Two more sources (Rodney Paul 2017 IJSF on humidity vs. market totals rejecting efficiency; nflanalytic.com's own admission that its wind-bucket comparison can't separate wind's effect from cold-weather teams building run-heavy rosters) were read at abstract/summary depth only (paywalled / WebFetch-summarized), flagged as such. Five new-capability candidates: (1) two-way fixed-effects panel regression replacing the 3 constants, identified off within-team weather variation to kill the roster-selection confound; (2) add humidity+pressure to the already-working Open-Meteo pipeline and test the Paul (2017) claim on Gridiron's own data rather than trust the abstract; (3) synthetic-control estimate of Denver's altitude effect (N=1 treated unit — explicitly not a causal-forest problem) focused on 2nd-half fatigue per the acclimatization mechanism; (4) a wind-surprise (forecast-lead vs. realized) signal built entirely from tables/functions that already exist and are already wired to the wrong consumer; (5) replace the flat wind constant with the per-team wind_epa_delta Gridiron already computes, shrunk empirical-Bayes style as a cheap stepping stone toward a real CATE/causal-forest model later. All fixes_finding = "none — new capability" per this agent's assigned bucket (none of tonight's 12 verified defects names weather/venue handling). Do-not-do list centers on: don't add a fourth unvalidated flat constant, don't launder a raw stratified-mean comparison as "causal," don't run a causal forest on Denver's N=1 altitude treatment (use synthetic control), cluster errors by week (weather is spatially/temporally correlated across a Sunday slate), and don't ship candidates 2/4 without passing their stated Gridiron-data exit test first.

sources.title: Weather and the NFL (Houghton-Berry, Park & Pierce — Stanford STATS50 class project)
sources.key_result: Lasso regression on 2009-2015 NFL games (~1,800), interacting weather (temp/wind/rain/snow/indoor/turf) with team pass/rush YPA strength rather than team identity; MSE 12.5 pts on score differential, 67.3-68.6% win accuracy on 2015 holdout. Explicitly states it could not separate weather effects from unmodeled home-field advantage — a stated limitation, not a hidden flaw.
sources.sample: 2009-2015 seasons, ~1,800 games, train 2009-2014 / test 2015
sources.authors: Rory Houghton-Berry, Edwin Park, Kathy Pierce

sources.title: Preparation for Endurance Competitions at Altitude: Physiological, Psychological, Dietary and Coaching Aspects
sources.key_result: Performance decrements from altitude begin as low as ~700-1600m depending on event duration, driven by VO2max reduction; partial acclimatization takes 5-7 days, near-complete by 2 weeks; explicitly notes team-sport sprint-recovery windows may be insufficient even after individual-athlete acclimatization periods. Not NFL-specific (endurance/individual-sport altitude camps at 1,780-4,300m) — used here only for the causal mechanism, with that limitation stated.
sources.sample: Narrative review synthesizing multiple altitude-training studies, exposures 1,780-4,300m

sources.title: The Impact of Atmospheric Conditions on Actual and Expected Scoring in the NFL
sources.key_result: Per abstract/indexed summary only (403 paywalled, ResearchGate also blocked): humidity has a statistically significant relationship to the gap between actual NFL scoring and the market total; wagering strategies on humidity, wind, and both combined are reported to reject market efficiency. Full regression form, exact sample size, and ROI figures could not be verified — flagged as unread in the notes file.

sources.title: Weather & NFL Scoring: It's the Wind
sources.key_result: Descriptive stratified-mean comparison over 7,276 games (1999-2025): 44.7 pts at 0-5mph wind vs 40.5 pts at 16+mph. Explicitly admits, in its own words, that it cannot separate the wind effect from cold-weather franchises building run-leaning rosters — the exact confound this research addresses. Read via WebFetch summary, not raw full text.

candidates.candidate: Two-way fixed-effects panel regression for the weather-on-total causal effect, replacing the three flat constants in weather_total
candidates.mechanism: Regress realized game total on wind/temp/precip x roof-type dummies with team-offense FE, team-defense FE, and season FE, using nfl_game_weather joined to game_lines. Identification comes from within-team variation in weather across a team's own away games, which directly resolves the roster-selection confound (comparing Buffalo-in-wind to Buffalo-in-calm, not Buffalo-in-wind to Miami-in-calm).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-ensemble.js:581-595 (weather_total component) consuming nfl_game_weather + game_lines; implementable as plain OLS-with-dummies in JS, no new dependency.
candidates.expected_value: Turns weather_total from three unvalidated guesses into a component with real standard errors and out-of-sample calibration, feeding the ensemble honestly instead of via constants nobody has ever backtested.
candidates.exit_test: Out-of-sample RMSE and interval coverage on 2024-2025 held-out weeks vs. current three-constant weather_total and vs. dropping the component entirely (must beat both).

candidates.candidate: Fetch and store humidity + surface pressure from Open-Meteo; test as a marginal totals signal net of wind/temp/dome
candidates.mechanism: Add relative_humidity_2m and surface_pressure to the existing Open-Meteo hourly query; add columns to nfl_game_weather; backfill 2022-2025 from the same archive endpoint already used for wind/temp. Test humidity's marginal contribution inside the candidate-1 fixed-effects regression, directly probing the Paul (2017) abstract-level claim on Gridiron's own data.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-weather.js hourAt()/forecastHourAt() (currently requests only temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m,wind_gusts_10m,precipitation) and the nfl_game_weather schema in server/db/schema/nfl-n-to-z.js:598.
candidates.expected_value: Cheap to test (the API and ingestion pattern already exist); if it survives its own exit test, gives a signal source competitors likely aren't tracking either.
candidates.exit_test: Does adding humidity to the candidate-1 regression reduce out-of-sample total RMSE by a real margin, not just move in-sample R^2? If not, log the null result and drop it.

candidates.candidate: Synthetic-control estimate of Denver's altitude effect (N=1 treated unit) focused on the 2nd-half/fatigue window
candidates.mechanism: Join the already-ingested nfl_stadiums.altitude into nfl-features.js's venue context. Because Denver is the only high-altitude team, team-FE regression can't identify an altitude coefficient (perfect collinearity) — use synthetic control instead: build a synthetic 'Denver' from a weighted blend of similarly-styled sea-level teams' own home performance, and compare against real Denver's home scoring / 4th-quarter differential, weighted toward road-team 2nd-half fatigue per the acclimatization mechanism (VO2max decrements, ~2-week acclimatization vs. teams arriving 1-2 days out).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/db/schema/mlb-model-misc.js:244-248 (nfl_stadiums.altitude, populated by server/services/nfelo.js:195-220 but never consumed elsewhere) joined into nfl-features.js's venue builder (~lines 350-390) and nfl-ensemble.js.
candidates.expected_value: Denver is a well-known but currently completely unmodeled (zero altitude term anywhere) home-field/total effect; a validated synthetic-control estimate with a placebo test would be a genuinely new, defensible signal rather than folklore.
candidates.exit_test: Placebo test (running the identical procedure on a random sea-level 'fake-treated' team should show ~0 effect) plus split-by-half-of-season stability check before trusting the point estimate.

candidates.candidate: Wind-surprise (forecast-lead vs. realized) signal reusing nfl_game_weather_forecast_history, currently wired to the wrong consumer
candidates.mechanism: nfl_game_weather_forecast_history already stores wind at 5/3/2/1/0 day leads before kickoff via forecastHistoryFeatures(); the market total is set mostly off the ~3-5 day lead forecast. The gap between that early forecast and the realized (lead-0/archive) wind is a much cleaner causal quantity than raw realized wind, because it isolates the part of the weather the market didn't get to price, sidestepping the roster-selection confound that contaminates raw wind readings.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-weather-history.js (forecastHistoryFeatures) currently consumed only by server/services/line-move-study.js:206-210 for studying market line movement — never fed into a totals prediction or dedicated betting signal.
candidates.expected_value: Nearly free — the data and extraction function already exist; this is purely a new consumer plus a backtest.
candidates.exit_test: Does the wind-surprise gap (lead0 minus lead3/5) show any relationship to closing-total-vs-actual-total error across the historical sample, and is it economically meaningful net of vig on 2,000+ games (not just statistically nonzero)?

candidates.candidate: Replace the flat wind constant with Gridiron's own already-computed per-team wind_epa_delta, empirical-Bayes shrunk, as a stepping stone to a full causal-forest CATE
candidates.mechanism: nfl-features.js already computes dome_epa_delta and wind_epa_delta per team (EPA/play indoors minus outdoors, windy minus calm) but weather_total ignores them and applies -2.4 to every team uniformly. Replace with a per-team wind sensitivity, shrunk toward the population mean for teams with few windy-game observations (empirical Bayes) — the practical, buildable-today version of the heterogeneous treatment effect the Stanford project's team-strength interaction already suggests is real (wind hurts pass-heavy offenses more).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-features.js:194-211,350-388 (dome_epa_delta, wind_epa_delta already computed) feeding server/services/nfl-ensemble.js's weather_total component, which currently discards them.
candidates.expected_value: Cheapest of the five to ship (data already exists, just unused); directly testable against the current flat constant.
candidates.exit_test: Does per-team wind sensitivity beat the flat -2.4 on out-of-sample total RMSE, specifically split on high-pass-rate vs high-rush-rate teams, where the flat constant should be most wrong?

repos.what_it_does: Python implementation of the synthetic control estimator and diagnostics (placebo tests, weight fitting).
repos.adoption_path: Read for the weight-optimization/placebo-test design used in candidate 3; reimplement the (small) quadratic weight-fitting routine natively in JS rather than adding a Python runtime to the Node backend.

repos.license: Other (Microsoft Research-derived; check terms before commercial redistribution)
repos.what_it_does: Doubly-robust / double-ML causal forests and orthogonal ML for conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimation.
repos.adoption_path: Use only as an algorithmic reference for a possible future full-CATE upgrade of candidate 5 (e.g. an offline Python batch job producing a static per-team-x-weather CATE table consumed by the JS ensemble); the empirical-Bayes shrinkage version in candidate 5 is the Node-native stepping stone to try first.

repos.what_it_does: Alternative Python synthetic-control implementation.
repos.adoption_path: Considered as an alternative to pysyncon for candidate 3; pysyncon preferred (more recently active, more narrowly scoped) so this is noted but not the primary reference.

do_not_do: Do not add another flat constant (e.g. "+0.5 for altitude") alongside the existing three — that repeats the exact defect this research targets instead of removing it.

Do not treat nflanalytic.com's raw wind-bucket average-total comparison, or any raw stratified mean, as a causal estimate wired into the ensemble — it is precisely the roster-selection-confounded comparison the source itself admits it cannot resolve.
Do not run a causal forest / per-observation CATE model on the altitude question — there is exactly one treated unit (Denver), a classic small-N causal-inference trap; use synthetic control instead.

Do not treat forecast-lead readings or same-week weather observations as independent when computing standard errors — games in the same week share synoptic weather systems; cluster by week or the false-precision problem already flagged elsewhere in Gridiron (missing conformal/calibrated intervals) reappears here.

Do not ship the humidity signal (candidate 2) or the wind-surprise signal (candidate 4) on literature alone — both are explicitly untested-on-Gridiron's-own-data hypotheses; require the stated exit test to pass on the 2022-2025 sample first.

Do not touch the live fantasy-football-dashboard database, run its migrations, or execute any of its code — this research was produced by reading files only; implementation requires a follow-up session with explicit write access, not inferred permission from these notes.

result.label: N18 — social-media / market-sentiment signals
result.summary: Read the actual literature on social/market sentiment predicting betting lines or fantasy value: it is thin, old, and mostly negative. The one cited positive (Sinha et al., tweet-volume features, 55.6% ATS on 252 games, no multiplicity correction) is marginal and unreplicated; the load-bearing negative (Lachanski & Pav's replication of Bollen's Twitter-mood-predicts-stocks paper) shows the effect vanishes as data-snooping once the full sample is used — the exact failure mode Gridiron's own missing trial registry would let recur. The one effect that does replicate (Feddersen/Humphreys/Soebbing: Facebook-likes popularity bias in bookmaker pricing) is a price-shading symptom, not a standalone tradeable signal, and it already has a natural home in Gridiron's one demonstrated-working edge (sharp-vs-rec book divergence, nfl-sharp.js) rather than as a new pipeline. Fantasy-specific social sentiment has zero published evidence either way. Gridiron already has a deliberately non-sentiment insider-tweet pipeline (twitter-ingest.js, nfl-news-signal.js) and an existing but dormant tweet-to-line-move correlator (nfl-tweet-line-correlation.js) plus an unused 12.4M-row Polymarket quote tape (polymarket_quotes) and a proliferating, uncoordinated CLV layer (4+ files) that any new signal would need to plug into. Verdict: do not build a general sentiment-scoring pipeline; the two things worth actually trying are narrow, cheap, and strictly gated.

sources.title: Predicting the NFL using Twitter
sources.authors: Shiladitya Sinha, Chris Dyer, Kevin Gimpel, Noah A. Smith
sources.sample: 252 NFL games, one season, tweet-volume + lexicon-sentiment features per team pre-kickoff
sources.key_result: Tweet-based features alone reached 55.6% accuracy against the closing spread via logistic regression, matching/exceeding a traditional game-stats model; authors themselves flag small sample and coarse (non-validated) sentiment extraction as limitations — a marginal, single-season edge with no multiplicity correction applied.

sources.title: Shy of the Character Limit: "Twitter Mood Predicts the Stock Market" Revisited
sources.sample: Replication of Bollen, Mao & Zeng (2011): original Feb–Nov 2008 Twitter/DJIA sample extended backward to include 2007 tweets the original authors had collected but discarded
sources.key_result: The originally 'significant' Twitter-mood → market Granger-causal relationship reproduces only on the truncated original subsample and vanishes on the fuller backward-extended sample — 'a result consistent with data snooping.' No out-of-sample predictive power found; paper notes Derwent Capital's hedge fund built on this signal failed and closed in 2012.

sources.title: Sentiment Bias and Asset Prices: Evidence from Sports Betting Markets and Social Media
sources.authors: Arne Feddersen, Brad R. Humphreys, Brian P. Soebbing
sources.sample: Two seasons of prices/outcomes across seven professional sports leagues in Europe and North America; Facebook 'Likes' per team as sentiment/popularity proxy
sources.key_result: Bookmakers shade prices favorably toward teams with more Facebook likes (measurable sentiment bias in price-setting), but favorably-priced popular teams do not actually win more often — the bias is a real, replicated price distortion, not by itself an exploitable inefficiency; it shows up as a symptom in the price rather than a standalone signal. (Note: full PDF body not text-extractable from host; findings verified from abstract/results summary on the paper's own repository pages, not full body text.)

sources.title: Highly Regarded Investors? Mining Predictive Value from the Collective Intelligence of Reddit's WallStreetBets
sources.sample: WallStreetBets posts/comments, multi-year corpus
sources.key_result: Search-level read only (abstract/summary, not full body): converges with adjacent literature that sentiment polarity has weak correlation with subsequent price moves while volume/attention metrics (post count, Google Trends) are a modestly more reliable signal; no fantasy-sports-specific social-sentiment study was found anywhere in this search — that absence is itself an honest finding for the fantasy side of this topic.

candidates.candidate: Route any future sentiment-vs-line-move test through ONE canonical CLV grader instead of adding a 6th competing implementation
candidates.fixes_finding: Five independent, disagreeing CLV (closing-line-value) implementations exist over four different tables with different math and sign conventions.
candidates.mechanism: nfl-tweet-line-correlation.js currently detects a post-tweet line move itself (against nfl_line_snapshots, its own noise-floor logic) rather than calling nfl-clv.js's grading function. Before any sentiment/social signal is judged 'did this produce value,' it must be graded through one canonical, sign-consistent CLV path — otherwise a 6th disagreeing implementation gets created the moment this topic's candidates are built.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Refactor server/services/nfl-tweet-line-correlation.js's move-detection to call into server/services/nfl-clv.js (or a designated canonical wrapper) instead of computing its own delta; require any new sentiment feature module to report through the same path before it can be scored.
candidates.expected_value: Not a new signal itself, but a prerequisite: without it, every sentiment experiment below produces a locally-consistent but globally-incomparable number, exactly the failure mode that already produced 5 disagreeing CLV implementations.
candidates.exit_test: After refactor, running the existing tweet-line-move backtest and a prop-CLV backtest through the same call path produces CLV numbers with matching sign convention on a shared sample of games — verified by a script comparing both outputs on 20 overlapping events.

candidates.candidate: Mine the already-collected 12.4M-row polymarket_quotes tape for order-flow sentiment (trade aggressor side, size, block-trade flag) instead of leaving it idle
candidates.fixes_finding: A 12.4-million-row Polymarket quote tape exists and is essentially unused for anything beyond spread-ladder construction.
candidates.mechanism: prediction-markets.js already states the hypothesis (aggressive on-exchange flow leads sportsbook line movement) but says it 'needs accumulated observations to answer.' The observations already exist in polymarket_quotes/polymarket_price_history (mlb-model-misc.js:562) — this is a market-sentiment signal (order-flow imbalance, not social text) that is strictly data Gridiron already paid to collect and is not using.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Add a feature extractor reading polymarket_quotes for trade-side imbalance and size around NFL games, join against nfl_line_snapshots by kickoff time, and route the resulting 'did aggressive flow lead the book' test through the F1 canonical CLV path.
candidates.expected_value: Genuinely unknown but cheap to test — the data is already paid for and sitting idle; a null result (the stated risk in the module's own comments — 'we are watching the same move arrive by a different route') is itself useful information for closing this avenue for good.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest over one season: does polymarket order-flow imbalance lead sportsbook line moves by a statistically detectable lag (Granger-style, pre-registered lag window) on held-out games — if r² is near the 0.0016 the project already measured for its own opening-line disagreement, kill it.

candidates.candidate: Use prediction-market implied probabilities as the exogenous observation feeding nfl-team-strength.js's update, replacing the hand-tuned preseason/in-season blend
candidates.fixes_finding: Team-strength ratings (nfl-team-strength.js) mix stale preseason priors with in-season data via a hand-tuned blend, not a principled state-space/Bayesian update.
candidates.mechanism: Kalshi/Polymarket win probabilities are a real-time, continuously-updating crowd (market) consensus already partially ingested by prediction-markets.js. Feeding that as the observation in a proper Kalman/Bayesian filter for team strength replaces an arbitrary blend weight with a principled update that decays the stale prior automatically as new market information arrives — this is a market-sentiment signal used as a MODEL INPUT, not a new bet.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-team-strength.js — replace the hand-tuned blend coefficient with a state-space update where prediction-markets.js's implied win probabilities are one noisy observation alongside game results.
candidates.expected_value: Improves calibration of a rating that currently has no principled uncertainty tracking, which matters more for props and fantasy inputs than for beating the closing line directly.
candidates.exit_test: Out-of-sample season backtest: does the state-space team-strength rating produce better calibrated (lower Brier score) win-probability forecasts than the current hand-tuned blend, on weeks the current model has already been backtested against?

candidates.candidate: Rec-book popularity-bias detector: build a simple team-popularity index (search interest / follower counts, NOT sentiment polarity) and test whether it predicts extra staleness in REC_BOOKS lines vs SHARP_BOOKS, feeding the existing sharp-vs-rec divergence engine
candidates.mechanism: Feddersen/Humphreys/Soebbing's one well-replicated finding is that bookmakers shade prices for popular teams without a corresponding change in win probability — i.e., popularity bias is a real but market-priced distortion. Gridiron's nfl-sharp.js already profits from measurable sharp-vs-rec gaps; the hypothesis is that popularity bias specifically WIDENS that gap for high-attention teams (Cowboys, Chiefs, etc.), giving nfl-sharp.js an extra, orthogonal reason to trust a divergence signal for popular teams over unpopular ones.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-sharp.js — add a team-popularity covariate (built from something cheap and free, e.g. Google Trends index or existing Twitter follower counts already fetched for insider-handle verification) as a weight/confidence multiplier on divergence signals, gated behind the same discovery→ablation→validation pipeline every other candidate feature goes through here.
candidates.expected_value: Low-to-moderate — this is testing whether a documented, real but market-priced bias creates extra edge specifically at the sharp/rec seam, which is a narrower and more defensible claim than 'sentiment predicts outcomes' generally.
candidates.exit_test: Does adding the popularity weight to nfl-sharp.js's divergence score improve realized CLV on divergence-flagged bets for high-popularity teams vs a no-popularity-weight control, over one season of forward paper bets? If no lift, drop it — do not add it to production staking.

candidates.candidate: Tweet-VOLUME (not sentiment polarity) as a gated, forward-only experimental feature in the existing tweet-line-correlation module
candidates.mechanism: Sinha et al.'s one positive result used tweet VOLUME features more than polarity, and the broader WSB literature agrees volume/attention outperforms sentiment polarity as a signal. This respects twitter-ingest.js's existing design principle (no sentiment score ever enters model features) by using only a count, not a valence judgment, and reuses the already-built nfl-tweet-line-correlation.js forward-accumulation framework rather than building a new pipeline.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Extend server/services/nfl-tweet-line-correlation.js to also log per-team tweet-volume spikes (using the existing twitterapi-io.js budget-capped client, curated handle list — no new keyword search) as a second, independent trigger alongside the current single-tweet baseline capture, and grade both through F1's canonical CLV path once enough forward observations accumulate.
candidates.expected_value: Low — the strongest supporting paper is a single 252-game sample with no multiplicity correction, and the effect (55.6% ATS) is close to the ~52.4% break-even line; this is worth a cheap, capped-budget forward test, not a resourced build.
candidates.exit_test: After N≥100 forward observations (this codebase's own stated bar for treating a correlation as more than noise, per nfl-tweet-line-correlation.js's own comments), does volume-spike-flagged CLV beat a no-signal control at conventional significance? If not, sunset the volume trigger and keep only the existing single-tweet correlation.

candidates.candidate: Fantasy-specific crowd-consensus signal (start/sit %, waiver-add rate on public platforms) as an ensemble input to the fantasy engine — explicitly flagged as an unexplored, low-confidence experiment
candidates.mechanism: No paper anywhere in this search studies social/crowd sentiment for fantasy football specifically — positive or negative. Given Nick's fantasy-over-betting priority, this is worth a genuinely cheap experimental probe rather than being dismissed on the (irrelevant) betting-market literature, but it must be held to the same registered-hypothesis discipline given there is zero prior evidence either way.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: A new, narrowly-scoped module reading public start/sit percentage or waiver-add-rate feeds (not raw social text) as one additional candidate_head alongside the existing ones in server/services/player-week-engine.js's candidatePlayerHeads(), gated the same way any other candidate head is — never given authority until it passes ablation.
candidates.expected_value: Unknown/speculative — explicitly the point of flagging it: this is the one place in the whole topic where the literature is silent rather than negative, so the honest recommendation is a cheap probe, not a build-out.
candidates.exit_test: Does adding this candidate head measurably improve out-of-sample player-week projection accuracy (MAE/Brier vs the existing heads) over a full season backtest? If it adds no lift over the existing recency/season-average heads, drop it — do not let an untested-but-not-yet-disproven signal linger as dead weight in the ensemble.

do_not_do: Do not build a general-purpose social-media sentiment-scoring pipeline (polarity classifier over broad NFL/team keyword search) — this is the exact shape of the one well-replicated failure (Bollen/Lachanski-Pav) and violates twitter-ingest.js's own explicit design principle that a tweet earns claim-level trust, never a sentiment score.

Do not treat Sinha et al.'s 55.6% ATS result as production-ready — it is a single 252-game, single-season sample with no multiplicity correction; treat it as a hypothesis to forward-test cheaply (N2), not a signal to weight into live picks.

Do not add a 6th CLV implementation for grading any new sentiment/market signal — route everything through the F1 canonical path first, or the existing five-implementation mess (FOUND) gets worse, not better.

Do not spend the twitterapi.io budget on broad keyword search for 'crowd mood' — the curated insider-handle approach already in twitter-ingest.js is the only justified use of that spend; a new sentiment feature competing for the same $10 cap needs its own explicit budget carve-out and sign-off, not silent reuse.
Do not build fantasy-sentiment (N3) as anything beyond a cheap gated probe — there is no evidence base either way, so it does not deserve resourcing beyond a single ablation-gated experiment.

Do not conflate 'market sentiment' (Kalshi/Polymarket order flow, already partially built in prediction-markets.js) with 'social-media sentiment' (Twitter/Reddit text) when reporting results — they have different evidence quality (moderate vs weak-to-negative) and mixing them in one dashboard metric would hide that difference.

Do not skip pre-registration on any of these: given the honestly negative-leaning literature, an untracked multi-model search here is exactly how Gridiron would recreate its own missing-trial-registry problem (FOUND) inside a brand-new feature area.

result.label: GF06-copula-dependence-code
result.summary: Cloned and read 4 real dependence-modeling codebases (one genuine NFL SGP parlay-correlation study, plus the three general-purpose copula libraries named in the task).
