result.label: GN04-dfs-optimizer-code
result.summary: Read pydfs-lineup-optimizer (MIT, 447 stars, code stale since 2021-09-27 despite a 2024 API pushed_at) plus sansbacon/pangadfs (MIT, actively maintained, genetic-algorithm portfolio optimizer with a real score+diversity+ownership fitness function) and its two satellites pangadfs-showdown (stale, captain-rule only) and pangadfs-simslate (empty skeleton, one 2021 commit, no code at all). None of the three model within-lineup correlation as a joint distribution: pydfs enforces stacks as hard MILP group constraints, pangadfs's "field ownership" fitness is a linear per-player sum, and simslate never shipped. Cross-checked against the actual Gridiron repo (read-only) and found no DFS salary-cap optimizer exists anywhere, but `server/services/correlation.js` already fits archetype (position-pair x same-team/opponent) correlations on residual fantasy points via a Gaussian copula, exposes a reusable `correlatedSampler(players, sortedSamples)` that Cholesky-factorizes once and draws jointly-correlated outcomes cheaply, and is already wired into `season-sim.js` and `draft-lookahead.js` in production. That sampler is a strictly better correlation engine than anything in the three repos surveyed. The new-capability gap is a lineup-selection/portfolio layer (MILP or GA) plus DK/FD salary ingestion (free, not paid) and a self-generated ownership proxy (chalk = value rank), for which pydfs's TeamStack/GameStack constraint vocabulary and pangadfs's multi-objective (score, diversity, ownership) portfolio fitness are the two concrete design patterns worth borrowing.

repos.last_commit: 2021-09-27 (master+develop both; note: GitHub API pushed_at shows 2024-03-01, a metadata artifact — no commit newer than 2021-09-27 exists on either branch)
repos.what_it_does: Single-lineup MILP (PuLP/MIP) salary-cap optimizer with per-site roster rules (sites_registry.py); stacks.py provides TeamStack/PositionsStack/GameStack as hard min/max-from-group constraints (not a correlation matrix); exposure_strategy.py caps % of multi-lineup exports a player/group appears in via exclude-and-resolve. No ownership model, no Monte Carlo, no GPP simulation anywhere in the package.
repos.adoption_path: Copy the TeamStack/GameStack/PositionsStack constraint vocabulary and the min/max-exposure-across-lineups pattern into a new JS lineup-selection module; do not port the Python/PuLP code itself.

repos.what_it_does: Pandas/numpy genetic-algorithm lineup optimizer with a plugin architecture. fitness_multioptimizer_field_ownership.py + optimize_multioptimizer_field_ownership.py jointly evolve a portfolio ('set') of N lineups scored on three weighted, min-max-normalized components: score (top-k + total), diversity (pairwise Jaccard/Hamming overlap across the portfolio), and ownership (contrarian/leverage = minimize summed ownership, balanced = maximize ownership variance across the set). Verified by grep: no stacking or within-lineup correlation logic anywhere in pangadfs/*.py — ownership is a plain linear per-player sum, not a joint model.
repos.adoption_path: Reimplement the score+diversity+ownership multi-objective portfolio fitness (not the GA machinery) in JS as the objective function for a new lineup-portfolio builder, feeding it Gridiron's own correlated point draws instead of pangadfs's independent per-player ownership sum.

repos.what_it_does: DK-Showdown captain-multiplier roster rules plugin for pangadfs; no correlation or ownership logic. Confirmed stale and narrow by directory listing.
repos.adoption_path: Only relevant if/when Gridiron adds DK Showdown-format slates; not otherwise actionable.

repos.what_it_does: README claims 'plugin to simulate optimal lineups on slate' but the repo contains a single initial commit with only .gitignore/LICENSE/README — zero Python files, verified by full directory listing and git show --stat.
repos.adoption_path: None — dead skeleton. Cited only as evidence that a correlated field/slate simulator is a known-desired but never-shipped open-source feature in this space.

candidates.candidate: Correlation-aware DFS lineup builder using Gridiron's existing correlated sampler
candidates.mechanism: Feed a candidate player pool + their sortedSamples (already produced by projections.js) into the existing correlatedSampler(players, sortedSamples) from server/services/correlation.js — already Cholesky-factorized and copula-driven, already production-wired into season-sim.js and draft-lookahead.js. For a fixed lineup, run N draws (e.g. 5,000) to get a simulated distribution of lineup fantasy-point totals instead of a naive sum-of-means, which understates variance for stacked lineups (QB+WR same-team positive correlation) and overstates it for anti-correlated ones (two same-backfield RBs). Score/rank candidate lineups by simulated percentile outcomes (e.g. 90th-percentile score, or P(beat X points)) appropriate to cash-game vs GPP objectives, not just mean projection.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New module server/services/dfs-lineup-sim.js that imports correlatedSampler from correlation.js and sortedSamples-producing logic from projections.js; exposes simulateLineup(playerIds, weekCtx) -> {mean, p50, p75, p90, p10} used by a new lineup-builder route. No changes to correlation.js or season-sim.js required.
candidates.expected_value: Turns an already-built, already-fitted correlation engine (previously used only for season simulation and draft lookahead) into the scoring backbone of a genuinely new fantasy surface (DFS-style lineup construction) at near-zero incremental modeling cost — the hard statistical work is done and in production already.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest against 2-3 completed weeks: build lineups from historical player pools + real DK salaries for those weeks (salaries can be sourced retroactively for free), compare simulated-percentile-ranked lineups' actual realized scores against lineups ranked by naive mean-sum; a real signal shows the correlation-aware ranking beating naive-mean ranking on GPP-style upper-percentile finishes across at least 2 of 3 backtested weeks.

candidates.candidate: Salary-cap lineup selector (MILP or greedy-ILP) with pydfs-style stacking constraints
candidates.mechanism: Borrow pydfs-lineup-optimizer's stacking vocabulary (TeamStack: N players from one team; GameStack: N players split across both teams in a shootout; PositionsStack: force specific position combos like QB+WR from the same team) as hard constraints layered on top of a salary-cap knapsack/MILP solve over Gridiron's own player pool + projections. This is the piece nothing in the current codebase provides (verified: no salary_cap/lineup-optim code exists anywhere in fantasy-football-dashboard).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/dfs-optimizer.js implementing a simple ILP (e.g. via a small JS solver like javascript-lp-solver, or a greedy+local-search heuristic given roster sizes are small) that takes {salaries, projections, stackRules} and returns the salary-maximizing-projection lineup subject to position slots and stack constraints named in the pydfs style (min N from team X, min N split across game Y). Requires new: DK/FD salary ingestion module (free CSV/JSON export per slate, not a paid API) stored in a new dk_salaries table.
candidates.expected_value: Without this layer, GN04-C1's correlation scoring has nothing to rank — this is the load-bearing new capability; pairs directly with C1 (simulate) and C3 (portfolio) to form the full builder.
candidates.exit_test: Given one completed week's real DK salaries + Gridiron's own week-of projections, the solver must produce a valid lineup (salary ≤ cap, correct position counts, stack constraints satisfied) in under 2 seconds for a ~150-player pool; correctness checked by hand against 3 known-good historical optimal lineups.

candidates.candidate: Multi-lineup GPP portfolio builder with score+diversity+ownership-proxy objective (pangadfs-style)
candidates.mechanism: Port pangadfs's multi-objective portfolio fitness — jointly score a SET of lineups on (a) top-k + total simulated score from GN04-C1, (b) pairwise Jaccard diversity across the portfolio so 20 submitted lineups aren't near-duplicates, (c) an ownership term — since Gridiron has no real ownership feed (that's genuinely paid/scraped on most sites), use a self-generated chalk proxy: rank players by value = projection/salary and treat high-value/low-salary players as high-presumed-ownership, rewarding lineups that fade chalk (contrarian) or deliberately balance exposure (leverage/balanced), exactly as pangadfs's three named strategies do, but clearly labeled as a proxy, not real field data.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New function buildPortfolio(pool, targetLineups, weights) in dfs-optimizer.js that repeatedly calls the GN04-C2 selector with randomized/perturbed constraints (or a small local-search/genetic loop over lineup sets, mirroring pangadfs's optimize_multioptimizer_field_ownership.py structure) and scores full sets using the score/diversity/ownership-proxy blend. Ship behind an explicit 'ownership is a heuristic proxy, not real field data' label in the UI per Nick's evidence-honesty pattern seen elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. nfl-prop-correlation.js's own header caveats).
candidates.expected_value: Moderate — the diversification/portfolio logic is genuinely useful for any multi-entry GPP play, but the ownership component's value is capped until/unless a real ownership feed is added; ship it clearly labeled as a chalk-proxy so it isn't mistaken for calibrated field data.
candidates.exit_test: Portfolio diversity check: with 20 requested lineups, no single non-chalk player should appear in more than max_exposure% of them (verifiable directly from output) and lineup-to-lineup player overlap should show a real Jaccard spread (not all-identical), confirmed by unit test before any real-money claim is made.

do_not_do: Do not port pydfs-lineup-optimizer's Python/PuLP solver code directly — it is stale since 2021 and Gridiron's stack is Node/JS; reimplement the small set of concepts worth keeping (stack constraint vocabulary, exposure-cap pattern) natively instead of bridging languages.

Do not claim or purchase a real DFS ownership feed to satisfy the 'ownership-aware' framing — that would violate the no-paid-API constraint; ship the value/salary chalk-proxy explicitly labeled as a heuristic, not real field ownership, until/unless a free source is found.

Do not build a new correlation-fitting module for this feature — server/services/correlation.js already does this on fantasy points and is production-tested via season-sim.js and draft-lookahead.js; reuse correlatedSampler, do not duplicate the archetype-fitting logic.
Do not treat pangadfs-simslate as a usable reference — it is an empty repo (verified: no .py files exist at all); do not cite it as having implemented anything beyond its own README claim.

Do not touch or import from fantasy-football-dashboard during this research (read-only per hard rules) — any prototyping of GN04-C1/C2/C3 must happen in a new, separate module/branch, never edited into the live repo while Week 1 games are being captured.

result.label: GN06-mixture-density-neural-code
result.summary: Read 4 repos (NGBoost, tonyduan's Mixture Density Network, zuko normalizing flows, nflows) to specify a probabilistic margin-forecast head for Gridiron's NFL model. Confirmed via reading (not README) that the current "predictive distribution" in server/services/nfl-ensemble.js:207-252 (predictiveDistribution) is a bootstrap over historical residuals — no model, no closed-form pdf/cdf — and self-labels calibration_state:'research_distribution_only', production_eligible:false. All three actionable candidates share one output contract: same margin_quantiles/interval/win-probability/cover-probability fields as today for backward compatibility, plus new pdf/cdf/sample functions and a training_metadata/calibration_state block, replacing counted-resample estimates with exact closed-form values from a real conditional distribution.
do_not_do: Do not make a normalizing flow (zuko/nflows) the first production head — it is the highest-overfitting-risk option on a few-thousand-game NFL dataset; ship NGBoost-Normal or the ported MDN first and only add the flow if held-out log-likelihood/CRPS actually beats both.

Do not embed PyTorch/Python inference synchronously in the hot request path for NGBoost or the MDN — train offline, serve a precomputed lookup or a small ported JS forward pass at request time; only the flow needs a live local (localhost-only) sidecar because its spline transform is too complex to hand-port to JS.

Do not conflate this fix with the ensemble's blend-collapse defect (forecast ≈ 0.68 + 0.632·market) — that is a separate point-forecast-combination problem; this candidate only replaces the distribution wrapped around whatever point forecast survives that fix.
Do not keep the sample_size/conditional_cohort diagnostic fields once a real model is in place — they were only meaningful because the old 'distribution' was literally the resampled cohort itself.

candidates.candidate: Replace nfl-ensemble.js's bootstrap-residual predictiveDistribution() with an NGBoost Normal head trained offline on the same historical (context, margin) rows, producing per-game closed-form (loc, scale) instead of a resampled point cloud.
candidates.mechanism: NGBRegressor(Dist=Normal, Score=CRPScore or LogScore) fits gradient-boosted decision trees per distribution parameter using the natural gradient (verified in ngboost/scores.py: Score._natural_gradient solves metric@x=grad via the Fisher-information metric, not a raw gradient step), with a line search (ngboost.py:line_search) that only commits a step if it actually reduces total score. The fitted Normal (ngboost/distns/normal.py) wraps scipy.stats.norm and transparently exposes .pdf/.cdf/.ppf/.rvs via __getattr__ — a genuine closed-form conditional distribution per row, not a discrete resample.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Nightly offline Python batch job reads the same teamWeeks()/hist rows nfl-ensemble.js already filters, fits NGBRegressor(Dist=Normal, Score=CRPScore), writes a per-game (loc,scale) lookup table (or a small feature->params function serialized to JSON); server/services/nfl-ensemble.js's predictiveDistribution() looks up (loc,scale) and computes margin_quantiles/margin_interval_80/50/home_win_probability/home_cover_probability analytically via a normal CDF instead of counting resampled points, keeping the exact same return-object field names.
candidates.expected_value: Turns a self-admittedly non-production, uncalibratable resample into a scoreable, closed-form distribution with almost no new infra (offline Python job + a lookup table); CRPScore is a proper scoring rule so it can be backtested against realized margins directly, unlike the current cohort-count approach which has no likelihood to evaluate.
candidates.exit_test: Held-out (last 2-3 completed weeks) CRPS/log-likelihood of the NGBoost Normal head must beat the current bootstrap's implied CRPS (computed by treating its resampled points as an empirical distribution) before calibration_state can move off research_distribution_only.

candidates.candidate: Port tonyduan/mixture-density-network's ~130-line Gaussian-mixture MDN (context -> mixture of 2-3 Gaussians over margin) to capture genuine multimodal margin outcomes (e.g. competitive-game vs. garbage-time-blowout regimes) that a single-Normal head cannot represent.
candidates.mechanism: Read in full: MixtureDensityNetwork.forward(x) runs two small MLPs from the context producing log_pi (softmax mixture weights) and per-component (mu, sigma=exp(raw+eps)); .loss() is exact stable Gaussian-mixture NLL via torch.logsumexp(log_pi + normal_loglik); .sample() does exact ancestral sampling (categorical draw via searchsorted on cumsum(exp(log_pi)), then a Gaussian draw). The included 1D example fits a genuinely multimodal x->y relationship a unimodal head cannot represent, which is the same shape as a margin that can plausibly land in two very different game-script buckets.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Train this near-unmodified script offline in Python on (context features, realized margin) pairs; export the two MLPs' weight matrices as JSON. Write a ~40-line JS forward-pass evaluator inside server/services/ (matmul + ReLU + softmax + exp only, no ML runtime) that computes log_pi/mu/sigma per game at request time inside predictiveDistribution(); derive margin_quantiles via bisection on the mixture CDF sum_k pi_k*Phi((x-mu_k)/sigma_k) (~15 lines), replacing the resampled-cohort quantile() calls with the same output field names.
candidates.expected_value: Small, well-verified reference implementation (read in full, not skimmed) with zero training-time-only dependencies once ported to a JS forward pass; captures multimodality that both today's bootstrap and the NGBoost-Normal alternative structurally cannot represent, at minimal inference cost (a few small matrix multiplies per game, ≤16 games/week).
candidates.exit_test: Held-out log-likelihood of the fitted 2-3 component MDN must exceed the NGBoost-Normal head's held-out log-likelihood on the same split before it replaces (rather than sits alongside) the Normal head; if it doesn't beat Normal, the added complexity isn't earning its keep.

candidates.candidate: Stand up probabilists/zuko's Neural Spline Flow (NSF) as a local Python sidecar giving an exact, arbitrarily-shaped (skewed/fat-tailed/multimodal) conditional density over margin, called over localhost HTTP by nfl-ensemble.js as the highest-capacity, gated-behind-backtest option.
candidates.mechanism: Verified by reading zuko/lazy.py and zuko/flows/spline.py (cross-checked against the README's own usage example): the core abstraction LazyDistribution.forward(c) -> torch.distributions.Distribution means a context vector in yields a real object exposing .log_prob(x), .sample((n,)); zuko.flows.NSF(features=1, context=N) is a masked-autoregressive flow whose per-dimension transform is a MonotonicRQSTransform (monotonic rational-quadratic spline) with knot parameters output by a learned conditioner network on the context — an exactly invertible, exact-density transform, not a fixed parametric family picked in advance.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Run a small always-local (no external network, no paid API) FastAPI/Flask process loading a trained zuko NSF(1, context_dim) checkpoint; nfl-ensemble.js's predictiveDistribution() calls it over localhost HTTP with the game's context vector and receives {pdf grid or callable, cdf via numerical integration, quantiles, samples}; per-request Python latency is irrelevant at ≤16 games/week. Ship this only as an optional third head behind the same output contract, not as a replacement for NGBoost/MDN.
candidates.expected_value: Highest theoretical flexibility (genuinely shape-free conditional density) of the three, but the method itself (read from the code, not assumed) is data-hungry and Gridiron's own diagnostics put total playable NFL history at a few thousand games — real risk this overfits or underperforms the two simpler heads on so little data; only worth the sidecar-infra cost if backtesting proves it earns it.
candidates.exit_test: Held-out log-likelihood must beat both the NGBoost-Normal and MDN heads on the same held-out weeks before it is enabled in production; if it doesn't clear that bar within one full season of backtesting, drop it rather than carry the extra sidecar-process operational cost.

candidates.candidate: Once any of the above heads exposes a real cdf(), add a genuine calibration audit (Probability Integral Transform histogram + KS test) that today's resample-only approach structurally cannot support.
candidates.mechanism: NGBoost's Normal.__getattr__ (ngboost/distns/normal.py) delegates to a scipy.stats.norm object, so .cdf is available for free; the ported MDN's mixture CDF is derived via the bisection described above; zuko's flow exposes .log_prob directly (cdf via numerical integration of the density). For each held-out completed game, compute u = cdf(realized_margin); if the model is well-calibrated, the u-values across many games should be ~Uniform(0,1) — this is the standard PIT calibration check, impossible to run against the current implementation because it has no cdf, only a fixed-size resampled point list.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Add a scheduled job (weekly, after games settle) that pulls each of that week's pre-game predictive distributions (whichever head produced them) and the realized margins, computes PIT values via the head's exposed cdf(), and runs a KS test against Uniform(0,1); persist the KS statistic/p-value alongside model_fit_pit_checked vs model_fit_uncalibrated in the calibration_state field so the governance gate mentioned in Nick's standing priorities has a real, automatable check instead of eyeballing quantile plots.
candidates.expected_value: This is the cheapest of the four to build (no new model, just a scoring job) and is the only way to make calibration_state:'model_fit_pit_checked' mean something real rather than aspirational; directly closes the 'no conformal or otherwise honestly-calibrated uncertainty interval exists anywhere in the pipeline' gap for whichever margin head ships first.
candidates.exit_test: KS test p-value on a rolling window of held-out weeks must stay above a fixed threshold (e.g. 0.05, adjustable) for the head to remain calibration_state:'model_fit_pit_checked'; a head that fails the KS test drops back to model_fit_uncalibrated and should not be used for staking-relevant probabilities until re-fit.

result.label: GN05-prediction-market-client-code
result.summary: Read Polymarket's official py-clob-client (Python) and clob-client (TypeScript) and Kalshi's official kalshi-starter-code-python. All three are almost entirely authenticated-trading surfaces (order signing, RFQ, wallet/balance management) that are irrelevant or explicitly out of scope for Gridiron, which never places bets on these venues. The one genuinely portable piece is mechanism knowledge, not code to vendor: (1) Polymarket's neg-risk contract (confirmed via clob-client's on-chain addresses) forces the sum of YES prices across a complete leader/futures/award field to converge on ~1.00 — a real combinatorial arbitrage, not a statistical one — and Gridiron's existing polymarket_markets classification (kind='leader_prop'/'futures'/'award') plus the already-captured 12.4M-row polymarket_price_history tape can replay this with zero new API calls; (2) py-clob-client's calculate_market_price shows how to walk the full order-book depth (already fetched by Gridiron's captureOrderBooks but discarded down to top-of-book) into a size-aware fill price, which is exactly the "quoted price you cannot get filled at in size is not a price" gap the file's own docstring names; (3) the same client's tick_size/price_valid logic shows Polymarket ladder prices are quantized per-market, which polymarket-lines.js's isotonic-crossing interpolation currently treats as continuous. Kalshi's starter code needs an authenticated/funded account and offers nothing Gridiron's existing unauthenticated elections-API reads don't already have; its websocket pattern is real but needs new infrastructure, so it's rejected. An arXiv paper on Polymarket NBA arbitrage (2605.00864) independently confirms the same class of opportunity exists but is liquidity-constrained in practice, matching Gridiron's own stated caveat.
do_not_do: Port or call any order-signing/trading code from py-clob-client or clob-client — Gridiron places no bets on Polymarket and doing so needs a funded wallet and private keys, which is out of scope tonight.
Stand up Kalshi's websocket ticker client — real idea but requires a persistent connection process (new infrastructure) and an authenticated API key Gridiron doesn't have for that surface.
Adopt py-clob-client's RFQ (request-for-quote) module — institutional block-trade negotiation, irrelevant to a historical-tape signal.

Treat neg-risk sum-of-prices deviations as free money without depth-checking them first — per the arXiv NBA-arbitrage paper and Polymarket.js's own docstring, these are liquidity-constrained and a quoted top-of-book price is not an executable one.

sources.title: Arbitrage Analysis in Polymarket NBA Markets
sources.key_result: Detects arbitrage in Polymarket NBA markets via a combinatorial approach — summing implied probabilities across mutually exclusive outcomes and flagging sums below 1.0 as risk-free trades. Confirms such opportunities exist but states liquidity/order-depth constraints are the primary barrier to actually executing them, and that snapshot-to-execution transitions lose the opportunity during volatile periods.
sources.sample: Polymarket NBA game-outcome and related markets, transaction-level order-book data

candidates.candidate: Neg-risk complementary-set consistency scanner over the existing Polymarket tape
candidates.mechanism: Polymarket's on-chain NegRiskAdapter (address confirmed in Polymarket/clob-client src/config.ts) converts a NO share on any outcome of a multi-outcome event into 1 YES share on every other outcome in that event, which contractually forces the sum of YES prices across a complete field (leader/futures/award markets) toward ~1.00 minus a small vig. Gridiron already classifies these markets (kind='leader_prop'|'futures'|'award') and groups them by event_title in polymarket_markets, and already has 12.4M rows of per-market price history in polymarket_price_history. A new module can join markets by event_title + captured_at/ts bucket, sum mid-YES across the field, and flag captures where |sum-1| exceeds a vig-adjusted threshold as a mechanical (not statistical) mispricing.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New server/services/nfl-negrisk-arb.js reading polymarket_markets (group by event_title, kind) joined to polymarket_price_history/polymarket_quotes — zero new API calls, zero new tables required for the detection pass (a new table only needed to log flagged windows).
candidates.expected_value: Identifies a genuine, code-verified arbitrage class Gridiron has never checked for; per arXiv:2605.00864 on the analogous Polymarket NBA case, real opportunities exist but are liquidity-constrained, so expected value is a measurement/monitoring capability first, executable edge only where candidate 2's depth data says the size is real.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest over the 12.4M-row tape: report the distribution of |sum(YES)-1| across all NFL leader/futures/award event-fields, and what fraction of flagged windows had order-book depth (from candidate 2) sufficient to fill a $200 position on the cheap side. If under 5% of flagged windows are fillable at that size, this is a monitoring tool, not an execution edge — say so and stop there.

candidates.candidate: Depth-aware executable price at capture time
candidates.mechanism: py_clob_client.client.calculate_market_price (and order_builder.calculate_buy_market_price) walks the full bid/ask ladder returned by the CLOB /book endpoint to compute the size-weighted fill price for a target dollar amount, rather than reading only the top of book. Gridiron's captureOrderBooks (server/services/polymarket.js:140-190) already fetches that exact full ladder every sweep but discards everything except best_bid/best_ask.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Extend captureOrderBooks in server/services/polymarket.js to compute and store fill price at fixed tranches (e.g. $50/$200/$1000) from the bids/asks arrays already in memory before they go out of scope — no new API calls, just retained arithmetic on data already fetched.
candidates.expected_value: Turns polymarket.js's own stated gap ("a quoted price you cannot get filled at in size is not a price") into a measured cost curve, and gives candidate 1's arbitrage scanner and nfl-execution-edge.js's cost comparisons a real size dimension instead of a top-of-book assumption.
candidates.exit_test: For the 60 markets already swept per captureOrderBooks call, compare best-bid/ask spread cost vs. $200-tranche fill cost; if they differ by less than a few bps on the median market, the top-of-book approximation already in use was fine and this is not worth keeping.

candidates.candidate: Tick-size-aware ladder crossing for polymarket-lines.js
candidates.mechanism: py_clob_client.utilities.price_valid and the TickSize type confirm every Polymarket book carries a per-market tick_size (commonly 0.01, tighter near 0/1) that quantizes prices — a market-structure fact, not sampling noise. polymarket-lines.js's isotonic()/crossing() functions currently interpolate the 50%-crossing spread/total as if the ladder were continuous, so some of what they treat as thin-book noise near key numbers is mechanical rounding.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: The /book payload already fetched in captureOrderBooks (same call as candidate 2) includes tick_size per market; thread it through to polymarket-lines.js's crossing() so extrapolated (off-ladder) crossings can be flagged by how many ticks away the nearest real quote sat, rather than treated as equally reliable to an interior crossing.
candidates.expected_value: Improves confidence calibration on the implied-line series signal-latency.js and the movement panel already consume; does not change model skill, only how much the crossing estimate should be trusted near the ladder's edges.
candidates.exit_test: Re-score existing extrapolated crossings by tick-distance-to-nearest-quote; if extrapolated crossings already cluster near the ladder edge (small tick distance) the current code is already fine in practice and this is a documentation-only fix, not a code change.

result.label: Time-series foundation model code: Chronos-2, TimesFM, Lag-Llama
result.summary: Cloned and read the source (not just READMEs) of amazon-science/chronos-forecasting, google-research/timesfm, and time-series-foundation-models/lag-llama. Chronos-2 (Apache-2.0, code+weights, 5.8k stars, last commit 2026-09-08) is architecturally the best fit for Gridiron's short/cross-sectional NFL panels: pipeline.py's predict(cross_learning=True) is explicitly built for "individual time series with limited historical context" pooling information across a batch (e.g. all 32 teams at once), and it has native past/future covariate support plus a first-class DataFrame API. TimesFM (32.3k stars, Apache-2.0 code, weights Apache-2.0 through v2.5 but v3.0 weights are non-commercial-only) offers a real in-context XReg regression-blend module (src/timesfm/utils/xreg_lib.py) for 2.5, and native multivariate-with-covariates in 3.0 — useful for modeling same-game leg correlation instead of assuming independence. Lag-Llama (Apache-2.0, 1.6k stars) is 15+ months stale, univariate-only with no covariate support, and its actual minimum-history requirement (context_length + max lag, read directly from run.py) works against short NFL-season panels — verdict: avoid for this use case. All claims of zero-shot quality on short panels are architectural feasibility from reading the code, not measured results; every candidate below needs a real backtest against the current baseline before trust.

sources.title: Chronos-2 technical report
sources.key_result: Abstract confirms group-attention in-context-learning architecture enabling zero-shot univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed forecasting, evaluated on fev-bench/GIFT-Eval/Chronos Benchmark II; claims 'outperforms baselines by a wide margin' on covariate tasks but the abstract itself carries no numeric deltas (those are in body tables not fetched) — treat as a vendor claim pending our own backtest.
sources.sample: n/a (abstract only)

sources.title: Lag-Llama: Towards Foundation Models for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
sources.key_result: Abstract confirms Lag-Llama is univariate-only (decoder-only transformer over lagged values) and claims 'strong zero-shot generalization' vs unspecified baselines; consistent with the code (no covariate path anywhere in run.py/data/*.py).
sources.sample: n/a (abstract only)

repos.what_it_does: Chronos/Chronos-Bolt/Chronos-2 pretrained time-series foundation models. Chronos2Pipeline (src/chronos/chronos2/pipeline.py) does zero-shot univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed quantile forecasting; predict() accepts mixed-length series in one batch with categorical+numeric past/future covariates, and cross_learning=True explicitly pools information across series with limited individual history (pipeline.py docstring, ~line 540-548). Chronos2Dataset (dataset.py ~203-236) uses min(context_length, history_length) with no hard minimum enforced. First-class pandas DataFrame API (predict_df, df_utils.py) keyed by item_id/timestamp.
repos.adoption_path: pip install chronos-forecasting; weekly Python batch job that cross-learns over all 32 teams' weekly scoring-differential series (or all active RBs' weekly touches), writes quantile-forecast JSON, consumed by server/services/nfl-team-strength.js as an added feature/prior alongside (not replacing) the existing hand-tuned blend.

repos.license: Apache-2.0 code; weights Apache-2.0 through v2.5, v3.0 weights under timesfm-non-commercial-license-v1.0 (non-commercial/non-production only)
repos.what_it_does: TimesFM 3.0 (src/timesfm3/) adds native multivariate forecasting with past+future dynamic covariates, no per-task tuning. TimesFM 2.5-era code (src/timesfm/utils/xreg_lib.py, Apache-2.0 weights) implements in-context regression (XReg): two literal modes 'timesfm + xreg' and 'xreg + timesfm' that fit a closed-form regression on named covariates and either residual-correct or detrend around the TimesFM forecast — real ~150-line numpy/jax implementation, not just a README claim. XReg path depends on jax/jaxlib + scikit-learn, a heavier stack than Chronos's pure PyTorch.
repos.adoption_path: Use TimesFM 2.5 (Apache-2.0 weights) XReg blend as an alternative to the hand-tuned preseason/in-season blend in nfl-team-strength.js; prototype TimesFM 3.0's native multivariate head (non-commercial weights, fine for a personal-project pilot) for jointly forecasting correlated same-game legs (QB pass yards + WR receiving yards + game total) instead of teaser-leg-rates.js's independence assumption.

repos.what_it_does: GluonTS-based train/eval harness (run.py) for a decoder-only transformer over lagged values. Univariate only — grepped the whole repo, zero covariate references in run.py/utils/utils.py/data/*.py. Actual minimum history required is context_length + max(lags_seq) (run.py ~line 277), materially more than the 'try context length from 32' README advice suggests, since lags_seq can extend to a full periodicity cycle. No cross-series/cross-learning at inference (only at training, via GluonTS ListDataset) and no DataFrame API.
repos.adoption_path: Not recommended for Gridiron: 15+ months stale, univariate/no-covariate, and its real minimum-history requirement works against single-season NFL panels even before considering it lacks Chronos-2's short-panel cross-learning advantage. Time is better spent validating Chronos-2.

candidates.candidate: Weekly Chronos-2 cross-learning batch forecast for all 32 teams' scoring-differential series, fed as an additional feature into nfl-team-strength.js
candidates.mechanism: Chronos2Pipeline.predict(inputs=list_of_32_team_series, cross_learning=True) pools information across all 32 teams' short (~1-17 week) histories via group attention in-context learning, producing zero-shot quantile forecasts without any training run, per pipeline.py's own documented design for series with limited individual history.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New nightly/weekly Python job (pip install chronos-forecasting) reads the same weekly team-scoring table nfl-team-strength.js already builds, emits a JSON quantile forecast per team, and nfl-team-strength.js consumes it as one more input signal/prior alongside its current hand-tuned preseason/in-season blend — not a replacement on day one.
candidates.expected_value: A genuinely out-of-sample, principled forecast to compare against and potentially blend with the current ad hoc blend; low downside since it's additive, not a rip-and-replace.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest Chronos-2's weekly team-strength forecast against the existing blend on held-out 2024-2025 weeks using the same error metric nfelo already tracks; kill it if it doesn't beat the blend's out-of-sample error, or if cross_learning doesn't measurably outperform per-team independent forecasting on this data.

candidates.candidate: Chronos-2 covariate-conditioned quantile distributions for player props, replacing point-estimate projections with a full predictive distribution
candidates.mechanism: predict() accepts per-player dicts with target (weekly stat history) plus past_covariates/future_covariates (opponent pass-defense strength, implied team total, snap share) and returns quantile forecasts (pipeline.py:468-560) — a nonparametric alternative to hand-building a negative-binomial/hierarchical model, using a pretrained backbone instead of fitting one from scratch on Gridiron's own limited player-week data.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Wrap Chronos2Pipeline.predict_df in a Python service keyed by player_id/week the way the existing props module is keyed; output full quantile bands instead of a point estimate, compared against the props module's already-measured +27% Brier skill on 2+ TD markets as the baseline to beat.
candidates.expected_value: Props is the one module with measured skill; giving it real calibrated quantiles (versus a point estimate) directly targets the flagged gap ('no negative-binomial/hierarchical/calibrated model') without discarding the existing signal — run both and compare.
candidates.exit_test: Compare Chronos-2 quantile calibration (PIT histogram / pinball loss) against the current point-estimate-plus-assumed-distribution approach on held-out weeks; adopt only if calibration measurably improves, since zero-shot quality on <20-week player histories is unproven in Chronos-2's own benchmarks.

candidates.candidate: TimesFM 2.5 in-context XReg regression blend as an alternative, already-implemented technique for combining a foundation-model forecast with known covariates
candidates.mechanism: xreg_lib.py implements two literal modes ('timesfm + xreg', 'xreg + timesfm') that fit a closed-form regression against named covariates and either residual-correct the TimesFM forecast or detrend before forecasting the residual — an actual runnable alternative to a hand-tuned linear blend, using Apache-2.0-licensed 2.5 weights (avoiding TimesFM 3.0's non-commercial-only weight license).
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Prototype against the same weekly team-scoring panel as the Chronos-2 candidate, using home/away, rest days, and Vegas implied team total as covariates; compare its residual-correction approach directly against nfl-team-strength.js's current hand-tuned preseason/in-season blend on the same backtest window.
candidates.expected_value: A second, architecturally different candidate (regression-on-residual vs. Chronos-2's pure in-context pooling) to triangulate against — if both agree the current blend is beatable, that's stronger evidence than either alone; requires the heavier jax/scikit-learn dependency stack, which is the real cost here.
candidates.exit_test: Run head-to-head against the Chronos-2 cross-learning candidate and the current blend on the same held-out weeks; drop whichever of the two foundation-model approaches doesn't clear the current blend's error, keep at most one to avoid maintaining two parallel foundation-model pipelines.

candidates.candidate: TimesFM 3.0 native multivariate forecasting as a pilot for modeling same-game leg correlation instead of assuming independence
candidates.mechanism: TimesFM 3.0's transformer (src/timesfm3/model.py, transformer.py) natively forecasts multiple channels jointly with shared covariates rather than per-series independently; sampling a joint multivariate quantile forecast for e.g. QB pass yards + WR receiving yards + game total in the same call captures some cross-leg correlation for free, without hand-building a copula.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Small offline pilot only: pick 3-5 known-correlated same-game leg pairs, forecast them jointly with TimesFM 3.0 vs. independently, and compare the joint sample correlation against the actual realized correlation in nflverse play-by-play — directly tests whether teaser-leg-rates.js's independence assumption is materially wrong and whether this model captures the gap.
candidates.expected_value: Speculative but cheap to test — if the joint forecast's implied leg correlation tracks realized correlation even roughly, it's a concrete, non-hand-tuned alternative to teaser-leg-rates.js's independence assumption; TimesFM 3.0 weights are non-commercial-only, acceptable for a personal-project pilot but a real constraint if ever productized.
candidates.exit_test: If TimesFM 3.0's implied same-game leg correlation doesn't track realized historical correlation (from the 251,591-row play-by-play table) better than the flat-independence assumption, drop it — this is the most speculative candidate here and should not proceed past a one-week pilot without a clear signal.

do_not_do: Do not use Lag-Llama for this task — 15+ months stale, univariate-only with zero covariate support anywhere in the code, and its real minimum-history requirement (context_length + max lag, read from run.py) works against single-season NFL panels; it is strictly dominated by Chronos-2 on every axis that matters for short cross-sectional data.

Do not adopt TimesFM 3.0's pretrained weights for anything that could become commercial/production — they are licensed non-commercial-only (timesfm-non-commercial-license-v1.0), unlike TimesFM 2.5 and all Chronos weights which stay Apache-2.0; fine for tonight's personal-project pilot, not a safe long-term default.

Do not trust any vendor benchmark table (fev-bench, GIFT-Eval, Chronos Benchmark II) as evidence of zero-shot quality on Gridiron's actual short NFL panels — these benchmarks are dominated by series far longer than an 18-week NFL season and were not independently re-verified here; every candidate above requires its own backtest against the current baseline before being trusted.

Do not run these models as a live per-request inference path in the Node server — they're Python/PyTorch (or jax) models with real (if modest, 28M-200M param) compute cost; keep them as offline/batch jobs producing JSON the existing Node services read, not inline synchronous calls.

Do not let a foundation-model forecast silently replace nfl-team-strength.js's existing blend on day one — treat every candidate here as an additive signal to compare/blend, since none of their short-panel behavior has been measured on Gridiron's own data yet.

result.label: GN03: transformer-on-PBP for next-drive-outcome
result.summary: Cloned and read (not just skimmed READMEs of) 4 repos: SumerSports/SportsTrackingTransformer (real, benchmarked spatial self-attention-over-a-player-set for tackle prediction — 20.2% ADE improvement over the 2020 BDB "Zoo" CNN baseline on their own held-out set), ebrown-32/Deep-Learning-NFL-QB-Stat-Predictor (a genuine temporal transformer over play-by-play sequences with a feature vocabulary that near-exactly matches Gridiron's nfl_play_by_play + nfl_play_formations columns, but zero disclosed evaluation metrics anywhere in the repo), mpchang/uncovering-missed-tackle-opportunities (BDB2024 — verified by reading the notebook that despite "Sequence"-named PyTorch classes, the actual trained model is XGBoost + SHAP, not any kind of sequence model), and juancamilocampos/nfl-big-data-bowl-2020 (faithful reproduction of the pre-transformer 2020 BDB winning CNN/interaction-network solution, useful only as the historical baseline the SumerSports paper measures against). Read Gridiron's actual nfl_play_by_play schema (server/db/schema/nfl-a-to-m.js:306-333, populated by nfl-espn-pbp.js) directly: 24 columns, no drive_id, ordered by `sequence` within event_id. Found that nfl-live-ledger.js already has the drive-boundary heuristic (offense-change) and a settled-outcomes calibration table (nfl_live_possession_settlements / liveLedgerCalibration()) that a next-drive-outcome model can be scored against for free, in parallel with the buggy Monte Carlo simulateRemainder() in nfl-drive-sim.js, without touching the live capture path. Specified a concrete "Drive-Outcome Transformer": per-play categorical+continuous token embedding -> transformer encoder (2-3 layers) with a learned in-drive positional embedding -> attention-pooling (borrowed from ebrown-32) -> multi-task heads (7-way drive outcome, points regression, auxiliary next-play-type). Also checked two arXiv abstracts (EventGPT, axial-transformer soccer forecasting) for architectural corroboration only — neither disclosed benchmark numbers in the abstract, so graded as moderate not strong evidence.

candidates.expected_value: Marginal representation-quality improvement for the same DOT model at near-zero extra cost, since the tables already exist and are already joined nowhere in the current pipeline for this purpose.
candidates.exit_test: Ablation: train DOT with vs without the set-attention formation sub-module on identical data/splits; ship only if it improves the same walk-forward Brier/log-loss from C1's exit test, since this is a minor architectural add with weak a-priori evidence of transfer from the (very different) tracking-data task it was verified in.

candidates.expected_value: A free-to-compute auxiliary signal that both improves the main DOT task (multi-task regularization, per the ebrown-32 pattern) and gives the props/teaser modules a same-drive tendency feature they do not currently have, without requiring a second model to be trained.

Do not trust any of these architectures' reported numbers as transferable to Gridiron's drive-outcome task — every disclosed benchmark (SumerSports' 20.2% ADE) is a same-repo, same-institution, different-task (tackle location, not drive outcome) comparison, not an independently reproduced result on this problem.

result.label: GN02: GNN sports-prediction repos — roster/snap-share graph for Gridiron
result.summary: Cloned and read 4 GNN sports-prediction repos (code, not READMEs). Two are directly attachable to Gridiron's existing weekly usage tables today (no new data needed): joewilaj/nbaGNNs (MIT, 62-node NBA offense/defense graph + node2vec + spektral GNN + market line, plus a learned "trust the model vs. Vegas" discriminator) and stevenbliu/Project-NBA-Rankings-Prediction (vendors real GraphSAGE; team-node/schedule-edge graph for rank classification, but its own hand-rolled GCN side-path trains and tests on identical data with zero split — its 88% accuracy claim is leakage, not evidence). Two are per-play spatial-tracking GNNs (sanjeevnara7/FootballPassPrediction, GATv2 over player x/y with distance-decayed edges, MIT, active; juancamilocampos/nfl-big-data-bowl-2020, Interaction Network over rusher-vs-defender relative features, no license, reached top-3% CV on the actual Kaggle 2020 leaderboard) — both are reference-only until Gridiron ingests Next Gen Stats tracking data, since it has no player x/y today. Verified Gridiron's own schema (player_week_usage, player_week_snaps/nfl_snaps, nfl_depth, nfl_roster_snapshots/nfl_player_roster_events) supports a concrete heterogeneous roster graph immediately: player nodes (target_share/offense_pct/EPA features) + team-offense/defense nodes, with teammate-competition, depth-chart-hierarchy, player-to-team-membership, weekly-matchup, and roster-transaction edges — directly mirroring nbaGNNs' 62-node design and Project-NBA-Rankings-Prediction's team-schedule-graph design, both buildable from tables Gridiron already populates weekly.

candidates.candidate: Build a weekly 64-node NFL offense/defense graph (32 teams x 2) from player_week_usage + nfl_snaps, run a small GNN (GraphSAGE or spektral GINConv) plus market-line feature to output team-strength embeddings and matchup point-differential, replacing nfl-team-strength.js's ad hoc prior/in-season blend.
candidates.fixes_finding: Team-strength ratings (nfl-team-strength.js) mix stale preseason priors with in-season data via a hand-tuned blend, not a principled state-space/Bayesian update.
candidates.mechanism: Directly ports joewilaj/nbaGNNs' verified architecture (62-node offense/defense graph, row-normalized weighted edges from box-score-style stats, node2vec or learned embeddings, spektral GNN layer, Game_Vec matchup extraction concatenated with the market line) from NBA/point-differential to NFL/player_week_usage, and stevenbliu/Project-NBA-Rankings-Prediction's team-node+schedule-edge GraphSAGE framing (using its vendored MIT GraphSAGE library, not its leaky hand-rolled GCN path) for the team-rating side.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New service nfl-team-strength-gnn.js: build the 64-node graph nightly from player_week_usage/nfl_snaps aggregated to team-offense/team-defense feature vectors, edges = that week's schedule (team vs opponent) plus a decayed self-loop to prior weeks; run node2vec/learned embedding + 1-2 GNN layers (PyTorch Geometric, since Gridiron is Node/JS -- run as a Python subprocess or ONNX-exported model called from nfl-team-strength.js) to get team embeddings; feed embeddings + market spread into a small regressor for point-differential, replacing the current hand-tuned blend. Must use a strict walk-forward split (same season-day retraining loop as nbaGNNs) to avoid stevenbliu's leakage bug.
candidates.expected_value: A principled, learnable team-strength signal that combines market and internal signal the way nbaGNNs demonstrably does (uses the line as a feature, not a shrinkage target) -- directly attacks the -2.28 CLV / 0.68+0.632*market collapse by giving the ensemble an actual second opinion instead of another market-shrunk component.
candidates.exit_test: Walk-forward test (rolling day-by-day retrain, held-out future weeks only) must beat the current nfl-team-strength.js blend's MAE on score differential and show CLV != 0 in at least one full season backtest before touching live picks; if it converges to just re-predicting the closing line, kill it -- same failure mode as the current ensemble.

candidates.candidate: Add a learned 'trust the model vs. the market' discriminator, mirroring nbaGNNs' second-stage Model-Graph/GIN discriminator, as an explicit governance gate on top of any Gridiron betting model's picks.
candidates.mechanism: nbaGNNs builds a third graph from its own primary model's historical prediction errors vs. Vegas ('Model Graph'), embeds it with node2vec + GIN, and trains a binary classifier that predicts whether the model or the market will be closer for a given upcoming game -- i.e. a data-driven confidence/edge gate rather than a fixed threshold.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: A new nfl-pick-confidence-gnn.js consuming the existing nfl_pick_watch_log and historical picks/outcomes tables to build the same 'model graph' (nodes = games, edges = similarity in team/market-state at pick time) and train a small GIN classifier gating which picks are allowed to size up, sitting alongside (not replacing) the existing staking guardrail so it adds a second, independently-trained veto rather than a single point of failure.
candidates.expected_value: A concrete, testable alternative to whatever ad hoc confidence heuristic currently gates bet sizing; if it reliably identifies the subset of picks where the model actually beats the close, it directly improves realized CLV even with zero change to the underlying forecast.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest the discriminator's accept/reject decisions against the full pick history: it must show positive CLV on its accepted subset and no CLV improvement (or negative) on its rejected subset, out of sample, before being wired into live staking.

candidates.candidate: Build a heterogeneous weekly roster graph (player nodes + team-offense/defense nodes; teammate-competition, depth-chart-hierarchy, snap-share-membership, and weekly-matchup edges) from player_week_usage, player_week_snaps, and nfl_depth, and run GraphSAGE node regression to predict weekly target/carry share and role changes -- directly serving fantasy, not betting.
candidates.mechanism: Combines stevenbliu/Project-NBA-Rankings-Prediction's team-node/schedule-edge graph-construction pattern (nodes = entities-per-week, edges = who-played-whom, using its vendored MIT GraphSAGE) with FootballPassPrediction's edge-weighting-by-relationship idea (team-onehot + distance decay becomes teammate-onehot + depth-chart-rank decay) to encode 'who absorbs the touches when a teammate is out' as message passing rather than the hand-tuned heuristics in role-changepoint.js.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New service nfl-roster-graph.js: build the graph described in the notes file (player nodes from player_week_usage/player_week_snaps with target_share/offense_pct/EPA features; depth-chart edges from nfl_depth.pos_rank; team-membership edges; opponent-matchup edges) each week, run 1-2 GraphSAGE layers to propagate role/usage signal across the depth chart, and use the resulting player embeddings as a new feature block into whatever consumes nfl_player_week_features today (offseason-model.js, role-changepoint.js). Since Nick's stated priority is fantasy over betting, this is the highest-leverage of the four candidates.
candidates.expected_value: A learned, graph-aware alternative to role-changepoint.js's hand-tuned heuristics for redistributing usage after an injury/trade/benching -- the depth-chart-hierarchy edge type is a natural inductive bias for exactly that problem and costs nothing in new data ingestion.
candidates.exit_test: Hold out weeks where a known usage-redistribution event occurred (injury/trade) and compare the GNN's predicted target/snap-share shift for the backup vs. role-changepoint.js's current heuristic prediction, against actual realized shares; ship only if it reduces error on that held-out event set.

candidates.candidate: Flag Next Gen Stats player-tracking ingestion as a prerequisite research item: if/when Gridiron ever ingests x/y tracking data, adopt the GATv2 distance-decayed-edge pattern (FootballPassPrediction) or the Interaction-Network rusher-vs-defender pattern (nfl-big-data-bowl-2020) rather than hand-building spatial features.
candidates.mechanism: Both repos verified as real, working per-play spatial GNNs: FootballPassPrediction uses GATv2Conv/GCNConv over a fully-connected player graph with edge_attr = exp(-(distance/25)^2) gating attention; nfl-big-data-bowl-2020 uses a DeepMind graph_nets EdgeBlock->NodeBlock Interaction Network over rusher-vs-defender relative position/velocity, trained on the actual competition CRPS loss and reaching top-3% CV on the real 2020 Kaggle leaderboard.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: No code to write tonight -- record as a forward-looking design note attached to whatever module would eventually consume NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data (none exists yet in the schema). When that ingestion exists, the concrete edge-construction code in gnn/gnn_datagen.py (sanjeevnara7/FootballPassPrediction, MIT) is directly adaptable: swap soccer pitch dimensions (105x68) for NFL field dimensions and re-key node features to [x, y, speed_x, speed_y, direction, is_ballcarrier].
candidates.expected_value: Prevents reinventing a worse spatial-graph design later; low cost now (just a documented pointer), meaningful savings whenever tracking data lands.
candidates.exit_test: No action needed until Next Gen Stats ingestion is scheduled; re-open this candidate at that time and re-clone both repos to confirm they still build against current PyG/graph_nets versions.

do_not_do: Do not cite or reuse stevenbliu/Project-NBA-Rankings-Prediction's '~88% accuracy' claim -- its GCN_Trainer.py trains and evaluates on identical, unsplit, full-season-aggregated features/labels (verified in src/models/GCN_Trainer.py); it is leakage, not a validated result.

Do not vendor code from juancamilocampos/nfl-big-data-bowl-2020 verbatim into Gridiron -- the repo has no LICENSE file (default all-rights-reserved); treat it as a design reference only, or ask the author before reuse.

Do not attempt to attach FootballPassPrediction or nfl-big-data-bowl-2020's spatial-tracking GNN patterns to any current Gridiron table -- Gridiron has no player x/y tracking data ingested today (verified: no such table in server/db/schema/*.js), so there is nothing for a per-frame spatial graph to consume yet.

Do not run nbaGNNs' training loop as-is (retrains a fresh model every single day of the test window, batch_size=1, TF1-era Keras + spektral + old node2vec fork) -- port the architecture, not the code, and budget for a full walk-forward retrain schedule rather than assuming it's cheap.

Do not let a GNN team-strength or roster-graph candidate go anywhere near live betting stakes or fantasy lineup submission before an out-of-sample walk-forward backtest -- per Nick's fantasy-over-betting priority and the standing betting governance-gate rule, these are modeling research artifacts until proven, not production signals.

result.label: GN09 — Injury-impact / depth-chart-propagation network models
result.summary: Searched ~25 GitHub query variants plus open-web/academic queries for real injury-impact or depth-chart-propagation network models in sports analytics. None exist: public repos fall into four buckets — injury epidemiology toolkits (burden/incidence, single-player, no roster propagation), individual injury-risk ML classifiers, naive fantasy injury-shock simulators with no redistribution logic, and stale/unlicensed WAR/replacement-value single-player metrics. Nothing joins "Player A is out" to "Players B/C/D's usage moves by X" via depth-chart edges. Cloned and read lzumeta/injurytools (MIT, 7 stars, active — real injury-epidemiology R package, no network/depth-chart concept; risk-matrix chart borrow-idea only) and chanzer0/NFL-DFS-Tools (no license, 49 stars — zero injury-awareness in the code, confirmed by grep, avoid). Checked ryurko/nflWAR (no license, 38 stars, stale since 2018, built on retired nflscrapR — replacement-level methodology is a real, relevant idea but no network structure, borrow-idea only), joewlos's Monte Carlo draft simulator (avoid — random injury shocks, no redistribution), cbratkovics/fantasy-football-ai and jjti/ff (reference-only, unrelated scope). Grepped Gridiron's own (read-only) fantasy-football-dashboard repo and confirmed it already has every ingredient a propagation model needs — nfl_depth (depth chart), nfl_snaps (snap share), who-plays.js (availability/expected-snaps-lost), role-changepoint.js (retrospective role-change detector as ground truth) — but nfl-player-value.js only computes a single-player replacement-value gap against a hand-tuned constant table, with no propagation to specific teammates. Proposed an original bounded design: a depth-chart graph with edges weighted by empirically observed historical usage redistribution (targets/carries/snaps) when a same-slot teammate was out, fit and backtested against role-changepoint.js's existing labeled events, shipped shadow-only per the codebase's existing convention, using only tables Gridiron already populates.

sources.title: nflWAR: A Reproducible Method for Offensive Player Evaluation in Football
sources.authors: Ron Yurko, Samuel Ventura, Maksim Horowitz
sources.key_result: Defines NFL player value as WAR via a roster-based replacement-level definition and a multilevel model on nflscrapR play-by-play; the replacement-level methodology (not the code, which is stale/unlicensed) is the reusable idea.
sources.sample: NFL play-by-play, nflscrapR era (through ~2017 seasons)

candidates.candidate: Build a depth-chart usage-propagation graph: nodes are (player, position, team) from nfl_depth, edges connect same-position-group teammates, edge weights are empirically fit shares of vacated targets/carries/snaps that historically moved to each teammate the last N times that depth slot was out, computed from player_week_usage + nfl_snaps + nfl_depth.
candidates.mechanism: Directed weighted graph over the existing depth-chart table; weights = conditional usage-share transfer probabilities estimated from historical vacancy events, validated against a naive equal-split / depth-order-only baseline.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New service reading nfl_depth, nfl_snaps, player_week_usage; triggered by who-plays.js's expected_snaps_lost as the vacancy signal; backtested against role-changepoint.js's existing labeled role-change events; output stored as a shadow feature alongside nfl-player-value.js, not replacing it.
candidates.expected_value: Turns 'this player's absence costs X fantasy points' (already computed) into 'and specifically these teammates gain Y/Z of it' — the actual lineup-decision question Nick asked who-plays.js to answer but that file explicitly stops short of.
candidates.exit_test: Backtest on held-out weeks: does the graph's predicted redistribution beat equal-split and depth-order-only baselines on actual next-game target/carry/snap share for the teammates involved, measured by MAE on share points?

candidates.candidate: Replace nfl-player-value.js's hand-tuned POSITION_VALUE constant table with an empirically fit, position-group-specific replacement-level baseline derived from Gridiron's own historical backup-player production, borrowing nflWAR's roster-based replacement-level definition as methodology only (no code port — repo is unlicensed and stale).
candidates.mechanism: Fit replacement-level production per position group from the distribution of actual backup output in player_week_usage/nfl_snaps history, instead of the current fixed point-scale priors (QB 4.8, WR 1.0, etc.) that the file's own comment admits are 'a monotone prior, not production coefficients.'
candidates.how_in_gridiron: server/services/nfl-player-value.js — recalibrate POSITION_VALUE from an empirical query over player_week_usage joined to nfl_depth depth-order, refreshed periodically rather than hardcoded.
candidates.expected_value: Removes a hand-tuned constant from a production-adjacent value calculation with real historical data Gridiron already has; low-cost, low-risk correctness upgrade.
candidates.exit_test: Compare backtest accuracy of value-gap estimates (predicted vs. actual production drop-off) using the empirical baseline vs. the current hand-tuned constants over held-out weeks.

candidates.candidate: Extend the propagation graph beyond skill positions to offensive-line/front-seven units: model interior-OL group health as a unit node whose degradation propagates to QB pressure-adjusted value and RB efficiency, using existing nfl_snaps position-group aggregates rather than individual OL fantasy value (which is near-zero and not worth modeling player-by-player).
candidates.mechanism: Unit-level (not player-level) node for the interior OL / front-seven, with edges into QB and RB value nodes weighted by historical sack-rate/pressure-rate shifts when snap-weighted starter continuity on that unit drops, computed from nfl_snaps.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Second graph layer on top of GN09-1, reading nfl_snaps position-group rollups; feeds into the QB/RB nodes of the same propagation graph rather than being a standalone feature.
candidates.expected_value: Captures a real fantasy-relevant effect (bad O-line week hurts QB/RB value) that the current single-player nfl-player-value.js structurally cannot represent, since it only tracks the departing player's own line.
candidates.exit_test: Does adding the OL-unit propagation term reduce out-of-sample error on QB/RB weekly fantasy-point projections versus the model without it, on weeks with a confirmed OL starter change from nfl_depth?

candidates.candidate: Borrow the risk-matrix (severity x frequency) visualization idea from lzumeta/injurytools as a diagnostic/monitoring chart for the propagation graph's calibration coverage by position group — not a modeling change, a QA view.
candidates.mechanism: 2D chart of injury frequency vs. fantasy-value severity per position group, sourced from nfl_injuries + nfl-player-value.js outputs, to visually flag which position groups have too few historical vacancy events for GN09-1's edge weights to be trustworthy.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: A small dashboard panel reading nfl_injuries and the GN09-1 graph's per-edge sample counts; purely a visibility/QA tool, gates nothing in production.
candidates.expected_value: Cheap guardrail against silently trusting propagation edges fit on 2-3 historical events for thin-sample position groups (e.g., long snapper, kicker).
candidates.exit_test: Does the chart correctly flag the position groups GN09-1's backtest already shows have unstable/high-variance edge weights due to small sample size?

repos.what_it_does: R toolkit for sports injury epidemiology: incidence/prevalence/burden statistics, survival-style time-loss analysis, and a 2D risk-matrix (severity x frequency) chart. Verified by reading R/gg_riskmatrix.R and R/utils.R (grep for network/graph/propagation/depth-chart/substitution hits only unrelated prose in those two files) — no roster, depth-chart, or teammate-substitution concept anywhere in the package; treats each player's injury history in isolation.
repos.adoption_path: Reuse only the risk-matrix chart concept (GN09-4) for a QA/coverage diagnostic; the package solves surveillance, not propagation, and is R against Gridiron's JS stack.

repos.what_it_does: R package computing WAR for NFL offensive players via a multilevel model on nflscrapR play-by-play, using a roster-based definition of replacement level. Checked via GitHub API metadata and the companion arXiv paper (1802.00998); not cloned since no license permits porting code and the underlying nflscrapR data source has been retired for years. Single-player point-value metric — no network/propagation structure.
repos.adoption_path: Take only the replacement-level methodology (empirically defined from the observed backup pool) to recalibrate nfl-player-value.js's hand-tuned POSITION_VALUE constants (GN09-2); do not port any code (unlicensed, stale, wrong data source).

repos.what_it_does: FastAPI/TypeScript Monte Carlo fantasy draft simulator. Randomly assigns injuries/setbacks to simulated players from historical base rates during simulated seasons — an injury simply zeroes the player's future simulated value; no depth-chart lookup, no redistribution to specific teammates. Confirmed via repo description and file structure; no network/propagation logic exists to evaluate further.
repos.adoption_path: Not applicable — no propagation logic to reuse.

repos.what_it_does: Python DFS lineup optimizer / GPP tournament simulator for DraftKings/FanDuel. Cloned and grepped all .py files for injury/depth-chart/out-probability/questionable terms — zero matches. No injury-awareness exists in the code at all; player exclusion from a lineup pool is a manual, user-driven step, not a modeled effect.
repos.adoption_path: Not applicable — confirmed no injury or depth-chart logic exists in the codebase to port or reference.

repos.what_it_does: Weekly NFL fantasy point prediction pipeline from nflverse data: as-of feature engineering, temporally validated RF models vs. a causal baseline, rolling-origin backtest evaluation, FastAPI + Next.js deployment. Checked via repo metadata/description only (not cloned) — scope is general forecasting, not injury propagation.
repos.adoption_path: Its rolling-origin backtest harness pattern is a possible reference for Gridiron's own forward-calibration practices, unrelated to injury-network modeling specifically.

repos.what_it_does: TypeScript fantasy draft assistant pulling ESPN/CBS/NFL projections and ranking players by Value Over Replacement (VORP), defined simply as projection minus the (n+1)th-ranked player at that position. Checked via repo metadata/description; no depth-chart join, no network, simpler replacement-level definition than Gridiron's existing nfl-player-value.js already implements.
repos.adoption_path: Nothing to port — Gridiron's existing replacement-value logic is already more sophisticated than this repo's.

do_not_do: Do not port ryurko/nflWAR code directly — it has no license (all rights reserved), is stale since 2018, and depends on the retired nflscrapR data source; only the replacement-level methodology idea is usable.

Do not treat lzumeta/injurytools as a propagation or depth-chart model — it is an injury-epidemiology/surveillance toolkit with no roster or substitution concept; only its risk-matrix chart type is reusable as a QA diagnostic.

Do not build the propagation graph as a production-facing feature immediately — ship it shadow-only per the codebase's existing convention (who-plays.js, news-fantasy-impact.js) until it clears a real forward backtest against historical usage-share redistribution.

Do not edit, run tests against, or otherwise touch the live fantasy-football-dashboard repo tonight — it is read-only while a live server captures Week 1 games through Sunday; this design is a handoff spec, not code to merge now.

Do not expand this into a full injury-risk-prediction model (predicting whether a player gets hurt) — that is a different, already-well-covered problem (bucket 2 of the search) and out of scope for what was asked (impact/propagation given an injury, not injury prediction itself).

result.label: GN08: genetic programming / symbolic regression
result.summary: Cloned and read gplearn, PySR, and srbench source directly (not their READMEs), then sized the real overfitting risk against Gridiron's actual sample counts (team-weeks in the low hundreds per season, prop feature tables in the low thousands, 251,591 PBP rows that are not independent observations at the level you'd model). Both gplearn and PySR are legitimate, actively-maintained implementations, verified by reading genetic.py/_program.py and sr.py respectively. The danger is not the algorithm: a default run evaluates 10,000-100,000+ candidate expressions against a table of a few hundred to a few thousand rows and then hands you the single best training-loss equation with no external holdout — structurally the same "no trial registry / no multiplicity correction" failure already flagged tonight for the 21-model historical search, just automated and repeated thousands of times per fit. gplearn ships a genuine built-in guard (bootstrap out-of-bag fitness tracking via max_samples<1, verified at genetic.py:139-151 and 449-546) that PySR entirely lacks (grepped pysr/*.py for cross_val|train_test_split|holdout|validation — zero generalization-checking hits; model_selection="best"/"score" are both training-loss-derived, sr.py:3405-3454). Candidates below specify a bounded pilot that uses gplearn's OOB signal as a first-pass alarm, wraps both libraries in an external nested walk-forward split modeled on SRBench's own protocol (30 reruns/dataset, held-out test R2), and restricts the pilot to feature-discovery/augmentation roles rather than replacing any model outright, so no symbolic candidate reaches production without clearing an honest out-of-sample bar.

sources.title: SRBench: A Living Benchmark for Symbolic Regression
sources.venue: GitHub repo; original benchmark paper NeurIPS 2021 Datasets & Benchmarks track
sources.key_result: Standard SR benchmark protocol: 25 tuned methods x 30 independent runs x 24 PMLB black-box datasets plus a first-principles (Feynman) set, scored on held-out test R2 (black-box) and exact ground-truth-equation recovery under noise (first-principles). The repo's own documented pattern is the thing worth porting: GP/SR methods can match black-box ML test R2 with much smaller models, but ground-truth recovery degrades sharply as noise rises and dataset size shrinks — exactly Gridiron's regime (small n, real noise, no known ground-truth equation).

sources.title: gplearn (genetic.py, _program.py, fitness.py source read directly)
sources.key_result: Real tournament-selection GP engine with sklearn-style API. Confirmed two genuine overfitting guards in the code: parsimony_coefficient (auto mode derives it each generation from cov(length,fitness)/var(length), genetic.py:507-509) and max_samples<1.0, which fits each program on a bootstrap subsample and computes oob_fitness_ on the complement (genetic.py:139-151), tracked per-generation in run_details_['best_oob_fitness']. No internal train/test split for final model selection exists, and a default run already evaluates population_size x generations = 20,000 candidate programs against one fitness function.

sources.title: PySR (sr.py source read directly, focused on idx_model_selection and calculate_scores)
sources.key_result: High-throughput multi-population evolutionary search producing a Pareto front of (complexity, loss); default model_selection="best" picks, among equations within 1.5x of minimum training loss, the one maximizing a training-loss-derived AIC-style 'score' (negated d(log-loss)/d(complexity), sr.py:3426-3454). Verified by grep that pysr/*.py contains zero train/test-split, cross-validation, or holdout logic anywhere — every generalization guarantee must be supplied externally by the caller.

candidates.candidate: Gridiron-SR-bench: a private nested walk-forward harness (season N train / N+1 test, N reruns per candidate) modeled on cavalab/srbench's protocol, required before any GP/SR output can be promoted out of the research lab.
candidates.mechanism: Wrap gplearn/PySR fits in an outer loop: fit on seasons 1..k, score strictly on season k+1 (never re-fit on test), repeat across all available season boundaries, and require >=10 independent reruns per candidate target to report a test-R2 (or test-Brier for props) distribution with a bootstrap CI rather than a single number. This directly ports SRBench's own methodology (30 reruns/dataset, held-out test scoring) rather than trusting either library's internal 'best' selection, which both are verified to compute from training loss.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: New module in the Python research lab, e.g. research/sr_bench.py; consumes the same season-partitioned tables server/services/nfl-team-strength.js and server/services/nfl-props-player-features.js already build, but only ever reads them (no writes to data.sqlite). Gate: nothing produced by GN08-C2/C3/C4 may be cited as a finding without a Gridiron-SR-bench report attached.
candidates.expected_value: Turns 'symbolic regression found this equation' into a claim with an actual out-of-sample number attached — the single biggest gap in every current model per tonight's findings (five disagreeing CLV implementations, hand-tuned team-strength blend, no trial registry) is exactly the absence of this kind of external check.
candidates.exit_test: If, across 3 independent target tables, GP/SR test-R2 (or test-Brier) is not reproducibly higher than a simple linear/logistic baseline fit on the same walk-forward splits, kill the harness investment and do not build GN08-C2/C3.

candidates.candidate: gplearn SymbolicTransformer as a feature-discovery front-end for the player-prop calibration heads (nfl-props-player-features.js), gated by Gridiron-SR-bench (GN08-C1) and by gplearn's own OOB-fitness alarm.
candidates.mechanism: Run SymbolicTransformer(max_samples=0.7, parsimony_coefficient='auto') on the existing engineered features per season; discover a small number (<=5) of nonlinear interaction terms whose generation-over-generation best_fitness vs best_oob_fitness gap stays small (verified code path: genetic.py:139-151, 449-546). Feed only the surviving terms as additional input columns into the existing calibrated prop model — never replace the model itself. Any transformer feature whose OOB gap is large, or that fails GN08-C1's walk-forward test, is discarded before it reaches the feature table.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Feature-injection point: server/services/nfl-props-player-features.js's per-season Map<gsis_id, features> build (verified at line 114, SELECT DISTINCT player_id FROM nfl_player_week_features). Props is flagged tonight as the project's one area of genuine measured skill (2+ TD Brier skill +27%) but under-measured against real prices — this is a low-risk place to try SR because the pilot only augments features, it cannot make an already-decent calibrated model worse on its own.
candidates.expected_value: If even one or two discovered interaction terms survive walk-forward validation, a modest Brier-skill lift on the strongest existing surface at near-zero downside since baseline model behavior is unchanged when no term survives.
candidates.exit_test: No SymbolicTransformer-derived feature that clears GN08-C1's walk-forward bar within 2 pilot seasons of feature tables -> drop this candidate; prop feature engineering stays manual.

candidates.candidate: PySR closed-form search for the team-strength preseason-to-in-season blend, run only inside Gridiron-SR-bench, never against raw training loss.
candidates.mechanism: Use PySR to search a small operator set (+, -, *, /, a few unary) over (prior_season_strength, in_season_stats, weeks_elapsed) to propose a closed-form blend function, scored exclusively by GN08-C1's held-out walk-forward test score — never by PySR's own model_selection='best', which is verified (sr.py:3405-3454) to be a training-loss/complexity heuristic with no generalization check. Cap maxsize<=12 and niterations modestly given the ~500-600 rows/season effective sample size.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Attachment point: server/services/nfl-team-strength.js's hand-tuned prior/in-season blend (priorPointsByTeam and the league-prior shrinkage logic around lines 88-260). Tonight's findings call this blend 'not a principled state-space/Bayesian update' — a searched closed-form candidate is a new capability to compare against it, not an automatic replacement.
candidates.expected_value: A closed-form equation that beats the current hand-tuned blend on held-out season test scores would be directly interpretable and auditable, unlike a black-box alternative; expected hit rate is modest given team-week n is only in the hundreds per season, which is exactly why GN08-C1 gating is mandatory here.
candidates.exit_test: If the best PySR candidate does not beat the current blend's held-out score across at least 2 season-boundary folds, do not touch nfl-team-strength.js; the hand-tuned blend stays as-is.

candidates.candidate: Cold-start feature synthesis for the fantasy weekly-learning loop using gplearn on prior-season-only features, evaluated by leave-one-season-out CV.
candidates.mechanism: The fantasy player_week_engine has never captured a forward snapshot (heads is null week 1, per tonight's findings) — a real cold-start strategy is needed rather than a silent no-op. Use gplearn's SymbolicRegressor restricted to only prior-season/preseason-available features (no current-season data, since none exists at cold start) to synthesize a week-1 prior function, validated by leave-one-season-out CV across however many prior seasons of player-week data exist, with max_samples<1 OOB tracking as the in-loop overfitting alarm.
candidates.how_in_gridiron: Targets the cold-start gap named in tonight's findings for the fantasy weekly-learning loop (player_week_engine.heads null at week 1). This is fantasy-side, which is Nick's standing top priority over betting.
